entries.assertion: Establish from Agencia Tributaria's own pages how a property gain is computed, and which rate regime applies to a seller taxed as a resident versus one taxed under IRNR — including whether the rate turns on the seller's passport, their EU/EEA status, or where they are tax resident.
entries.source_required: Agencia Tributaria's own IRNR guidance plus consolidated TRLIRNR art. 25 and LIRPF arts. 9 and 66
entries.source_opened: Agencia Tributaria, 'Ganancia patrimonial derivada de la transmisión' — https://sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es/Sede/no-residentes/irnr-sin-establecimiento-permanente/cuestiones-especificas-sobre-tributacion-inmuebles/ganancia-patrimonial-derivada-transmision.html ; BOE, consolidated TRLIRNR — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2004-4527 ; BOE, consolidated Ley 35/2006 LIRPF — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2006-20764
entries.locator: AEAT: gain = transfer value less acquisition value (purchase price plus improvements, acquisition costs and taxes, less tax depreciation); «El tipo de gravamen aplicable es el 19%», not varying by EU/EEA status. TRLIRNR art. 25.1.f).3º (19% on gains from transfers of assets) as against art. 25.1.a) (24% general, 19% for EU/EEA residents with effective exchange of information). LIRPF art. 9.1 (residence: 183 days, or main centre of economic interests in Spain) and art. 66 (savings scale)
entries.as_of: TRLIRNR consolidated to 25/05/2023; LIRPF consolidated to 02/09/2026; AEAT page read 2026-09-02
entries.final_wording: Establish from Agencia Tributaria's own pages how a property gain is computed, and which rate regime applies to a seller taxed as a resident versus one taxed under IRNR — including whether the rate turns on the seller's passport, their EU/EEA status, or where they are tax resident.
entries.note: Answered at source, and the answer is clean: the rate turns on tax residence alone. Nationality is not a criterion anywhere in LIRPF art. 9, and on a PROPERTY GAIN the EU/EEA line does not move the rate either — the 24/19 split in art. 25.1.a) governs imputed and rental income, not gains. A resident is instead taxed on the savings scale (art. 66).

entries.assertion: Note: the two research passes behind this brief DISAGREE on whether a non-EEA non-resident's property gain is taxed at the same rate as an EEA one.
entries.source_required: Consolidated TRLIRNR art. 25 in force, confirmed against AEAT's own page
entries.source_opened: BOE, consolidated RDLeg 5/2004 (TRLIRNR) — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2004-4527 ; Agencia Tributaria, 'Ganancia patrimonial derivada de la transmisión' — https://sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es/Sede/no-residentes/irnr-sin-establecimiento-permanente/cuestiones-especificas-sobre-tributacion-inmuebles/ganancia-patrimonial-derivada-transmision.html
entries.locator: TRLIRNR art. 25.1.f): «El 19 por ciento cuando se trate de: … 3.º Ganancias patrimoniales que se pongan de manifiesto con ocasión de transmisiones de elementos patrimoniales» — no EU/EEA qualifier. Contrast art. 25.1.a): 24% general, 19% for residents of an EU or EEA state with effective exchange of information. AEAT: «El tipo de gravamen aplicable es el 19%»
entries.as_of: TRLIRNR consolidated to 25/05/2023 (art. 25.1.f) last amended by art. 73.2 Ley 26/2009, effective 01/01/2010); read 2026-09-02
entries.final_wording: Settled at source: a non-resident's gain on the sale of Spanish property is taxed at a flat 19% under art. 25.1.f.3º TRLIRNR, whatever the seller's nationality and whether or not they are resident in the EU/EEA. The 24%/19% split in art. 25.1.a is a different rule and applies to imputed and rental income, not to the gain.
entries.note: Leaving a flagged disagreement inside a research instruction keeps the ambiguity alive downstream, so it is replaced with the resolved answer. This is the exact conflation the brief was right to be suspicious of. The EU/EEA line does bite elsewhere in the same sale — the reinvestment exemption (DA 7ª) and the deduction of expenses — but never on the headline rate.

entries.assertion: Establish who is legally liable for plusvalía municipal on a sale, whether that liability sits differently where the seller is a non-resident individual, and whether the amount is set municipality by municipality — so whether any province-wide figure can exist.
entries.source_required: Consolidated TRLRHL, arts. 59, 106 and 108
entries.source_opened: BOE, consolidated RDLeg 2/2004, Texto refundido de la Ley Reguladora de las Haciendas Locales — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2004-4214
entries.locator: Art. 106.1.b): on an onerous transfer the taxpayer is the person «que transmita el terreno» (the seller). Art. 106.2: the acquirer «tendrá la consideración de sujeto pasivo sustituto del contribuyente… cuando el contribuyente sea una persona física no residente en España». Art. 59.2: municipalities «podrán establecer y exigir» the IIVTNU. Art. 108.1: rate «fijado por cada ayuntamiento», capped at 30%; art. 108.4: ordenanzas may bonify up to 95%
entries.as_of: Consolidated text as last updated 03/06/2026 (art. 106 unchanged since Ley 18/2014, in force 17/10/2014); read 2026-09-02
entries.final_wording: Establish who is legally liable for plusvalía municipal on a sale, whether that liability sits differently where the seller is a non-resident individual, and whether the amount is set municipality by municipality — so whether any province-wide figure can exist.
entries.note: All three limbs check out, and the third answers itself: because the tax is optional for a municipality (art. 59.2) and its rate and bonificaciones are set locally (art. 108), no province-wide plusvalía figure can exist. The non-resident twist in art. 106.2 is real and is routinely mis-stated — the seller remains the taxpayer; the buyer becomes the substitute who must pay, which is why buyers of non-residents retain for it.

entries.assertion: Establish the mechanism by which a percentage of the price is retained from a non-resident seller: who pays it to whom, on what form, and by what route the seller recovers any excess.
entries.source_required: Consolidated TRLIRNR art. 25.2 plus Agencia Tributaria's own modelo 211/210 pages
entries.source_opened: BOE, consolidated RDLeg 5/2004 (TRLIRNR) — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2004-4527 ; Agencia Tributaria, 'Retención del adquirente de un inmueble' — https://sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es/Sede/no-residentes/irnr-sin-establecimiento-permanente/retenciones-irnr-sin-establecimiento-permanente/retencion-adquirente-inmueble.html and 'Ganancia patrimonial derivada de la transmisión' — https://sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es/Sede/no-residentes/irnr-sin-establecimiento-permanente/cuestiones-especificas-sobre-tributacion-inmuebles/ganancia-patrimonial-derivada-transmision.html
entries.locator: TRLIRNR art. 25.2: «el adquirente estará obligado a retener e ingresar el 3 por ciento… de la contraprestación acordada, en concepto de pago a cuenta del impuesto». AEAT: the buyer — resident or not — files modelo 211 and pays within one month of the transfer; the seller files modelo 210 declaring the gain and «se podrá obtener la devolución del exceso» where the 3% exceeds the tax due. Art. 25.2 also makes the property itself liable (afecto) if the retention is not paid in
entries.as_of: TRLIRNR consolidated to 25/05/2023; AEAT pages read 2026-09-02
entries.final_wording: Establish the mechanism by which a percentage of the price is retained from a non-resident seller: who pays it to whom, on what form, and by what route the seller recovers any excess.
entries.note: Every element is confirmed at source: 3%, buyer to Treasury, modelo 211 within one month, seller recovers via modelo 210. Two things to get right in copy: the buyer is the one who retains and files (not the notary, not the agency), and the buyer's own residence is irrelevant — the duty attaches because the SELLER is non-resident. The property is charged if the buyer fails to pay it in, which is why buyers insist.

entries.assertion: EEA (Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein) is a different question from EU membership, and Switzerland is its own regime again.
entries.source_required: Consolidated RD 240/2007 (scope and Swiss regime) and LO 4/2000 art. 1.3
entries.source_opened: BOE, consolidated Real Decreto 240/2007 — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2007-4184 ; BOE, consolidated Ley Orgánica 4/2000 — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2000-544
entries.locator: RD 240/2007 art. 1.1: covers nationals of EU member states «y de los restantes Estados parte en el Acuerdo sobre el Espacio Económico Europeo». Disposición adicional tercera.1: by virtue of the EC–Switzerland free movement agreement of 21 June 1999, «a los ciudadanos suizos y a los miembros de su familia les es de aplicación lo previsto en el presente real decreto». LO 4/2000 art. 1.3: those under the régimen comunitario are governed by their own rules
entries.as_of: RD 240/2007 consolidated to 09/11/2015; LO 4/2000 consolidated to 19/03/2025; read 2026-09-02
entries.final_wording: EEA (Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein) is a different question from EU membership, and Switzerland is its own regime again.
entries.note: Correct, but it is worth being explicit about which axis is being separated, because the answer flips between them. On IMMIGRATION, Switzerland rests on its own legal basis (DA 3ª RD 240/2007, the 1999 agreement) yet receives the same treatment as EU citizens. On TAX, Switzerland is genuinely outside: DA 7ª TRLIRNR extends the reinvestment exemption to EU and EEA residents only, and Switzerland is neither. So 'its own regime' means 'same outcome, different instrument' for entry and residence, and 'different outcome' for tax reliefs.

entries.assertion: Never publish an agency commission percentage as typical or standard: no rate is regulated in Spain and no verified Costa-Blanca-measured median exists.
entries.source_required: Primary text deregulating estate agency activity, plus a check for any official commission series
entries.source_opened: BOE, consolidated Real Decreto-ley 4/2000, de 23 de junio, de Medidas Urgentes de Liberalización en el Sector Inmobiliario y Transportes — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2000-11834
entries.locator: Art. 3, 'Condiciones para el ejercicio de la actividad de intermediación inmobiliaria': the activities listed in art. 1 of Decreto 3248/1969 «podrán ser ejercidas libremente sin necesidad de estar en posesión de título alguno ni de pertenencia a ningún Colegio oficial». No fee scale is set in that or any successor instrument

entries.final_wording: Never publish an agency commission percentage as typical or standard: no rate is regulated in Spain and no verified Costa-Blanca-measured median exists.
entries.note: Both halves hold. The activity has been free since 2000 with no reserved title and no tariff, so any published 'standard' rate would be a price signal, not a fact — and, given it would be an industry-wide figure, one worth keeping away from on competition grounds too. On the second half: neither the registry nor the notarial Alicante series records commission, so there is no instrument from which a Costa Blanca median could be drawn.

entries.locator: TRLIRNR DA 7ª ('Exención por reinversión en vivienda habitual'), ap. 1: contributors resident in an EU member state; ap. 4: extended to EEA states «con el que exista un efectivo intercambio de información tributaria»; ap. 3: the art. 25.2 retention and art. 28.1 filing still apply. Added by art. 1.13 Ley 26/2014, in force 01/01/2015. LIRPF art. 33.4.b) (over-65 exemption) sits in the residents' law; the AEAT IRNR page carries no over-65 exemption
entries.as_of: TRLIRNR consolidated to 25/05/2023; LIRPF consolidated to 02/09/2026; AEAT page read 2026-09-02
entries.final_wording: Establish separately, from the primary text, who each one reaches: the reinvestment exemption is extended to non-residents of the EU/EEA with effective exchange of information by DA 7ª TRLIRNR, while the over-65 relief has been read narrowly against non-residents.
entries.note: Substantively right, with one precision the wording blurs: the exchange-of-information condition in DA 7ª attaches only to the EEA extension (ap. 4), not to EU member states (ap. 1). On the over-65 point the primary-text position is stronger than 'read narrowly' suggests — there is simply no equivalent extension in TRLIRNR, and AEAT's own IRNR page does not mention one. Note too that DA 7ª still requires the 3% retention and the modelo 210 filing; the exemption is not self-executing at completion.

entries.assertion: Never state the current rate scale from memory: the top savings-base bracket changed with effect from 2025, and rates must be read from the amended article, not recalled.
entries.source_required: Consolidated LIRPF art. 66 with its amendment history

entries.locator: Art. 66 'Tipos de gravamen del ahorro'. Amendment note: «Se modifica, con efectos desde el 1 de enero de 2025, por la disposición final 7.1 de la Ley 7/2024, de 20 de diciembre». Art. 66.2 scale: 19% to 6.000 €, 21% to 50.000 €, 23% to 200.000 €, 27% to 300.000 €, 30% thereafter; the state half in art. 66.1 runs 9,5 / 10,5 / 11,5 / 13,5 / 15%

entries.final_wording: Never state the current rate scale from memory: the top savings-base bracket changed with effect from 2025, and rates must be read from the amended article, not recalled.
entries.note: Confirmed precisely: DF 7.1 of Ley 7/2024 raised the top savings bracket to 30% above 300.000 €, with effect from 1 January 2025. Two cautions when this scale is used in seller copy: it governs a SPANISH TAX RESIDENT's gain, not a non-resident's (that is the flat 19% of art. 25.1.f TRLIRNR), and art. 66.1 shows only the state half of a scale completed by the autonomous community's own tranche.

entries.assertion: In a Comunitat Valenciana residential sale, which documents and registry facts must be in place before a notary can authorise the deed — and which widely repeated 'requirements' in fact expose the seller only to a cost, a sanction, or a lower price, without blocking the signing?
entries.source_required: Consolidated LPH art. 9.1.e, RD 390/2021 art. 17, Ley Hipotecaria art. 20
entries.source_opened: BOE, consolidated Ley 49/1960 (LPH) — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-1960-10906 ; BOE, consolidated RD 390/2021 — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2021-9176 ; BOE, consolidated Ley Hipotecaria — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-1946-2453
entries.locator: LPH art. 9.1.e): «sin la cual no podrá autorizarse el otorgamiento del documento público, salvo que fuese expresamente exonerado… por el adquirente» — an express blocker. RD 390/2021 art. 17.2: registered certificate and label «se anexará al contrato de compraventa» — a duty, but no authorising bar. Ley Hipotecaria art. 20: tracto sucesivo — the transferor's right must already be registered or the Registrar «denegará la inscripción»
entries.as_of: LPH consolidated to 21/03/2026; RD 390/2021 to 23/07/2025; Ley Hipotecaria to 03/01/2025; read 2026-09-02
entries.final_wording: In a Comunitat Valenciana residential sale, which documents and registry facts must be in place before a notary can authorise the deed — and which widely repeated 'requirements' in fact expose the seller only to a cost, a sanction, or a lower price, without blocking the signing?
entries.note: A good question, and the distinction it draws is genuine and legally visible: LPH art. 9.1.e uses blocking language and RD 390/2021 art. 17 does not. Keep the two gates apart in the answer — the notary authorising the deed, and the Registrar inscribing it (Ley Hipotecaria art. 20 bites at the second gate, not the first). And note that the LPH blocker itself falls away if the buyer waives it.

entries.note: Correct for a sale, and the real 7-day rule is LPH art. 9.1.e (community-debt certificate, seven natural days). One nearby fact to hold so the guardrail is not over-applied: a seven-natural-day lender certificate DOES exist in art. 2 Ley 2/1994 — but only in CREDITOR subrogation, where a new lender takes over the loan. That is not a sale, and it is not the seller's mortgage-cancellation certificate. Nothing binds the bank to seven days on an ordinary sale.

entries.assertion: For heirs of a property in Alicante province, what has to be completed, and in what order, between a death and a buyer being able to register their purchase;
entries.source_required: Ley Hipotecaria art. 20 (tracto sucesivo) and the ISD filing deadline in the Reglamento
entries.source_opened: BOE, consolidated Ley Hipotecaria (Decreto de 8 de febrero de 1946) — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-1946-2453 ; BOE, consolidated RD 1629/1991, Reglamento del Impuesto sobre Sucesiones y Donaciones — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-1991-27678
entries.locator: Ley Hipotecaria art. 20: to register a transfer, the transferor's right must already be registered, and «En el caso de resultar inscrito aquel derecho a favor de persona distinta de la que otorgue la transmisión… los Registradores denegarán la inscripción solicitada». RISD art. 67.1.a): six months from the devengo (death) to file, with a prórroga regime in art. 68 (not available after the first five months, and carrying interés de demora)
entries.as_of: Ley Hipotecaria consolidated to 03/01/2025; RISD consolidated to 05/04/2023; read 2026-09-02
entries.final_wording: For heirs of a property in Alicante province, what has to be completed, and in what order, between a death and a buyer being able to register their purchase;
entries.note: Correctly posed, and the ordering it asks about is legally forced rather than customary: art. 20 Ley Hipotecaria means the heirs' title must be registered before the buyer's can be, which is what makes the acceptance-of-inheritance deed and the ISD filing gate the sale rather than run alongside it. The six-month ISD clock (RISD art. 67.1.a) runs from the death, not from the deed — that is the deadline that catches families.

entries.locator: Disposición transitoria segunda: «Con efectos desde el 1 de junio de 2026, el artículo 12 bis de la Ley 13/1997… tendrá la siguiente redacción», ap. 2: «bonificación del 25 por ciento» for Group III collaterals of the 2nd or 3rd degree by consanguinity. Disposición final cuarta: «Con efectos desde el 1 de junio de 2027», same ap. 2 at «bonificación del 50 por ciento». Art. 32 (the wording in force from the law's entry into force) carries no Group III bonificación at all. Groups I and II remain at 99% throughout
entries.as_of: Read at source 2026-09-02; the 25% step took effect 1 June 2026 and is superseded on 1 June 2027
entries.final_wording: The step that falls inside 2026 is now read at source: Ley 5/2025 (Generalitat Valenciana), Disposición transitoria segunda, gives Group III relatives (2nd/3rd-degree collaterals by consanguinity — siblings, uncles/aunts, nephews/nieces) a 25% bonificación for deaths from 1 June 2026, rising to 50% from 1 June 2027 under Disposición final cuarta. Groups I and II stay at 99%. Any Group III figure must be dated to the death, and the 25% expires on 31 May 2027.
entries.note: The caution was justified and is now discharged, but the resulting figure is itself time-limited, which is why this is TIME-SENSITIVE rather than VERIFIED. Two mechanics that decide which number applies: the trigger is the DEVENGO — the date of death — not the date of the deed or the filing, and the bonificación applies only to assets the taxpayer has declared. Before 1 June 2026 there was no Group III bonificación at all, so an estate opened in early 2026 is on a different rule from one opened in July 2026.

entries.assertion: Never assume heirs living abroad are in the same position as heirs living in Spain, or that an EEA-resident heir and a non-EEA-resident heir face identical treatment at either stage.
entries.source_required: Consolidated Ley 29/1987 DA 2ª (post-Ley 11/2021) and TRLIRNR for the later sale

entries.locator: LISD DA 2ª, Uno.1.b): where the deceased was resident in an autonomous community, «los contribuyentes no residentes tendrán derecho a la aplicación de la normativa propia aprobada por dicha Comunidad Autónoma» — no EU/EEA qualifier. Amendment note: «Se modifica el apartado Uno por el art. 4.6 de la Ley 11/2021, de 9 de julio», in force 11/07/2021. For the later sale: TRLIRNR art. 25.1.f).3º (19% for all non-residents) but DA 7ª (reinvestment exemption confined to EU and EEA residents)
entries.as_of: LISD consolidated to 28/12/2022 (DA 2ª last amended 10/07/2021, in force 11/07/2021); TRLIRNR consolidated to 25/05/2023; read 2026-09-02
entries.final_wording: Never assume heirs living abroad are in the same position as heirs living in Spain. But do not carry the EEA/non-EEA split into the inheritance tax itself: since Ley 11/2021 (in force 11 July 2021) amended DA 2ª of Ley 29/1987, non-resident heirs are entitled to the autonomous community's own rules regardless of whether they live in the EU, the EEA or a third country. The EEA line does still bite at the later SALE — the reinvestment exemption in DA 7ª TRLIRNR reaches EU and EEA residents only — so keep the two stages apart.
entries.note: Half right, half out of date, and the out-of-date half is the expensive one: a piece warning Group I/II heirs in the US or Canada that they may be shut out of the Valencian 99% bonificación would be wrong, and would frighten people into paying for advice they do not need. The original EU/EEA restriction in DA 2ª was struck by Ley 11/2021 following the Supreme Court line after C-127/12. The residence-abroad caution survives intact for other reasons (which community's rules apply, filing to the State administration, representation).

entries.assertion: Which instrument publishes the nationality of people registering home purchases in Alicante province, what exactly does it count (transactions or value;
entries.source_required: The registry series (Colegio de Registradores) and the notarial series, checked for the geography at which nationality is actually published
entries.source_opened: Colegio de Registradores de la Propiedad y Mercantiles de España, Estadística Registral Inmobiliaria, Cuarto Trimestre 2025 — https://www.registradores.org/documents/d/guest/eri_4t_2025 ; Consejo General del Notariado (Centro de Información / Centro Tecnológico del Notariado), 'Compraventa de Inmuebles de la provincia de Alicante', published by the Colegio Notarial de Valencia — https://valencia.notariado.org/portal/documents/81893/4712529/
entries.locator: ERI 4T 2025: nationality tables at NATIONAL level (p. 34: Reino Unido 7,93%, Países Bajos 6,77%, Alemania 6,65%…) and by COMUNIDAD AUTÓNOMA (p. 43); the PROVINCIAL table (p. 44) gives only the foreigners' SHARE — Alicante/Alacant 42,91%. ERI methodology, p. 118: «Los resultados no se adentran en el concepto de residencia… no se puede desagregar entre residentes y no residentes». Notarial Alicante report: 'Estadística anual por país extranjero' (p. 7) gives nationality counts for Alicante province 2018–2025 (2024: Reino Unido 3.594, Países Bajos 3.328, Bélgica 3.092, Polonia 2.933), plus per-municipality tables by nationality (pp. 7–8); 'Condiciones Particulares' (p. 11): counted on act 0501 compraventa de inmuebles, dwellings with an address in Alicante province, buyer typed Español/Extranjero (a mixed purchase is counted in both), deals over 15.000.000 € excluded
entries.as_of: ERI reference period Q4 2025; notarial series extraction date 13/11/2025, running to 2T 2025; read 2026-09-02
entries.final_wording: Which instrument publishes the nationality of home buyers in Alicante province — noting that the REGISTRY series (Colegio de Registradores' Estadística Registral Inmobiliaria) publishes nationality only nationally and by autonomous community, and gives the province just the foreigners' share, so province-level nationality comes from the NOTARIAL series (Consejo General del Notariado, published for Alicante by the Colegio Notarial de Valencia), which counts deeds rather than registrations. What exactly does it count (transactions or value;)
entries.note: The verb 'registering' quietly picks the wrong instrument. Registration and deed-signing are different events, different bodies and different lag, and the one that actually publishes nationality for Alicante province is the notarial one. Three further traps in the same sentence: the notarial series counts DWELLINGS (with mean declared amount reported separately, so transactions and value are distinct outputs); a purchase by a Spanish and a foreign buyer jointly is counted in BOTH groups, so shares do not sum to 100%; and both series record NATIONALITY, which the ERI states outright cannot be resolved into resident or non-resident.

entries.source_required: RD 240/2007 (scope and Switzerland), LO 4/2000 (short-stay regime and its carve-out), LIRPF art. 9 (tax residence)
entries.source_opened: BOE, consolidated Real Decreto 240/2007 — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2007-4184 ; BOE, consolidated Ley Orgánica 4/2000 — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2000-544 ; BOE, consolidated Ley 35/2006 (LIRPF) — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2006-20764
entries.locator: RD 240/2007 art. 1.1 (EU member states and «los restantes Estados parte en el Acuerdo sobre el Espacio Económico Europeo» — i.e. Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein) and DA 3ª.1 (Swiss citizens and their family members covered by the same decree, under the EC–Switzerland agreement of 21 June 1999). LO 4/2000 art. 1.3 (those under the régimen comunitario are governed by their own rules, this Law applying only where more favourable) and art. 30.1 («Estancia es la permanencia en territorio español por un período de tiempo no superior a 90 días»). LIRPF art. 9.1.a) (more than 183 days in the calendar year, counting sporadic absences unless tax residence elsewhere is evidenced) and 9.1.b) (main nucleus or base of activities or economic interests in Spain), with the rebuttable spouse-and-minor-children presumption
entries.final_wording: Establish from primary immigration and tax sources the boundaries a nationality alone cannot settle: which nationalities are EEA and therefore outside the 90/180 third-country clock, where Switzerland sits, and on what basis Spanish tax residence is determined.
entries.note: All three limbs verified against primary Spanish law. Norwegian, Icelandic and Liechtenstein nationals fall under RD 240/2007 by art. 1.1 and are outside the short-stay clock; Swiss nationals reach the same regime by DA 3ª.1. Tax residence turns on days or economic centre — never on nationality, and never on holding a residence card. One evidentiary gap to be honest about: I could not open the consolidated Schengen Borders Code on EUR-Lex (the pages returned empty), so the '90 in any 180' formulation is sourced here to Spanish law (LO 4/2000 art. 30.1, 90 days) rather than to Regulation (EU) 2016/399 art. 6.1 itself. If the piece states the rolling 180-day window, that specific wording still needs the EU regulation read at source. Add the point the registry series makes independently: nationality does not settle residence in either direction.

entries.final_wording: Which Alicante-province municipalities have price or transaction figures published by an official statistical instrument, what is the publication threshold and where is it stated, and what evidence about local demand exists for the towns that fall below it?
entries.note: Answerable, but the question's singular 'the publication threshold' will mislead whoever executes it: there is no single threshold. MIVAU's municipal TRANSACTION tables are not bound by it, INE stops at province regardless of size, and the Notariado portal goes below municipality entirely to postcode. Also note what the promise cannot deliver — INE ETDP publishes COUNTS only, no price, so 'how the two are actually selling' can be answered on volume from INE but needs a second, separately named source for price. Registered PRICE: not in INE ETDP at all — the registered-price index is a Colegio de Registradores product (ERI, quarterly/annual, repeat-sales methodology).
entries.final_wording: In Alicante province, how have new-build and second-hand transaction counts (INE ETDP / MIVAU) and the registrars' registered sale price index (Colegio de Registradores, ERI) moved relative to each other across the latest published periods — noting that the counts and the price come from different publishers on different calendars — and what does that split establish, and not establish, about the buyers a resale seller is competing for?
entries.note: Wrong as written in one specific way: it implies counts and 'registered sale prices' can be read off one series. They cannot. INE's ETDP is a count statistic with no price; the registered price index belongs to the Colegio de Registradores and is quarterly, so it will never share a reference period with a monthly count. Pairing a June 2026 monthly count against a first-quarter 2026 price and calling it a relative movement would be a fabrication. Separately, the 'and not establish' clause is the honest core of the question and should survive intact: a provincial new/second-hand split says nothing about whether the same buyer was choosing between the two, and new-build counts are recorded at deed/inscription, which for off-plan can be years after the buyer decided.

entries.note: Answerable, and the answer is asymmetric in a way that matters. The registrars' registered price does break out obra nueva vs segunda mano. The ministry's appraisal value does NOT split new vs used — it splits by ANTIGÜEDAD, the age of the dwelling, which is a proxy and not the same thing (a five-year-old flat resold is a second-hand sale of a nearly-new dwelling). Reporting MIVAU's antigüedad bands as a new/used split would be a quiet fabrication. Also keep the two apart on substance: a registered price is what someone paid; an appraisal value is what a tasadora certified under the ECO/805/2003 valuation rules, usually for mortgage purposes, on a self-selecting sample of mortgaged properties.

entries.final_wording: Establish what is published about new-build supply in the province and name precisely which measure it is — planning permits, starts, or completions — rather than describing it generically as 'supply'.
entries.note: The instruction is right and the province-level measures exist, but the three English words map imperfectly onto the Spanish series and the mapping should be written out. COMPLETIONS = certificaciones de fin de obra (tables 14–15 of the visados statistic), provincial. PERMITS = licencias municipales de obra, the Estadística de Construcción de Edificios — a separate product not carried in this boletín section, so it must be located and cited on its own before being quoted. STARTS have no direct Spanish series at all: visados de dirección de obra (obra nueva) are the conventional proxy, but a visado is a professional filing that precedes work and does not prove a shovel moved. Calling visados 'starts' without that caveat is the standard error in Spanish property journalism. None of these three is 'supply' in the sense a seller cares about, which is completed unsold units in their own town — a figure nobody publishes.

entries.note: €280,000 on a €250,000 purchase is a 12% cost load, and 12% is precisely the stale rule of thumb that the article's own guardrail at entry 220 forbids. entries.assertion: What does the buyer actually need liquid before completion on the Costa Blanca in 2026 — and why is the answer different for a resale and a new build?
entries.source_required: The Valencian ITP and AJD rates and the national IVA rate for housing
entries.source_opened: Generalitat Valenciana, Hisenda — Novedades tributarias 2026, https://hisenda.gva.es/es/web/tributos/novetats-tributaries-2026 ; BOE, Ley 37/1992 del IVA, consolidated, https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-1992-28740
entries.locator: GVA: TPO 9% on immovable property from 1 June 2026 (11% >€1M); AJD 1.4% from 1 June 2026. LIVA art. 91.Uno.1.7º: 10% reduced rate for 'edificios o partes de los mismos aptos para su utilización como viviendas'; consolidated text current to 28 February 2026.
entries.final_wording: What does the buyer actually need liquid before completion on the Costa Blanca in 2026 — and why is the answer different for a resale and a new build?
entries.note: The premise is sound and the two paths really are structurally different, not merely differently priced. A resale is a transfer between private parties: ITP/TPO at 9% (11% above €1,000,000), no AJD on the purchase deed itself. A new build bought from the developer is a first delivery: 10% IVA under art. 91.Uno.1.7º LIVA plus AJD at 1.4%, i.e. 11.4% on this path against 9% on the resale path. Two further asymmetries worth carrying: IVA is paid to the seller at completion while ITP is self-assessed and paid to the Generalitat afterwards, which changes what must be liquid ON the day; and the article should say 'Comunitat Valenciana', not 'Costa Blanca', since the rates are regional and the Costa Blanca is not an administrative unit.

entries.final_wording: The ITP rate in force in the Comunitat Valenciana on the date of writing, with its effective date and whether the rate is set by the deed date or the private-contract date (the general rate on immovable property moved 10% → 9% for taxable events accruing from 1 June 2026, under Ley 5/2025 de 30 de mayo; the 11% rate is RETAINED where the value exceeds €1,000,000, and reduced rates of 3%–8% exist for defined buyer profiles)
entries.note: The 10% → 9% move and the 1 June 2026 date are confirmed on the Generalitat's own page. Corrected because a bare '9%' is wrong for two large slices of the Costa Blanca market: anything valued above €1,000,000 is still taxed at 11%, and buyers who qualify on profile pay 3%, 4%, 6% or 8%. On the date question the instruction is asking the right thing and the answer is the DEED date — Ley 5/2025 applies to hechos imponibles devengados from 1 June 2026, and under art. 49 TRLITPAJD accrual runs from the transmission, which for a property sale is the escritura pública, not the private contract or the arras. One further trap: the 9% is applied to the taxable base, which under art. 10.2 TRLITPAJD is the cadastral valor de referencia where that exceeds the agreed price — so the rate cut does not guarantee a lower bill.

entries.note: Both legs confirmed at primary level: 10% IVA under art. 91.Uno.1.7º LIVA, and the Valencian general AJD rate of 1.4% from 1 June 2026 (down from 1.5%) under Ley 5/2025. Three qualifications to carry into the copy. The 10% applies to the FIRST delivery of the dwelling by the developer; a second or later delivery is exempt from IVA and falls into ITP/TPO instead, which is what makes a 'new build' that has already been deeded once a resale for tax purposes. Garages beyond two units and commercial annexes bought with the dwelling do not necessarily share the 10%. entries.note: Corrected on the framing, which is the part that would have misled. The gate is not nationality, not immigration status, and not tax residence — it is whether the dwelling becomes the buyer's vivienda habitual. A buyer who will not live in the property cannot reach any of these rates whatever their passport, and a foreign national who moves in can. That distinction is exactly the nationality/residence conflation this ledger exists to catch. Also corrected for completeness: the profile list omits disability and gender-violence victims, both of which carry 3%/4%, and the whole schedule is banded at €180,000, so 'the under-35 rate' is 6% or 8% depending on value, not a single number. Two things I did NOT verify and which must be checked in the article text of Ley 13/1997 before publication: the income limits (a combined general + savings taxable-base ceiling has historically applied to several of these rates, and law-firm pages give conflicting figures), and the minimum holding/occupation period. entries.assertion: The legal basis in the IRNR and the imputed base: 1.1% or 2% of cadastral value, and which coefficient applies to this property, which turns on its cadastral value and the applicable general collective revision rules — not on a rate each municipality chooses.
entries.source_required: AEAT's current non-resident manual (and DA 55ª LIRPF for the 2023–2025 special rule)
entries.source_opened: Agencia Tributaria, Manual de tributación de no residentes, 'Rentas imputadas de bienes inmuebles urbanos', https://sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es/Sede/ayuda/manuales-videos-folletos/manuales-practicos/manual-tributacion-no-residentes/capitulo-03-tributacion-rentas-comunes-nr/rentas-imputadas-bienes-inmuebles-urbanos.html
entries.locator: Manual updated 1 July 2026 (edition covering July 2026). 1.1% where the municipality's cadastral values were revised, modified or determined by a general collective valuation procedure taking effect within the tax period or the 10 preceding tax periods (the special 'since 1 January 2012' cut-off applied for 2023, 2024 and 2025); 2% otherwise. No cadastral value or none notified by 31 December: base is 1.1% of 50% of the greater of acquisition price or the administratively checked value. Rates: 'Residentes UE, Islandia, Noruega y, desde 11-07-2021, Liechtenstein: 19%'; 'Resto de contribuyentes: 24%'.
entries.as_of: 2026-07-01 (AEAT manual edition)
entries.final_wording: The legal basis in the IRNR (art. 24.5 TRLIRNR, by reference to art. 85 LIRPF) and the imputed base: 1.1% or 2% of cadastral value. Which coefficient applies turns on WHEN the municipality's cadastral values were last revised, modified or determined by a general collective valuation procedure — 1.1% if that took effect in the tax period or the 10 preceding tax periods, 2% otherwise — and not on the size of the property's own cadastral value, nor on a rate each municipality chooses. Where there is no cadastral value or it has not been notified by 31 December, the base is 1.1% applied to 50% of the greater of the acquisition price or the administratively checked value. For 2026 the ordinary 10-year rule governs: the 'revised since 1 January 2012' cut-off in DA 55ª LIRPF was written for 2023, 2024 and 2025 and must not be carried into 2026 without checking.
entries.note: Corrected on two points. First, the assertion says the coefficient 'turns on its cadastral value' — it does not. The amount of the cadastral value sets the BASE, not the percentage; the percentage turns solely on the timing of the municipality's general collective valuation. Getting this backwards would produce advice that varies the rate with the property's value, which is wrong for every reader. Second, the DA 55ª trap flagged in the brief is real and I checked it specifically rather than carrying it forward: DA 55ª fixed the cut-off at 1 January 2012 for 2023–2025 only, and the AEAT manual as updated 1 July 2026 states the ordinary rule (revision in force in the tax period or the 10 preceding ones) alongside that time-limited exception. This is legislatively unsettled — RDL 16/2025 and then RDL 2/2026 (3 February 2026) each sought to extend the arrangement and neither was ratified by Congress, with AEAT issuing a clarifying note in April 2026 on the effects for 2025 — so the 2026 position should be re-confirmed against AEAT before publication and should carry a date. Finally, keep the imputed-income rate split straight: 19% for EU/Iceland/Norway/Liechtenstein residents and 24% for others applies to IMPUTED and rental income. A non-resident's capital gain on selling the property is a flat 19% regardless — the 19/24 split does not reach it.

entries.final_wording: Art. 85 LIRPF sets the imputation at 2% of cadastral value, dropping to 1.1% only where a general collective cadastral revision took effect in the tax period itself or in the ten preceding tax periods. The friendlier 'revised since 1 January 2012' cut-off sits in DA 55ª LIRPF, and as at 1 September 2026 the consolidated text of DA 55ª in force covers the 2023 tax period ONLY. It was not extended to 2026 — and the 2024/2025 extensions were themselves annulled: Congress derogated RDL 16/2025 on 27 January 2026 (BOE-A-2026-2024) and RDL 2/2026 on 26 February 2026 (BOE-A-2026-4667). For 2026, apply art. 85's ten-preceding-tax-periods test, not the 2012 date.
entries.note: Two errors in the assertion. (1) 'written for 2023-2025' describes wording that no longer exists in the law — the 2023-2025 heading came from RDL 16/2025 and RDL 2/2026, both derogated; the surviving text says 2023 only. (2) The implied answer 'check if extended to 2026' has a definite answer today: no. Practical effect on the Costa Blanca is large — a municipality whose last general revision predates 2016 falls to 2% for 2026 on the statute as it stands. AEAT has separately argued (nota of April 2026) that the 31 December accrual rule keeps the extension alive for 2025; it has published nothing applying that reasoning to 2026. Flag to a tax adviser before publishing a rate.

entries.assertion: Never say a Spanish resident pays the same imputed tax as a non-resident.
entries.source_required: Consolidated art. 85 LIRPF (resident imputation, taxed in the IRPF general base) and art. 25.1.a) TRLIRNR (non-resident flat rate)
entries.source_opened: BOE, texto consolidado Ley 35/2006, bloque 'a85' — https://www.boe.es/datosabiertos/api/legislacion-consolidada/id/BOE-A-2006-20764/texto/bloque/a85 ; BOE, texto consolidado RDLeg 5/2004, bloque 'a25' — https://www.boe.es/datosabiertos/api/legislacion-consolidada/id/BOE-A-2004-4527/texto/bloque/a25
entries.locator: Art. 85.1 LIRPF (2%/1.1% of cadastral value, 'excluida la vivienda habitual') vs art. 25.1.a) TRLIRNR (flat 24%, or 19% for EU/EEA-with-mutual-assistance residents)
entries.final_wording: Never say a Spanish resident pays the same imputed tax as a non-resident.
entries.note: Correct, and worth spelling out why: the imputed AMOUNT is computed the same way under art. 85 LIRPF, but a Spanish tax resident adds it to the IRPF general base and pays at their progressive rate with personal allowances, while a non-resident pays a flat 19%/24% under IRNR on a separate Modelo 210 with no allowances. Same base, different tax.

entries.assertion: Never apply 24% to an EU or EEA owner, or 19% to a UK owner
entries.source_required: Consolidated art. 25.1.a) TRLIRNR plus AEAT Anexo V list of EEA states with mutual assistance
entries.source_opened: BOE, texto consolidado RDLeg 5/2004, bloque 'a25' — https://www.boe.es/datosabiertos/api/legislacion-consolidada/id/BOE-A-2004-4527/texto/bloque/a25 ; AEAT Manual de Tributación de No Residentes, Anexo V — https://sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es/Sede/ayuda/manuales-videos-folletos/manuales-practicos/manual-tributacion-no-residentes/anexos/paises-ue-eee.html
entries.locator: Art. 25.1.a) TRLIRNR, in force since 01/01/2015; AEAT Anexo V (manual edition July 2026): Iceland, Norway, Liechtenstein
entries.final_wording: Never apply 24% to an owner tax-resident in the EU or in Iceland, Norway or Liechtenstein, and never apply 19% to an owner tax-resident in the UK. And check that the owner is a non-resident at all — a British national who is tax-resident in Spain files IRPF, not Modelo 210.
entries.note: As written it says 'EU or EEA owner' and 'UK owner', which reads as nationality. It is tax residence that sets the rate. Two live traps on the Costa Blanca: a Dutch national tax-resident in the UK pays 24%; a British national tax-resident in Spain leaves the IRNR system entirely. Also 'EEA' only qualifies where mutual assistance applies — for the EEA that is Iceland, Norway and Liechtenstein, all three confirmed by AEAT.

freshness.source_locator: Art. 25.1.a) TRLIRNR, in force since 01/01/2015; AEAT Anexo V (manual edition July 2026): Iceland, Norway, Liechtenstein

entries.assertion: Your Spanish neighbour gets an 80% mortgage.
entries.source_required: Banco de España guidance on the financing percentage relative to appraisal value, or a named lender's published maximum
entries.source_opened: Banco de España, Portal Cliente Bancario, blog post 'La tasación no solo es un mero trámite', published 12/03/2024 — https://clientebancario.bde.es/pcb/es/blog/la-tasacion-no-solo-es-un-mero-tramite.html
entries.locator: BdE Cliente Bancario, verbatim: the loan amount is tied to the appraisal value, 'normalmente, hasta un máximo del 80%' of it; the amount also depends on the entity's commercial policy, the applicant's financial capacity, the property type and additional guarantees
entries.final_wording: A Spanish resident buying their main home can normally borrow up to 80% of the valuation — Banco de España says lenders do not usually go above that. It is a ceiling, not an entitlement: the bank lends on the lower of price and valuation, and only if your income supports it.
entries.note: Three things wrong with 'gets an 80% mortgage': it is a maximum not a grant, it is anchored to the appraisal (banks apply it to the lower of price and appraisal), and it is the habitual-residence figure — your neighbour's holiday flat would not get it either. There is no statutory LTV cap in Spain; 80% is supervisory and commercial practice.

entries.assertion: As a non-resident you get 60%.
entries.source_required: A named Spanish lender publishing its maximum LTV for non-residents, or Banco de España
entries.source_opened: CaixaBank HolaBank, 'Housing Mortgage Guide' (NRI 7119-2024/09542) — https://www.caixabank.es/particular/holabank/housing-mortgage-guide.html ; Banco Santander, non-resident mortgage page — https://www.bancosantander.es/particulares/hipotecas/no-residentes
entries.locator: CaixaBank HolaBank guide, verbatim: 'HolaBank offers up to 70% financing for the property excluding additional fees such as taxes (VAT, Capital Gains Tax [ITP]), and other associated expenses.' Santander's non-resident mortgage page publishes no LTV figure at all.
entries.final_wording: Non-residents are financed at a lower percentage than residents, but there is no single number. The one Costa Blanca-facing lender that publishes a figure is CaixaBank's HolaBank, at up to 70% of the property value; Santander publishes none. Assume you must fund 30%+ of the price plus roughly 12-15% in taxes and costs, and get the figure from your own lender.
entries.note: 60% is not sourced anywhere I could open. It circulates on broker and estate-agency blogs, which are leads, not proof. No law caps non-resident LTV; it is each lender's credit policy, which is why a single headline number cannot be right.

Do not build EU / non-EU / UK / US / Swiss LTV bands — no lender I could open publishes them. Where residence outside the EU changes anything published, it changes the application channel, the documentation and the term available on a non-euro income, not the LTV.
entries.note: The instruction as written sends the writer to find three bands that do not exist, which is exactly how invented numbers get published. It also mislabels 'Swiss' as a category of its own — Switzerland is neither EU nor EEA, and CaixaBank in fact treats the Swiss franc as a mainstream currency for term purposes.

entries.assertion: Age and term limits typically imposed on non-resident borrowers
entries.source_required: A named lender publishing maximum term and maximum age at maturity for non-resident mortgages
entries.source_opened: CaixaBank HolaBank Housing Mortgage Guide — https://www.caixabank.es/particular/holabank/housing-mortgage-guide.html
entries.locator: CaixaBank HolaBank representative example, verbatim: 'Maximum term of 20 years for deposits in euros and other currencies (1), and maximum term of 15 years for deposits in other currencies allowed (2)'. No maximum age at maturity is published on that page.
entries.final_wording: Term limits published by a named lender for non-resident borrowers — CaixaBank HolaBank caps the term at 20 years for euro and major-currency income and 15 years for other permitted currencies, against the 30 years commonly available to residents. Report an age-at-maturity limit only where the lender publishes one; HolaBank does not, so do not assert one.
entries.note: Term is verifiable and is a bigger constraint than most buyers expect — a 20-year cap raises the monthly payment sharply against a resident's 30 years. Age caps are real in the market but I could not open a published one, so pairing them as equally established would launder an unsourced figure. Note too that the term depends on the CURRENCY of income, not on nationality.

entries.assertion: do not assert an EU-versus-non-EU LTV band unless a named lender publishes one, since third-country status drives AML and documentation requirements rather than the LTV cap
entries.source_required: Lender publications (to test whether an EU/non-EU LTV band exists) and consolidated Ley 10/2010 on the actual trigger for enhanced due diligence
entries.source_opened: CaixaBank HolaBank Housing Mortgage Guide — https://www.caixabank.es/particular/holabank/housing-mortgage-guide.html ; BOE, texto consolidado Ley 10/2010 de prevención del blanqueo de capitales, bloque 'a11' — https://www.boe.es/datosabiertos/api/legislacion-consolidada/id/BOE-A-2010-6737/texto/bloque/a11
entries.locator: Art. 11.1 Ley 10/2010 (version BOE-A-2018-12131, in force 04/09/2018): enhanced due diligence applies to countries with strategic AML/CFT deficiencies appearing on the European Commission list adopted under art. 9 of Directive (EU) 2015/849 — not to third countries generally; art. 11.2 adds a risk-based test. CaixaBank HolaBank publishes one LTV for all non-residents.
entries.final_wording: Do not assert an EU-versus-non-EU LTV band unless a named lender publishes one — none that I could open does. What residence outside the EU actually changes is documentation and the application channel, plus the term available where income is in a non-euro currency. Enhanced anti-money-laundering checks are not triggered by third-country status as such: under art. 11 Ley 10/2010 they attach to countries on the European Commission's high-risk list, and otherwise on a risk assessment.
entries.note: The operative rule is right and worth keeping. The rationale as written is not: it implies every third country triggers AML escalation, which art. 11 Ley 10/2010 does not say. Left uncorrected it invites copy telling a US or Canadian buyer they are an AML risk by definition — CaixaBank in fact treats US and Canadian residents as eligible for its fastest online channel.

entries.assertion: What a derrama is, and why your vote doesn't save you.
entries.source_required: Consolidated Ley 49/1960 (LPH) arts. 9, 10 and 17 on who is bound by a junta resolution and when a dissenting owner is protected
entries.source_opened: BOE, texto consolidado Ley 49/1960 de Propiedad Horizontal, bloques 'anoveno' and 'adiecisiete' — https://www.boe.es/datosabiertos/api/legislacion-consolidada/id/BOE-A-1960-10906/texto/bloque/anoveno and .../texto/bloque/adiecisiete
entries.locator: Art. 17.4 LPH (current consolidated text, last amended by disposición final 1 RDL 7/2026 de 20 de marzo, BOE-A-2026-6544, in force 22/03/2026): where a 3/5 majority approves innovations, new installations, services or improvements NOT required for the building's adequate conservation, habitability, safety and accessibility, and the cost exceeds three ordinary monthly common-charge instalments, 'el disidente no resultará obligado, ni se modificará su cuota'. Art. 17.1: cost of telecom/renewable-energy infrastructure cannot be charged to owners who did not vote in favour.
entries.final_wording: What a derrama is — and when your vote saves you and when it doesn't. Vote against a non-essential improvement costing more than three months' ordinary fees and art. 17.4 LPH means you don't pay. Vote against essential conservation, safety, habitability or accessibility work and you pay anyway.
entries.note: 'Your vote doesn't save you' is wrong as a flat statement, and it is the single most-repeated piece of bad Spanish community-law copy. Art. 17.4 LPH gives the dissenting owner an express exemption for non-required improvements above the three-monthly-instalment threshold, and art. 17.1 protects those who did not vote in favour of telecom/renewables infrastructure. The true point is narrower and still striking: for work required to keep the building safe and habitable, your vote is irrelevant. Re-read art. 17 against the consolidated text each time — it has changed twice in the last fifteen months (Ley Orgánica 1/2025 with effect 3 April 2025, and RDL 7/2026 in force 22 March 2026, after RDL 7/2025's version was annulled by Congress in July 2025).

entries.assertion: Before you spend one euro on yourself: the real yearly cost of owning a €250,000 coastal flat, line by line.
entries.source_required: An official source establishing a single annual running cost for a Costa Blanca flat — which would have to overcome the fact that IBI rates are set municipality by municipality
entries.source_opened: BOE, texto consolidado RDLeg 2/2004 (TRLRHL), bloque 'a72' — https://www.boe.es/datosabiertos/api/legislacion-consolidada/id/BOE-A-2004-4214/texto/bloque/a72 ; Ayuntamiento de Torrevieja, Ordenanza fiscal reguladora del IBI, BOP de Alicante nº 247 de 29/12/2020 — https://torrevieja.es/sites/default/files/repositorio-archivos/IBI.pdf

entries.final_wording: Before you spend one euro on yourself: the real yearly cost of owning a €250,000 coastal flat in [named town], line by line.
entries.note: 'The real yearly cost' promises a single number that cannot exist, because the largest fixed line — IBI — is a municipal rate spanning 0.4% to 1.1% by law, and community fees are set building by building. Naming the town is what makes the headline honest and is also what makes it useful. The €250,000 is a worked example and should read as one.

entries.assertion: What does it actually cost to own a €250,000 coastal flat for a year on the Costa Blanca — and what actually differs between a Spanish tax resident and a non-resident owner, given that both are imputed on a second home?
entries.source_required: Consolidated art. 85 LIRPF to confirm that a Spanish tax resident is imputed on a non-habitual home, and art. 25 TRLIRNR for the non-resident treatment
entries.source_opened: BOE, texto consolidado Ley 35/2006, bloque 'a85' — https://www.boe.es/datosabiertos/api/legislacion-consolidada/id/BOE-A-2006-20764/texto/bloque/a85 ; BOE, texto consolidado RDLeg 5/2004, bloque 'a25' — https://www.boe.es/datosabiertos/api/legislacion-consolidada/id/BOE-A-2004-4527/texto/bloque/a25
entries.locator: Art. 85.1 LIRPF applies the imputation to urban property 'excluida la vivienda habitual' — so a resident's second home IS imputed; art. 25.1.a) TRLIRNR sets the non-resident flat rate (24%, or 19% for EU/EEA-with-mutual-assistance residents)
entries.final_wording: What does it actually cost to own a €250,000 coastal flat for a year on the Costa Blanca — and what actually differs between a Spanish tax resident and a non-resident owner, given that both are imputed on a second home?
entries.note: The embedded premise is correct and is the fact most guides get backwards: art. 85 LIRPF excludes only the habitual residence, so a Spanish tax resident with a coastal second home is imputed too. The genuine differences are the tax vehicle (IRPF general base at progressive rates with allowances vs flat 19%/24% IRNR), the return (annual IRPF vs Modelo 210), and the filing window. Answering it also requires naming a town, per id 250.

entries.final_wording: How IBI is derived from cadastral value and the fact that the tipo de gravamen is set by each municipality — so the figure must be tied to a named town
entries.note: Confirmed: the ayuntamiento sets the urban rate anywhere from 0.4% to 1.10%, so an unnamed-town IBI figure can be wrong by a factor of nearly three. Two refinements for accuracy: the rate is applied to the base LIQUIDABLE, not the raw cadastral value, wherever a reduction under arts. 66-67 TRLRHL is still running after a general revision; and art. 72 also carries a surcharge for permanently unoccupied residential property, which a second-home owner should be told exists.

entries.assertion: Which of the lines are genuinely non-resident-specific (Modelo 210 imputed income, fiscal representation) versus paid by everyone
entries.source_required: Consolidated art. 10 TRLIRNR on when a non-resident must appoint a fiscal representative, and art. 85 LIRPF on whether imputation is non-resident-specific
entries.source_opened: BOE, texto consolidado RDLeg 5/2004 (TRLIRNR), bloque 'a10' — https://www.boe.es/datosabiertos/api/legislacion-consolidada/id/BOE-A-2004-4527/texto/bloque/a10 ; BOE, texto consolidado Ley 35/2006, bloque 'a85' — https://www.boe.es/datosabiertos/api/legislacion-consolidada/id/BOE-A-2006-20764/texto/bloque/a85
entries.locator: Art. 10.1 TRLIRNR (version BOE-A-2021-11473, in force 11/07/2021): only taxpayers NOT resident in another EU Member State must appoint a representative, and then only where they operate through a permanent establishment, in the arts. 24.2/38 cases, or where the Administration so requires; the duty does not apply to EEA States covered by mutual assistance on exchange of information and recovery. Art. 85 LIRPF imputes non-habitual urban property to residents too.
entries.final_wording: Which lines are genuinely non-resident-specific versus paid by everyone. The imputed income itself is NOT non-resident-specific — art. 85 LIRPF imputes a second home to Spanish tax residents as well. What is specific to the non-resident is the vehicle: a separate Modelo 210 self-assessment at a flat 19%/24% with no personal allowances. Fiscal representation is not a standard non-resident cost either: under art. 10 TRLIRNR it is required only of owners resident outside the EU and outside the mutual-assistance EEA, and then only in defined cases or when the tax office demands it.
entries.note: Two errors that would cost readers money. Listing 'Modelo 210 imputed income' as non-resident-specific contradicts topic 5's own question (id 248), which correctly says both are imputed on a second home. And presenting fiscal representation as a routine non-resident line would sell an EU-resident owner a service art. 10 TRLIRNR does not require of them — an EU-resident owner never falls under the appointment duty, and nor does an Icelandic, Norwegian or Liechtenstein resident.

Art. 85 LIRPF imputes non-habitual urban property to residents too.

entries.assertion: Your €250,000 flat cost £213,000 in January and £224,000 in June — same flat.
entries.source_required: ECB euro foreign exchange reference rates for GBP (the published daily official series), for the dates asserted
entries.source_opened: European Central Bank Data Portal, series EXR.D.GBP.EUR.SP00.A (Pound sterling/Euro ECB reference exchange rate, 2.15 pm CET), 25/08/2025-01/09/2026 — https://data-api.ecb.europa.eu/service/data/EXR/D.GBP.EUR.SP00.A?startPeriod=2025-08-25&endPeriod=2026-09-02&format=csvdata
entries.locator: ECB daily reference rate, monthly means: January 2026 = 0.8683 GBP/EUR (€250,000 = £217,070); June 2026 = 0.8637 (€250,000 = £215,930). Twelve-month extremes: 0.8846 on 14/11/2025 (£221,150) and 0.84873 on 16/07/2026 (£212,182). 261 daily observations.
entries.final_wording: Your €250,000 flat cost about £217,100 in January and about £215,900 in June — same flat. Over the past twelve months the sterling price of that €250,000 has swung between roughly £212,200 and £221,200 on the ECB's daily reference rate: a spread of about £9,000.
entries.note: Wrong in both figures AND in direction. £213,000 implies 0.852 and £224,000 implies 0.896; neither rate occurred in January or June 2026, and 0.896 did not occur at any point in the twelve months to 1 September 2026 (the high was 0.8846 on 14 November 2025). Sterling STRENGTHENED between January and June 2026, so the flat got slightly cheaper in pounds, not £11,000 dearer. Rebuild any FX hook from the ECB series with the dates stated; the real swing is still a genuine £9,000 story.

entries.assertion: How far has GBP/EUR actually moved over the last twelve months, and what does that swing add to or take off a €250,000 purchase?
entries.source_required: An official daily exchange-rate series — the ECB euro foreign exchange reference rates, or Bank of England spot rates
entries.source_opened: European Central Bank Data Portal, series EXR.D.GBP.EUR.SP00.A — https://data-api.ecb.europa.eu/service/data/EXR/D.GBP.EUR.SP00.A?startPeriod=2025-08-25&endPeriod=2026-09-02&format=csvdata
entries.final_wording: How far has GBP/EUR actually moved over the last twelve months, and what does that swing add to or take off a €250,000 purchase? Name the source and both dates — the ECB publishes a daily reference rate — and recompute at publication.
entries.note: A sound question, but any answer expires the day it is written: the ECB republishes the reference rate every working day at 2.15pm CET. As at 1 September 2026 the twelve-month answer is a swing between roughly £212,200 and £221,200 on €250,000, about £9,000 or 4.2%. Two traps for the copy: the ECB reference rate is not the rate a buyer gets (a bank or broker spread sits on top), and a rolling 'last twelve months' must be re-anchored to fixed dates before publication.

entries.assertion: When you sell, the buyer's lawyer keeps 3% of your money and hands it to the taxman before you see it.
entries.source_required: Consolidated TRLIRNR (RDLeg 5/2004) art. 25.2 and the IRNR Regulation (RD 1776/2004) art. 14, on who bears the withholding obligation
entries.source_opened: BOE, Real Decreto Legislativo 5/2004 (TRLIRNR), texto consolidado — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2004-4527 ; and BOE, Real Decreto 1776/2004 (Reglamento IRNR), texto consolidado — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2004-14532
entries.locator: TRLIRNR art. 25.2 (consolidated, última actualización 25/05/2023; art. 25 last amended by Ley 26/2014, in force 1 Jan 2015): "el adquirente estará obligado a retener e ingresar el 3 por ciento… de la contraprestación acordada, en concepto de pago a cuenta del impuesto correspondiente a aquéllos". RIRNR art. 14.1 and 14.3 (última actualización 19/10/2019).
entries.final_wording: When you sell as a non-resident, the law makes the BUYER — not the buyer's lawyer — withhold 3% of the agreed price and pay it to the Agencia Tributaria within one month of completion. It is a payment on account of your own Spanish non-resident tax, not money anyone keeps.
entries.note: Two errors as written. (1) The obligated party is the adquirente (the buyer) — the lawyer may operate the mechanics but the statutory duty and liability are the buyer's. (2) 'Keeps' is wrong and is the exact thing guardrail 268 forbids: it is withheld and paid over to the Agencia Tributaria. Also add the non-resident condition — this does not apply to a Spanish-resident seller (RIRNR art. 14.2.a).

entries.locator: RIRNR art. 14.4 (consolidated, última actualización 19/10/2019): the non-resident declares and where applicable pays the definitive tax, offsetting the amount withheld, within three months from the end of the buyer's one-month period; the Administration refunds "el exceso retenido o ingresado a cuenta" after any checks it considers necessary.
entries.final_wording: How a non-resident settles up afterwards — and reclaims any excess.
entries.note: The heading promises recovery, which the statute does not. Art. 14.4 refunds only the EXCESS over the definitive tax, and only after AEAT's checks; where the gain is large the 3% is a part-payment and the seller pays MORE. As written it contradicts guardrail 269 in the same topic. TRLIRNR DA 7ª.3 confirms the 3% is withheld even where an EU reinvestment exemption is claimed.

entries.assertion: 3% of your sale price goes straight to the Spanish taxman before you see a cent.
entries.source_required: TRLIRNR art. 25.2 and RIRNR art. 14.1–14.2 on the trigger, base and exclusions
entries.source_opened: BOE, TRLIRNR texto consolidado — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2004-4527 ; BOE, RIRNR texto consolidado — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2004-14532
entries.locator: TRLIRNR art. 25.2 and RIRNR art. 14.1: 3% "de la contraprestación acordada", applying to transmissions by IRNR taxpayers acting without a permanent establishment. RIRNR art. 14.2.a): no withholding where the transferor evidences subjection to IRPF or Impuesto sobre Sociedades by certificate from the tax administration; 14.2.b) excludes contributions of property to Spanish company capital.
entries.final_wording: If you sell as a non-resident, 3% of the agreed price is withheld at completion and paid straight to the Spanish tax office before you see a cent.
entries.note: Unconditional as written, and therefore false for a Spanish-resident seller — precisely the resident/non-resident variable that has to stay separate. Two precisions: the trigger is the SELLER's non-residence (and it drops away on a certificate of IRPF/IS subjection under RIRNR art. 14.2.a), and the statutory base is the 'contraprestación acordada', not 'sale price' as a loose synonym.

entries.assertion: Is it a tax or a deposit, and what does a non-resident seller have to do — and by when — to get any of it back?
entries.source_required: TRLIRNR art. 25.2 (legal characterisation) and RIRNR art. 14.4 (seller's obligation and deadline)
entries.source_opened: BOE, TRLIRNR texto consolidado — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2004-4527 ; BOE, RIRNR texto consolidado — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2004-14532
entries.locator: TRLIRNR art. 25.2: "en concepto de pago a cuenta del impuesto". RIRNR art. 14.4: definitive declaration and payment within three months from the end of the buyer's one-month period, offsetting the withholding.
entries.final_wording: Is it a tax or a deposit, and what does a non-resident seller have to do — and by when — to get any of it back?
entries.note: Well-formed and answerable from primary law. The answer is 'neither': it is a pago a cuenta — a payment on account of the seller's own IRNR liability. The 'by when' is the RIRNR art. 14.4 window: three months from the end of the buyer's one-month period, i.e. roughly four months from completion. Keep 'any of it' — recovery is not guaranteed.

entries.assertion: That the obligation sits on the buyer, who files Modelo 211 and pays within one month of completion, and the seller's remedy if the buyer fails to do it
entries.source_required: RIRNR art. 14.3 and 14.5, plus the Orden approving Modelo 211
entries.source_opened: BOE, RIRNR texto consolidado — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2004-14532 ; BOE, Orden EHA/3316/2010 texto consolidado — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2010-19707
entries.locator: RIRNR art. 14.3 (última actualización 19/10/2019, redaction in force from 1 Jan 2007): the person obliged to withhold must file with the AEAT Delegación covering the property's location and pay "en el plazo de un mes a partir de la fecha de la transmisión". Art. 14.5: if unpaid, the transferred property is afecto al pago of the lesser of the withholding and the tax, and the Registrador records it by marginal note stating the sum the finca answers for. Modelo 211 approved by Orden EHA/3316/2010 (consolidated, última actualización 23/06/2026).
entries.final_wording: That the obligation sits on the buyer, who files Modelo 211 and pays within one month of the date of transmission, and what happens if the buyer fails to do it — art. 14.5 RIRNR does not give the seller a remedy: it charges the property itself (afección real, noted in the margin of the register), which bites the buyer.
entries.note: Buyer, Modelo 211 and the one-month deadline are all verified verbatim. The clause 'the seller's remedy' imports a remedy the tax rules do not create: art. 14.5 is a Treasury guarantee against the transferred property, not a seller's cause of action. Also, the statutory clock runs from 'la fecha de la transmisión' (the escritura), which is the practical meaning of completion but should be said that way.

entries.assertion: The seller's Modelo 210 deadline for reclaiming or settling, and precisely what is forfeited by missing it
entries.source_required: RIRNR art. 14.4 for the deadline, and Ley 58/2003 (LGT) arts. 31 and 66 for the consequence of missing it
entries.source_opened: BOE, RIRNR texto consolidado — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2004-14532 ; BOE, Ley 58/2003 General Tributaria, texto consolidado — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2003-23186
entries.locator: RIRNR art. 14.4: three months from the end of the one-month withholding period. LGT art. 66.c) and d) (consolidated, última actualización 21/12/2024): the right to request, and to obtain, refunds derived from each tax's own rules prescribes at four years. LGT art. 31.2 (amended by Ley 11/2021): once six months pass without payment of the refund for a cause attributable to the Administration, interest de demora accrues automatically.
entries.final_wording: The seller's Modelo 210 deadline — three months from the end of the buyer's one-month period (RIRNR art. 14.4) — and what actually happens if it is missed: the refund is not forfeited, it can still be claimed, and the right to claim it prescribes only after four years (LGT art. 66.c).
entries.note: The instruction carries a false premise. Nothing is 'forfeited' at the three-month mark. A late Modelo 210 with a refund result is still valid; the four-year LGT prescription is the real cliff edge. Writing 'you lose the 3% if you miss the deadline' is a foreseeable and damaging error this instruction invites.

entries.assertion: The current non-resident CGT rate on the gain, and a worked case where the 3% is less than the tax due so the seller owes more rather than receiving a refund
entries.source_required: TRLIRNR art. 25.1 consolidated text in force, distinguishing the gains rate from the imputed/rental rates
entries.source_opened: BOE, Real Decreto Legislativo 5/2004, texto consolidado — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2004-4527
entries.locator: TRLIRNR art. 25.1.f).3º (consolidated, última actualización 25/05/2023; letter f) in its Ley 26/2009 redaction with effect from 1 Jan 2010): 19% for "Ganancias patrimoniales que se pongan de manifiesto con ocasión de transmisiones de elementos patrimoniales". No later amendment to art. 25 appears in the consolidated text.
entries.final_wording: The current non-resident CGT rate on the gain, and a worked case where the 3% is less than the tax due so the seller owes more rather than receiving a refund
entries.note: 19% flat, and — this is the trap the ledger exists for — letter f) is unqualified by residence, so it is 19% for EU/EEA AND third-country sellers alike. The 24%/19% split in art. 25.1.a) belongs to imputed and rental income, not to gains. The worked case breaks at a clean threshold: 0.19·gain > 0.03·price, i.e. the seller owes more whenever the gain exceeds 15.79% of the price. Also flag TRLIRNR DA 7ª (reinvestment-in-main-home exemption, EU residents), whose apartado 3 confirms the 3% is still withheld.

entries.assertion: Realistic refund processing times and what the Agencia Tributaria requires (Spanish bank account, NIE, fiscal representative)
entries.source_required: The Orden approving Modelo 210 on refund accounts, TRLIRNR art. 10 on representatives, and an official source for processing times
entries.source_opened: BOE, Orden EHA/3316/2010 texto consolidado — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2010-19707 ; BOE, TRLIRNR texto consolidado — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2004-4527 ; BOE, LGT texto consolidado — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2003-23186
entries.locator: Orden EHA/3316/2010 art. 3.2 (consolidated, última actualización 23/06/2026), verbatim: "si el titular de la cuenta de devolución es el propio contribuyente, la cuenta puede estar abierta en una entidad de crédito en España o en el extranjero"; the preamble records that Modelo 210 refunds may be made by transfer to taxpayers' accounts held at financial institutions abroad. TRLIRNR art. 10.1: a resident representative is compulsory only for taxpayers not resident in another EU State, and only where they operate through a permanent establishment, in the arts. 24.2/38 cases, or where the Administration so requires. LGT art. 31.2: six months before interest de demora runs.
entries.final_wording: What the Agencia Tributaria actually requires for the refund: a Spanish NIF/NIE (or the identification code AEAT issues for the purpose), and a bank account in the seller's OWN name — which may be held in Spain or abroad. A fiscal representative is not a general requirement (TRLIRNR art. 10.1 imposes one only on non-EU residents in defined cases). On timing, no official processing-time statistic is published; the only official benchmark is LGT art. 31.2 — after six months AEAT owes interest de demora.
entries.note: Two of the three parenthetical 'requirements' are wrong and would be published as fact. A Spanish account is required only if the refund account belongs to the retenedor, responsable solidario or authorised legal representative rather than to the taxpayer. A fiscal representative is not needed by an EU-resident seller at all, and for a third-country seller only in the art. 10.1 cases. 'Realistic processing times' has no authoritative source — say so or drop it, do not quote an expat-forum figure.

TRLIRNR art. 10.1: a resident representative is compulsory only for taxpayers not resident in another EU State, and only where they operate through a permanent establishment, in the arts. 24.2/38 cases, or where the Administration so requires. entries.assertion: Who pays plusvalía municipal on a sale by a non-resident and whether the buyer can be made liable
entries.source_required: Consolidated TRLRHL (RDLeg 2/2004) art. 106 on sujetos pasivos of the IIVTNU
entries.source_opened: BOE, Real Decreto Legislativo 2/2004 (Texto Refundido de la Ley Reguladora de las Haciendas Locales), texto consolidado — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2004-4214
entries.locator: TRLRHL art. 106.1.b) and 106.2 (consolidated, última actualización 03/06/2026; art. 106 in its redaction in force since 17 Oct 2014 after Ley 18/2014 suppressed apartado 3): on onerous transmissions the contribuyente is the transferor; and "tendrá la consideración de sujeto pasivo sustituto del contribuyente… quien adquiera el terreno… cuando el contribuyente sea una persona física no residente en España".
entries.final_wording: Who pays plusvalía municipal on a sale by a non-resident and whether the buyer can be made liable
entries.note: Yes — and this is the single most commercially important line in topic 7. On a sale the seller is the taxpayer, but where that seller is a non-resident NATURAL PERSON the buyer becomes sustituto del contribuyente and the town hall can demand it from the buyer. Note the limit precisely: art. 106.2 says 'persona física', so it does not catch a non-resident company. The sustituto has a right of reimbursement against the contribuyente under LGT art. 36.3.

entries.assertion: Never present the 3% as automatically refundable;
entries.source_required: RIRNR art. 14.4 on the conditional nature of the refund

entries.note: Three independent reasons it is not automatic: only the EXCESS over the definitive tax is returned; it is returned only after AEAT's checks; and where the gain exceeds 15.79% of the price the seller owes more instead. It is also not automatic in the sense of being self-executing — the seller must file Modelo 210 to trigger it.

entries.assertion: Never assume the 3% is calculated on anything other than the declared sale price
entries.source_required: TRLIRNR art. 25.2 / RIRNR art. 14.1 statutory base of the withholding
entries.source_opened: BOE, TRLIRNR texto consolidado — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2004-4527 ; BOE, RIRNR texto consolidado — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2004-14532
entries.locator: TRLIRNR art. 25.2 and RIRNR art. 14.1: the base is "la contraprestación acordada".
entries.final_wording: Never assume the 3% is calculated on anything other than the agreed consideration ("la contraprestación acordada") — normally the price declared in the escritura. It is never taken on the cadastral value, the valor de referencia, or the seller's gain.
entries.note: The guardrail points the right way but uses a non-statutory term. 'Contraprestación acordada' is wider than a cash price: it takes in non-monetary consideration such as an assumed mortgage or a permuta, where the declared price alone would understate the base. Naming the statutory term keeps the writer accurate in the odd cases without loosening the ordinary one.

entries.assertion: What do they actually have to pay, and by when, before they can sell it — and does the Valencian 99% relief reach heirs who have never lived in Spain?
entries.source_required: Consolidated Ley 13/1997 (CV) art. 12 bis for the rate, and LISD Disposición adicional segunda for non-resident access to regional rules
entries.source_opened: BOE, Ley 13/1997 de la Generalitat Valenciana, texto consolidado — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-1998-8202 ; BOE, Ley 29/1987 del ISD, texto consolidado — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-1987-28141
entries.locator: Ley 13/1997 art. 12 bis.1.a) (consolidated, última actualización 02/07/2026, in force from 03/07/2026): 99% bonificación on the proportional part of the ISD quota for mortis causa acquisitions by relatives in groups I and II of art. 20.2.a LISD. LISD DA 2ª.Uno.1.a) (última actualización 10/07/2021): where the causante was non-resident, taxpayers are entitled to the rules of the Autonomous Community holding the greatest value of the estate's Spanish assets.
entries.final_wording: What do they actually have to pay, and by when, before they can sell it — and does the Valencian 99% relief reach heirs who have never lived in Spain?
entries.note: A properly framed question, and the answer is yes: never having lived in Spain does not bar the 99%. Keep the five variables apart when answering — what matters is the location of the assets and the causante's residence, not the heirs' nationality or immigration status. One condition the writer must not omit: art. 12 bis.2 restricts the bonificación to assets fully declared in a self-assessment filed either in time or before any AEAT requerimiento. The 'by when' (ISD filing deadline) was not verified in this pass and needs its own check against the RISD.
