entries.assertion: Plusvalía municipal on an inheritance: who pays, how it is now calculated, and the municipal deadlines
entries.source_required: Consolidated TRLRHL arts. 106, 107 and 110 in force
entries.source_opened: BOE, Real Decreto Legislativo 2/2004 (TRLRHL), texto consolidado — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2004-4214
entries.locator: TRLRHL (consolidated, última actualización 03/06/2026): art. 106.1.a) — on lucrative transmissions the sujeto pasivo is the person who acquires the land, i.e. the heir; art. 107.1–107.4 — base imponible by land value at accrual (IBI value) times the coefficient for the generation period, "sin perjuicio de lo dispuesto en el apartado 5"; art. 110.4 cross-refers to arts. 104.5 and 107.5 (the real-gain route and the non-subjection where there is no increase, both introduced by RDL 26/2021 after STC 182/2021); art. 110.2.b) — for acts by reason of death the declaration period is "seis meses prorrogables hasta un año a solicitud del sujeto pasivo".
entries.final_wording: Plusvalía municipal on an inheritance: who pays, how it is now calculated, and the municipal deadlines
entries.note: All three limbs are answerable from the consolidated TRLRHL, and the answers are: the heir pays; the base is either the objective coefficient method (art. 107) or, at the taxpayer's election, the real increase (art. 107.5), with no tax where there is no increase (art. 104.5); and the deadline is six months from death, extendable to one year on request. The word 'now' is doing real work — anyone answering from pre-2021 material will describe a method the Constitutional Court struck down. Two cautions: the coefficients are set annually in the Ley de Presupuestos and each ayuntamiento sets its own rate and may or may not operate autoliquidación, so no single national figure exists.

entries.assertion: Whether a Spanish will and a choice-of-law declaration under EU Regulation 650/2012 changes what the children face
entries.source_required: The Official Journal text of Regulation (EU) No 650/2012, arts. 21, 22 and 84 and the opt-out recitals
entries.source_opened: Regulation (EU) No 650/2012, OJ L 201, 27.7.2012, pp. 107–134, Spanish text as mirrored by the BOE — https://www.boe.es/doue/2012/201/L00107-00134.pdf (EUR-Lex itself was not reachable from this environment)
entries.locator: Reg. (EU) 650/2012, done at Strasbourg 4 July 2012, OJ L 201 of 27.7.2012: art. 21.1 — the law applicable to the succession as a whole is that of the State of the deceased's habitual residence at death, with the art. 21.2 manifestly-closer-connection escape; art. 22.1–22.2 — professio iuris for the law of a State of nationality held at the time of choosing or at death, made expressly in a disposition mortis causa; art. 84 — applies from 17 August 2015; recitals 82 and 83 — the United Kingdom, Ireland and Denmark are not bound by it.
entries.final_wording: Whether a Spanish will and a choice-of-law declaration under EU Regulation 650/2012 changes what the children face
entries.note: Legitimate and correctly cited, but it must be answered with one boundary stated out loud, or the copy will mislead: Regulation 650/2012 governs the SUCCESSION law — who inherits, and whether forced heirship applies — and has no effect on the Spanish inheritance TAX, which is set by the LISD and the Valencian rules regardless of the law chosen. Second point worth carrying: the UK is not bound by the Regulation, yet Spain applies it universally (art. 20), so a British national can still validly choose English law in a Spanish will. Only deaths from 17 August 2015 are covered.

entries.assertion: If the previous owner owed the community €5,000, you pay it.
entries.source_required: Consolidated Ley 49/1960 de Propiedad Horizontal art. 9.1.e) on the acquirer's liability and its limit
entries.source_opened: BOE, Ley 49/1960, de 21 de julio, sobre propiedad horizontal, texto consolidado — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-1960-10906
entries.locator: LPH art. 9.1.e) (consolidated, última actualización 21/03/2026), verbatim: the acquirer "responde con el propio inmueble adquirido de las cantidades adeudadas a la comunidad de propietarios… por los anteriores titulares hasta el límite de los que resulten imputables a la parte vencida de la anualidad en la cual tenga lugar la adquisición y a los tres años naturales anteriores. El piso o local estará legalmente afecto al cumplimiento de esta obligación."
entries.final_wording: If the previous owner left community debts, the flat itself answers for them — but only up to the amounts falling due in the elapsed part of the year you buy in plus the three preceding calendar years. Anything older stays the seller's problem, and the seller must hand over a certificate of debts before the notary unless you expressly waive it.
entries.note: Three defects. (1) The liability is capped in time: current annuity plus three calendar years, so a €5,000 arrears figure is not automatically inherited in full. (2) It is an afección real — the flat answers for it — not a personal debt transferred to the buyer; the former owner remains personally liable. (3) It omits the buyer's actual protection: art. 9.1.e) obliges the seller to declare and certify the debt state, and the notary may not authorise the deed without that certificate unless the buyer waives it. See also id 280 on the €5,000 figure itself.

El piso o local estará legalmente afecto al cumplimiento de esta obligación."

entries.assertion: Whether a derrama (special assessment) approved before the sale but billed after it transfers to the buyer, and how the approval date decides it.
entries.source_required: Consolidated LPH provisions allocating derramas between outgoing and incoming owner (arts. 9.1.e and 17.11)
entries.source_opened: BOE, Ley 49/1960 sobre propiedad horizontal, texto consolidado — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-1960-10906
entries.locator: LPH art. 17.11 (consolidated, última actualización 21/03/2026), verbatim: "Las derramas para el pago de mejoras realizadas o por realizar en el inmueble serán a cargo de quien sea propietario en el momento de la exigibilidad de las cantidades afectas al pago de dichas mejoras." LPH art. 9.1.e) separately fixes the acquirer's afección real at the elapsed part of the current annuity plus three calendar years.
entries.final_wording: Whether a derrama (special assessment) approved before the sale but billed after it transfers to the buyer, and how the statutory test decides it: LPH art. 17.11 makes derramas for improvements the liability of whoever owns the property when the instalments become EXIGIBLE — when they fall due — not when the junta approved them.
entries.note: The instruction hard-codes the wrong test and would produce confident, wrong copy. The statute's criterion is exigibilidad, and the practical consequence inverts the instruction's premise: a derrama approved before the sale but falling due after it lands on the BUYER. Two limits to keep straight: art. 17.11 is written for derramas 'para el pago de mejoras', so ordinary conservation charges run under art. 9.1.e); and whatever the allocation between the parties, the flat itself still answers under art. 9.1.e) within its three-year-plus-current-annuity window. Parties routinely contract around this, so say the default is contractually variable.

entries.assertion: The distinction between the pool never being declared/registered (declaración de obra nueva) and it never having been licensed by the town hall — these are separate problems with separate fixes.
entries.source_required: Consolidated state land law on declaración de obra nueva (TRLSRU art. 28) and Valencian planning law on licensing and restoration (TRLOTUP)
entries.source_opened: BOE, Real Decreto Legislativo 7/2015 (TRLSRU), texto consolidado — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2015-11723 ; BOE, Decreto Legislativo 1/2021 (TRLOTUP), texto consolidado — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=DOGV-r-2021-90283
entries.locator: TRLSRU art. 28 (consolidated, última actualización 25/05/2023): what notaries and registrars require to authorise and inscribe a declaración de obra nueva — a registry/notarial act. TRLOTUP arts. 255–257 (consolidated, última actualización 02/07/2026): the municipal licence, the caducidad of the restoration power, and the restoration measures — a planning act by the alcaldía or the Agencia Valenciana de Protección del Territorio.
entries.final_wording: The distinction between the pool never being declared/registered (declaración de obra nueva) and it never having been licensed by the town hall — these are separate problems with separate fixes.
entries.note: Correct and well drawn: two different bodies of law, two different authorities, two different remedies. The point that makes it matter commercially is TRLOTUP art. 256 — once the fifteen years run out the town hall can no longer order demolition, but "el mero transcurso del plazo… no conllevará la legalización", and while the breach persists no reform, extension or consolidation works may be carried out. So a pool can be registrable and still permanently unlawful. Correct regime confirmed too: the Valencian instrument is TRLOTUP, not the Andalusian AFO.

entries.assertion: 255 TRLOTUP, Decreto Legislativo 1/2021) on how long the town hall retains power to order restoration or demolition, and the classes listed in Art.
entries.source_required: Consolidated text in force of TRLOTUP art. 255, all apartados
entries.source_opened: BOE, Decreto Legislativo 1/2021 (TRLOTUP), texto consolidado — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=DOGV-r-2021-90283
entries.locator: TRLOTUP art. 255 "Obras terminadas sin licencia o sin ajustarse a sus determinaciones. Plazo de caducidad de la acción para ordenar la restauración de la legalidad urbanística", consolidated, última actualización 02/07/2026. Art. 255.1: fifteen years from total completion of the works or cessation of the use, exercised by the alcaldía and, where applicable, the Agencia Valenciana de Protección del Territorio, requiring the owner within two months to apply for authorisation or bring the works into line. Art. 255.5: the fifteen-year period does NOT apply — "no existirá plazo de caducidad de la acción" — to works on land classed as zonas verdes, viales, espacios libres or usos dotacionales públicos, land or buildings in the dominio público or in the Inventario General del Patrimonio Cultural Valenciano, "tampoco será de aplicación sobre suelo no urbanizable". Art. 255.6: the applicable period is the one in the planning law in force when the works finished.
entries.final_wording: Art. 255 TRLOTUP (Decreto Legislativo 1/2021) on how long the town hall retains power to order restoration or demolition — fifteen years from total completion under art. 255.1 — AND the cases in art. 255.5 where no period ever runs, which include zonas verdes, viales, espacios libres, usos dotacionales públicos, dominio público, the Inventario General del Patrimonio Cultural Valenciano and, critically for rural Costa Blanca property, suelo no urbanizable.
entries.note: Article number, instrument and subject are all correct. The correction is one of omission with real consequences: the instruction asks 'how long', which invites the answer 'fifteen years' full stop, when on suelo no urbanizable — where a great many Costa Blanca pools sit — the action never lapses at all. Two further points a writer must not lose: art. 255.6 means the period is the one in force when the works FINISHED, not today's; and the power is shared with the Agencia Valenciana de Protección del Territorio, so 'the town hall' alone understates who can act.

entries.assertion: Whether declaración de obra nueva por antigüedad is available in this situation, what it requires (architect's certificate, cadastral proof of age, notary, registry), and its realistic cost range from a sourced Spanish reference.
entries.source_required: Consolidated TRLSRU art. 28.4 for the requirements and the precondition, plus an official or professional-body Spanish source for costs
entries.source_opened: BOE, Real Decreto Legislativo 7/2015 (TRLSRU), texto consolidado — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2015-11723 ; BOE, TRLOTUP texto consolidado — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=DOGV-r-2021-90283 (no official cost source located)
entries.locator: TRLSRU art. 28.4 (consolidated, última actualización 25/05/2023): available for constructions "respecto de las cuales ya no proceda adoptar medidas de restablecimiento de la legalidad urbanística que impliquen su demolición, por haber transcurrido los plazos de prescripción correspondientes"; requires a certification from the Ayuntamiento or a competent technician, a notarial act describing the finca, or a graphic cadastral certification, showing completion on a determined date and matching the title; the Registrar must verify the absence of an anotación preventiva for a disciplinary planning file and that the land is neither demanial nor burdened by public-use servitudes.
entries.final_wording: Whether declaración de obra nueva por antigüedad is available at all — under TRLSRU art. 28.4 it is only available once demolition can no longer be ordered, which under TRLOTUP art. 255.5 never happens on suelo no urbanizable or protected land — and what it requires: certification from the Ayuntamiento or a competent technician, or a notarial descriptive act, or a graphic cadastral certification evidencing the completion date, plus a Registrar's check that no disciplinary anotación preventiva burdens the finca and that the land is not demanial. No official or professional-body cost range was located; give a cost only if a named Spanish source supports it, otherwise omit it.
entries.note: The requirements list in the instruction is broadly right but loosely worded — art. 28.4 offers three alternative proofs of age, not a cumulative set, and the Registrar's two negative checks are the part most often omitted. The availability question needs the TRLOTUP art. 255.5 gate stated explicitly, because that is what decides most rural cases. The cost element is UNSUPPORTED: I found no official or colegio-published range, and 'a sourced Spanish reference' will in practice be met by a law-firm or builder marketing page, which is a lead and not proof.

entries.assertion: The legal categories — allanamiento de morada versus usurpación — and where a foreign owner's regularly used holiday home falls, since a second home can qualify as morada and whether police can act immediately — establish what flagrancy actually requires under the LECrim and the Interior protocol, since no 48-hour rule exists in Spanish law.
entries.source_required: Consolidated Código Penal arts. 202 and 245 (BOE); consolidated LECrim art. 795 (flagrancy definition); a citable Tribunal Supremo judgment on whether a second home is 'morada'; the Ministerio del Interior operational protocol
entries.source_opened: Código Penal, texto consolidado, BOE-A-1995-25444 — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-1995-25444 (blocks a202, a245); Ley de Enjuiciamiento Criminal, texto consolidado, BOE-A-1882-6036 — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-1882-6036 (block a795). Interior protocol: NOT opened. TS 'segunda vivienda = morada' authority: NOT opened.
entries.locator: CP art. 202.1 ('El particular que, sin habitar en ella, entrare en morada ajena...' prisión de 6 meses a 2 años); CP art. 245.1 (violence/intimidation, prisión 1-2 años) and 245.2 (occupation without violence of an immueble 'que no constituyan morada', multa de 3 a 6 meses); LECrim art. 795.1.1ª defines delito flagrante. entries.final_wording: The legal categories — allanamiento de morada (CP art. 202) versus usurpación (CP art. 245) — and where a foreign owner's regularly used holiday home falls. Note that art. 245.2 CP applies only to an immueble 'que no constituyan morada', so the morada / non-morada line is the whole question; whether a regularly used second home counts as morada is decided case by case and must be backed by a citable Tribunal Supremo judgment before it is asserted. On immediate police action, apply the flagrancy definition in LECrim art. 795.1.1ª. There is no 48-hour rule anywhere in the Código Penal or the LECrim.
entries.note: Two limbs verified against primary text: the category line (CP art. 245.2's own words carve out morada) and the absence of any 48-hour rule. Two limbs not verified: 'a second home can qualify as morada' is asserted as settled but I opened no authority for it — and FGE Circular 1/2025, which I did open in full, gives no guidance on second homes; and I could not open any 'Interior protocol', so do not cite one.

entries.assertion: Never present 15 days as a general eviction deadline or target — it is a hearing-rescheduling window, and repeating it is how the 'Spain evicts squatters in 15 days' headline spreads.
entries.source_required: Consolidated LECrim arts. 800.3 and 802.2 (BOE)
entries.source_opened: Ley de Enjuiciamiento Criminal, texto consolidado, BOE-A-1882-6036 — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-1882-6036 (blocks as800, as802)
entries.locator: art. 802.2 LECrim = re-listing window ('no pueda celebrarse el juicio oral en el día señalado, o... no pueda concluirse en un solo acto'); art. 800.3 LECrim = initial señalamiento window ('hará el señalamiento para la celebración del juicio oral... dentro de los quince días siguientes')
entries.as_of: LECrim consolidated 09/04/2026; art. 802 version in force 03/04/2025, art. 800 version in force 04/05/2010; consulted 02/09/2026
entries.final_wording: Never present 15 days as a general eviction deadline or target. Two different 15-day periods exist inside the juicio rápido: art. 800.3 LECrim sets the initial trial date within 15 days, and art. 802.2 LECrim gives 15 days to re-list a hearing that could not be held or finished. Neither fixes when anyone leaves a property, and repeating them as an eviction promise is how the 'Spain evicts squatters in 15 days' headline spreads.
entries.note: The instruction's conclusion is right, its reasoning is not. Calling the 15 days purely 'a hearing-rescheduling window' is itself inaccurate — art. 800.3, which was not amended in 2025, sets the initial trial date within 15 days. Correcting this matters because an editor who checks the reasoning and finds it wrong will discard the whole caution.

entries.assertion: Whether you lose your €80,000 comes down to one piece of paper you should have demanded on day one.
entries.source_required: Consolidated Ley 38/1999 (LOE), disposición adicional primera, as in force (BOE)
entries.source_opened: Ley 38/1999 de Ordenación de la Edificación, texto consolidado, BOE-A-1999-21567 — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-1999-21567 (block daprimera via the BOE legislación-consolidada API)
entries.locator: LOE DA 1ª, Uno.1, version in force from 01/01/2016: developers must (a) 'Garantizar, desde la obtención de la licencia de edificación, la devolución de las cantidades entregadas más los intereses legales, mediante contrato de seguro de caución... o mediante aval solidario' AND (b) 'Percibir las cantidades anticipadas... a través de entidades de crédito en las que habrán de depositarse en cuenta especial, con separación de cualquier otra clase de fondos'
entries.as_of: LOE DA 1ª version in force since 01/01/2016; consulted 02/09/2026
entries.final_wording: Whether you get your money back off-plan turns on two things the law requires from day one — an individual bank guarantee or caución insurance policy in your name, and payment into the developer's separate special account (LOE, disposición adicional primera). And note the timing trap: since 1 January 2016 the guarantee obligation runs only 'desde la obtención de la licencia de edificación', so anything you hand over before the building licence is issued sits outside it. (€80,000 is illustrative only.)
entries.note: Wrong as written on two counts. It is not 'one piece of paper' — DA 1ª imposes both the guarantee and the special account, and the individual policy per buyer is a separate requirement (Dos.1.a). More importantly, the post-2016 guarantee starts at the building licence, not at signature — that is the single most consequential change from the old Ley 57/1968 regime and a headline promising 'demand one paper on day one' actively misleads a buyer paying a pre-licence reservation.

entries.assertion: What an owner receives when land is incorporated by a deslinde revision: the ex officio 75-year concession, no canon, existing uses respected under Ley 2/2013 — and what that concession does and does not permit (sale, inheritance, mortgage, works, renewal).
entries.source_required: Consolidated Ley 22/1988 de Costas, disposición transitoria primera and art. 66 (BOE); Ley 2/2013 artículo segundo (BOE)
entries.source_opened: Ley 22/1988, de Costas, texto consolidado, BOE-A-1988-18762 — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-1988-18762 (blocks primera, a66); Ley 2/2013, de 29 de mayo, texto consolidado, BOE-A-2013-5670 — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2013-5670 (block asegundo)
entries.locator: Ley 22/1988 DT 1ª.1: concession 'se otorgará por treinta años, prorrogables por otros treinta, respetando los usos y aprovechamientos existentes, sin obligación de abonar canon', and the holder 'deberá solicitar la correspondiente concesión en el plazo de un año'. DT 1ª.4 applies that same régimen where a new deslinde is carried out, the one-year clock running from approval of the deslinde. DT 1ª.2/1ª.3: registered owners protected by art. 34 LH caught by a deslinde get 30 years, again on application. DT 1ª.5 was struck down as unconstitutional by STC 233/2015. Ley 22/1988 art. 66.2: concessions 'en ningún caso podrá exceder de setenta y cinco años'. Ley 2/2013 art. segundo.1: prórroga granted 'a instancia de su titular', and applies to DT 1ª right-holders 'previa solicitud de la correspondiente concesión'; art. segundo.3: 'La duración de esta prórroga en ningún caso excederá de setenta y cinco años.'
entries.as_of: Ley 22/1988 DT 1ª version in force 11/12/2015; art. 66 version in force 31/05/2013; Ley 2/2013 art. segundo in force 31/05/2013; consulted 02/09/2026
entries.final_wording: What an owner receives when land is incorporated by a deslinde revision: not an automatic 75-year concession. Under disposición transitoria primera of Ley 22/1988 the owner becomes the holder of a right of occupation and must APPLY for the concession within one year of approval of the deslinde; the concession runs for thirty years, extendable by another thirty, free of canon, respecting existing uses and entries. Seventy-five years is the statutory ceiling on any concession (art. 66.2) and on the prórroga introduced by artículo segundo of Ley 2/2013, which is likewise granted only 'a instancia de su titular'. Then set out what the concession does and does not permit (sale, inheritance, mortgage, works, renewal), each against a cited provision.
entries.note: The phrase 'ex officio 75-year concession' is wrong twice over: nothing is granted ex officio — DT 1ª imposes a one-year application deadline and Ley 2/2013 art. segundo says 'a instancia de su titular' — and the base term is 30+30, with 75 being only the outer ceiling. An owner who reads 'automatic' and lets the year lapse loses the right. The 'no canon' and 'existing uses respected' limbs are correct for the DT 1ª.1/1ª.4 route. Note also DT 1ª.5 (added by Ley 2/2013) was annulled by STC 233/2015 — do not cite it.

entries.assertion: The servidumbre de protección — 100 metres as standard, 20 metres for land already classed urban when the 1988 law took effect — and what it actually restricts, since it touches far more Costa Blanca buyers than the DPMT itself.

DT 3ª.3: 'Los terrenos clasificados como suelo urbano a la entrada en vigor de la presente Ley estarán sujetos a las servidumbres establecidas en ella, con la salvedad de que la anchura de la servidumbre de protección será de 20 metros.'

entries.note: Both figures confirmed verbatim. Two qualifications to carry into the copy: art. 23.2 lets the State widen the strip by up to a further 100 metres (so up to 200), and art. 23.3 lets it narrow to 20 metres on tidal riverbanks; and disposición transitoria primera of Ley 2/2013 opened a two-year window (from 31/05/2013) for certain consolidated núcleos NOT classified urban in 1988 to obtain the 20-metre regime on application. entries.final_wording: Current €/m2 for the named coastal town and its named inland neighbour, from a dated source, stating which price it is — appraisal value (MIVAU valor tasado, or Tinsa), asking price (idealista), or registered transaction price — because these are different series and are routinely conflated. The official municipal series is MIVAU's 'Valor tasado medio de vivienda libre de los municipios mayores de 25.000 habitantes', quarterly, latest quarter provisional; it does not cover municipalities under 25,000 inhabitants, so for a small inland town no official municipal €/m² exists and the post must say so rather than substitute a regional average.

Second, and more practically, the official municipal series has a 25,000-inhabitant floor that excludes most of the inland towns this topic is about, so the instruction as written asks for a figure that in many cases does not exist. I did not open Tinsa, idealista or registradores.org, so I make no claim about their municipal coverage.

entries.assertion: The legal protection on off-plan stage payments under Ley 38/1999 as amended by Ley 20/2015: what a compliant guarantee/insurance must cover, when it must be in place, and the buyer's actual remedy on delay or non-delivery.
entries.source_required: Consolidated Ley 38/1999 (LOE), Disposición adicional primera
entries.source_opened: BOE, Ley 38/1999 de Ordenación de la Edificación, consolidated text, https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-1999-21567
entries.locator: LOE, Disposición adicional primera ('Percepción de cantidades a cuenta del precio durante la construcción'), introduced by Ley 20/2015 de 14 de julio, in force 1 January 2016, which also repealed Ley 57/1968. Required instrument: 'seguro de caución suscrito con entidades aseguradoras debidamente autorizadas' or 'aval solidario emitido por entidades de crédito'. Timing: 'desde la obtención de la licencia de edificación' and in force through delivery. Remedy: buyer may 'optar entre la rescisión del contrato con devolución de las cantidades entregadas a cuenta' plus statutory interest, or claim directly against insurer/guarantor after demanding repayment from the promoter and not obtaining it within thirty days.
entries.as_of: BOE consolidated text as consulted 2 September 2026
entries.final_wording: The legal protection on off-plan stage payments under Ley 38/1999 as amended by Ley 20/2015: what a compliant guarantee/insurance must cover, when it must be in place, and the buyer's actual remedy on delay or non-delivery.
entries.note: Citation is correct and unusually well-targeted — the common error is to cite Ley 57/1968, which Ley 20/2015 repealed with effect 1 January 2016. Two things the researcher must carry: the guarantee obligation bites from grant of the building licence (so pre-licence 'reservations' are the exposed part of the transaction), and Ley 57/1968 still governs contracts entered into before 1 January 2016.

entries.assertion: The Spanish tax-residence consequence of a trial year: the 183-day rule and what worldwide-income exposure it creates, plus Modelo 720 / asset-reporting obligations if residence is triggered.
entries.source_required: AEAT's current statement of the individual tax-residence test, and confirmation the Modelo 720 obligation subsists
entries.source_opened: AEAT, Manual de Tributación de No Residentes (julio 2026), cap. 1 'El contribuyente y la residencia' → 'La residencia de las personas físicas', https://sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es/Sede/ayuda/manuales-videos-folletos/manuales-practicos/manual-tributacion-no-residentes/capitulo-01-contribuyente-residencia/residencia-personas-fisicas.html ; AEAT, Modelo 720, https://sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es/Sede/procedimientoini/GI34.shtml
entries.locator: AEAT Manual, edition julio 2026: an individual is Spanish tax resident where they 'permanezca en España más de 183 días durante el año natural' (sporadic absences counted unless tax residence elsewhere is proved); or where the main base or centre of their economic activities or interests is in Spain, directly or indirectly; with a rebuttable presumption where the non-separated spouse and dependent minor children habitually reside in Spain. Residence attaches to the whole calendar year — a change of residence does not split the tax period. Modelo 720 remains a live AEAT procedure, with a separate Modelo 721 for virtual currencies held abroad (not required for 2022).
entries.as_of: AEAT manual edition July 2026; AEAT Modelo 720 procedure page as at 2 September 2026
entries.final_wording: The Spanish tax-residence consequence of a trial year: the 183-day rule and what worldwide-income exposure it creates, plus Modelo 720 / asset-reporting obligations if residence is triggered.
entries.note: Verified, with the trap that matters most for a 'trial year': Spanish tax residence is all-or-nothing for the whole calendar year, so a reader who crosses 183 days in October is treated as resident from 1 January of that year. Keep the five variables apart — triggering tax residence has nothing to do with holding a residence permit, and a person can be tax resident in Spain and in their home country simultaneously until a treaty tie-breaker resolves it. The €50,000 Modelo 720 threshold was not confirmed from the AEAT page I opened; confirm it before publishing a number. The penalty regime (not the obligation) was rewritten after CJEU C-788/19 by Ley 5/2022 — do not repeat the old sanction figures.

entries.assertion: The licence asymmetry that most comparisons miss: an apartment let to tourists in the Comunitat Valenciana needs the community of owners' express authorisation under state law — LPH art.
entries.source_required: Consolidated Ley 49/1960 de Propiedad Horizontal, art. 17.12

entries.locator: LPH art. 17.12, current wording: 'El acuerdo expreso por el que se apruebe, limite, condicione o prohíba el ejercicio de la actividad a que se refiere la letra e) del artículo 5 de la Ley 29/1994... requerirá el voto favorable de las tres quintas partes del total de los propietarios que, a su vez, representen las tres quintas partes de las cuotas de participación.' entries.final_wording: The licence asymmetry that most comparisons miss: since 3 April 2025 an apartment newly let to tourists needs an express community-of-owners agreement under state law — LPH art. 17.12 — while pre-existing tourist lets are not caught retroactively.
entries.note: The article and the requirement are confirmed against the BOE consolidated text. Two qualifications added. The reform is not retroactive to flats already carrying on the activity, which is the single most consequential point for a buyer looking at an existing rental apartment. And there is live doctrinal argument about whether art. 17.12 requires prior express approval to START the activity or only governs the majority needed when the community decides — the Valencian registration rules (entry 343) resolve it in practice for new registrations, but the copy should not overstate the state-law position as settled.

entries.assertion: How EU Regulation 650/2012 (Brussels IV) lets a foreign national elect their national law in a Spanish will, and what happens without one — including the post-Brexit position for UK nationals.
entries.source_required: Regulation (EU) 650/2012 itself — arts. 20, 21, 22 and the recital on UK participation
entries.source_opened: BOE (DOUE) text of Reglamento (UE) nº 650/2012 del Parlamento Europeo y del Consejo, de 4 de julio de 2012, https://www.boe.es/buscar/doc.php?id=DOUE-L-2012-81342
entries.locator: Art. 20 (aplicación universal): 'La ley designada por el presente Reglamento se aplicará aun cuando no sea la de un Estado miembro.' Art. 21(1): succession governed by the law of the State of the deceased's habitual residence at death; art. 21(2) exception for a manifestly closer connection. Art. 22(1): a person may choose the law of a State of their nationality, at the time of choosing or at death; multiple nationals may choose any of them. Recital 82: the United Kingdom and Ireland did not take part in the adoption of the Regulation and are not bound by it.
entries.as_of: Regulation as published in the OJ; consulted 2 September 2026
entries.final_wording: How EU Regulation 650/2012 (Brussels IV) lets a foreign national elect their national law in a Spanish will, and what happens without one — including the post-Brexit position for UK nationals.
entries.note: Verified, and the post-Brexit point has a counterintuitive answer worth stating plainly: because art. 20 gives the Regulation universal application, a Spanish notary or court applies it to a UK national's estate regardless of Brexit, and a UK national can still elect the law of their nationality under art. 22. The UK was never bound by the Regulation — it opted out at adoption (recital 82) — so Brexit changed nothing here. Without a choice, art. 21 sends the succession to the law of habitual residence at death, which for a retired reader living on the coast usually means Spanish law and Spanish forced heirship. Note also that 'UK law' is not one law: England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland are separate legal units for this purpose.

entries.assertion: The real cost of the company route for a single holiday home: corporate compliance and accounts, the benefit-in-kind/market-rent treatment of the owners' own use, loss of individual reliefs, the special 3% levy on entities resident in listed low-tax jurisdictions, and the extraction cost of getting money back out — and, honestly, the narrow cases where a company still wins.
entries.source_required: AEAT's statement of the Gravamen Especial sobre Bienes Inmuebles de Entidades no Residentes
entries.source_opened: AEAT, Manual de Tributación de No Residentes (julio 2026), cap. 6 'Gravamen especial sobre bienes inmuebles de entidades no residentes', https://sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es/Sede/ayuda/manuales-videos-folletos/manuales-practicos/manual-tributacion-no-residentes/capitulo-06-gravamen-especial-sobre-nr.html
entries.locator: AEAT Manual, edition julio 2026 (page updated 21 July 2026), cap. 6: applies to entities 'residentes en un país o territorio que tenga la consideración de paraíso fiscal', a reference which since 11 July 2021 is read as meaning a jurisdicción no cooperativa; rate 3%; taxable base normally the cadastral value; accrues 31 December each year; filed in January following accrual (1-25 January for direct-debit payment); Modelo 213; deductible as an expense for IRNR purposes. Exemptions: foreign States and public institutions, international organisations, entities carrying on a continuous or habitual differentiated economic activity in Spain beyond mere ownership or letting, and entities listed on recognised secondary securities markets.
entries.as_of: AEAT manual edition July 2026, page updated 21 July 2026
entries.final_wording: The real cost of the company route for a single holiday home: corporate compliance and accounts, the benefit-in-kind/market-rent treatment of the owners' own use, loss of individual reliefs, the special 3% levy under arts. 40-45 TRLIRNR on entities resident in a jurisdicción no cooperativa (declared on Modelo 213, 3% of cadastral value, accruing 31 December and filed the following January, with exemptions including entities carrying on a real economic activity in Spain and listed companies), and the extraction cost of getting money back out — and, honestly, the narrow cases where a company still wins.
entries.note: The 3% figure is right; the trigger described is not. It is not 'listed low-tax jurisdictions' — it is Spain's list of jurisdicciones no cooperativas, the successor concept to paraíso fiscal since 11 July 2021, and a jurisdiction can be low-tax without being on it (and on it without being low-tax). Getting this wrong in either direction is expensive: it tells a Luxembourg or Malta structure it owes a levy it does not, or tells a listed-jurisdiction structure it is clear when it is not. The exemption for entities with a real Spanish economic activity is also material and was missing.

Applies to imputed income for tax year 2026 onwards (so 2026 income is filed from 1 April 2027); 2025 imputed income keeps the old window (1 January - 31 December 2026). entries.final_wording: How the ownership split between spouses flows into annual non-resident obligations (Modelo 210 — each co-owner declares their own share, imputed income) and into the future Spanish succession-tax calculation. Note the deadline change under Orden HAC/623/2026: imputed income for 2026 onwards is filed from 1 April to 31 December of the following year, so 2026 imputed income is declared from 1 April 2027; imputed income for 2025 kept the old 1 January - 31 December window.
entries.note: The substance holds — Modelo 210 is the right form, imputed income the right head, and each co-owner is taxed on their own share — but the timing is in motion and the instruction as written carries none of it. What expires: the pre-2026 filing calendar. From 2026 accruals the window opens 1 April of the following year, and the rental-income grouping rules shifted separately in 2024. I could not open a primary source for the exact 'one self-assessment per owner per property' rule (that sits in the Modelo 210 order's agrupación conditions, which I did not read), so state the per-owner point but check the per-property filing mechanics before asserting it.

entries.source_opened: Generalitat Valenciana, consolidated Ley 13/1997 ('Texto actualizado a 11 de agosto de 2026'), https://hisenda.gva.es/documents/168162620/169398267/Ley+13_1997+a+4+de+marzo+de+2026.pdf ; BOE, Ley 29/1987 del Impuesto sobre Sucesiones y Donaciones, consolidated PDF, https://www.boe.es/buscar/pdf/1987/BOE-A-1987-28141-consolidado.pdf
entries.locator: Ley 13/1997 art. 12 bis 'Bonificaciones en la cuota': 99% for mortis causa acquisitions by Group I and II relatives; 99% for inter vivos acquisitions by spouse, parents/adopters, children/adopted, grandchildren and grandparents; 99% for acquirers with disability ≥65% (or recognised permanent intellectual/mental disability ≥33%), which excludes the (a) and (b) bonuses; 25% for Group III second- and third-degree blood collaterals, mortis causa and inter vivos. Conditions: assets fully declared in a return filed in the voluntary period or without prior administrative requerimiento; inter vivos requires a public document, and for cash/securities gifts the origin of funds must be evidenced and the means of delivery identified. Footnote 55: current wording given by art. 22 of Ley 5/2026 de 31 de julio; art. 25 of that law amends DF 4ª of Ley 5/2025 to give a new wording with effect from 1 June 2027. Ley 29/1987 DA 2ª (consolidated, last modification 28 December 2022): non-resident taxpayers are entitled to apply the rules of the relevant Comunidad Autónoma — mortis causa where the deceased was non-resident (CA with the greatest value of the estate situated in Spain), mortis causa where the deceased was resident in a CA, and inter vivos gifts of Spanish immovable property (CA where the property lies). No EU/EEA limitation appears in the current text.
entries.as_of: Ley 13/1997 consolidated to 11 August 2026; Ley 29/1987 consolidated to 28 December 2022
entries.final_wording: The current Comunitat Valenciana inheritance and gift tax reliefs and their conditions in 2026 — 99% bonificación for Groups I and II mortis causa and for spouse/parents/children/grandchildren/grandparents inter vivos, 99% for acquirers with ≥65% disability, and 25% for Group III blood collaterals, all conditional on full declaration and (inter vivos) on a public deed and evidenced source of funds — including how they apply to non-residents, who under DA 2ª of Ley 29/1987 may apply the autonomous community's rules with no EU/EEA restriction. Re-check before publishing: art. 12 bis has a further wording taking effect on 1 June 2027.
entries.note: TIME-SENSITIVE because the current art. 12 bis wording comes from Ley 5/2026 of 31 July and a further wording bites on 1 June 2027 (art. 25 Ley 5/2026 amending DF 4ª Ley 5/2025) — anything written now needs a dated 'as at' and a diary note. Two corrections to what circulates: the Group III bonus is 25% in the text in force now, not a future promise; and the non-resident point is broader than usually stated — since the post-Ley 11/2021 wording, DA 2ª extends CA rules to non-residents generally, not only EU/EEA residents. Do not describe non-resident access as an EU-only benefit.

entries.assertion: You can pay cash — is there a case where a non-resident is still better off taking a Spanish mortgage?
entries.source_required: Primary Spanish tax law establishing whether a mortgage changes a non-resident's Spanish tax base at all

entries.final_wording: You can pay cash — is there a case where a non-resident is still better off taking a Spanish mortgage?
entries.note: The premise is legally real, not rhetorical: art. 9.Cuatro Ley 19/1991 makes a debt applied to acquiring the Spanish property deductible for a non-resident, so a mortgage can genuinely change the wealth-tax base. Do not let the piece imply a general cash-vs-mortgage rule.

entries.assertion: Whether mortgage interest is deductible against Spanish rental income, and the EU/EEA vs non-EU asymmetry (19% with deductible expenses vs 24% with none) that decides it.
entries.source_required: Consolidated TRLIRNR arts. 24.6 and 25.1.a, plus AEAT's own statement of practice
entries.source_opened: BOE consolidated RDLeg 5/2004 TRLIRNR — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2004-4527 ; AEAT sede, 'Rendimientos de inmuebles arrendados' — https://sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es/Sede/no-residentes/irnr-sin-establecimiento-permanente/cuestiones-especificas-sobre-tributacion-inmuebles/rendimientos-inmuebles-arrendados.html
entries.locator: TRLIRNR art. 24.6.1ª.a (EU residents may deduct LIRPF expenses directly and inseparably linked to the Spanish income; final paragraph extends this to EEA States with effective exchange of tax information); art. 25.1.a (general 24%, reduced to 19% for residents of another EU or EEA State with effective exchange of information). AEAT page updated 26-09-2024, listing 'UE, Islandia, Noruega y Liechtenstein: 19%; resto: 24%'
entries.as_of: BOE consolidated text in force at 2026-09-01; AEAT page updated 26-09-2024
entries.final_wording: Whether mortgage interest is deductible against Spanish rental income, and the EU/EEA vs non-EU/EEA asymmetry (19% with deductible expenses vs 24% with none) that decides it.
entries.note: Substance is right; the wording is not. Written as 'EU/EEA vs non-EU' it invites the exact error this ledger keeps catching: Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein sit on the 19%-with-deductions side, not the 24% side. The legal test is 'EU or EEA State with an effective exchange of tax information', not EU membership. The UK is on the 24%, no-deductions side since Brexit — which is what actually kills mortgage-interest relief for the typical British Costa Blanca landlord.

entries.final_wording: The Comunitat Valenciana tourist-let regime as it actually stands in 2026 (Ley 15/2018 as amended by Decreto-ley 9/2024): municipal urbanistic compatibility report, registration validity period (five years), whole-dwelling-only rule, and the requirement to declare the periods of the year the property is marketed — plus, from national law and not from the Valencian regime, the community-of-owners requirement in art. 17.12 LPH (express three-fifths agreement, applying since 3 April 2025).
entries.note: Four of the five elements are correctly attributed to the Valencian regime and were confirmed article by article. The fifth is misattributed: Decreto-ley 9/2024 does not require an authorisation from the community — it requires a certificación registral showing the estatutos do not prohibit non-residential use. The express three-fifths community approval for tourist lets comes from LPH art. 17.12 as rewritten by LO 1/2025, in force 3 April 2025 — national, not Valencian. Mixing the two will produce a wrong answer for any reader outside the Comunitat. Also note the decree-law is of 2 August 2024, not 5 August.

entries.assertion: The notary's statutory duties at a compraventa under the Ley del Notariado / Reglamento Notarial and current practice: identity and capacity, real-time Land Registry check (nota simple / registry telematic enquiry), warning of charges and encumbrances, cadastral reference, energy certificate, community-fee certificate, mortgage transparency (Ley 5/2019), and the non-resident seller 3% retention —
entries.source_required: Reglamento Notarial, Ley de Propiedad Horizontal, Ley 5/2019 and TRLIRNR — the several statutes that actually impose these duties
entries.source_opened: BOE consolidated Reglamento Notarial (Decreto de 2 de junio de 1944) — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-1944-6578 ; BOE consolidated Ley 49/1960 LPH — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-1960-10906 ; BOE consolidated Ley 5/2019 — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2019-3814 ; BOE consolidated RDLeg 5/2004 TRLIRNR — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2004-4527
entries.locator: Reglamento Notarial art. 175.1–175.3 (before authorising a purchase deed the notary must verify title and charges, telematically, at the moment closest to authorisation, incorporating the result into the matriz); LPH art. 9.1.e (transmitting owner must produce a certificación on the state of debts with the community, 'sin la cual no podrá autorizarse el otorgamiento del documento público', unless expressly waived by the buyer); Ley 5/2019 arts. 14.1 and 15 (ten calendar days' documentation, free acta notarial previa, deed cannot be authorised without it); TRLIRNR art. 25.2 ('el adquirente estará obligado a retener e ingresar el 3 por ciento')
entries.as_of: BOE consolidated texts in force at 2026-09-01
entries.final_wording: The duties triggered at a compraventa and where each one comes from: identity and capacity, and the real-time telematic Land Registry check of title and charges, under the Reglamento Notarial (art. 175); the community-fee certificate under art. 9.1.e LPH; mortgage transparency under Ley 5/2019 (arts. 14–15); the cadastral reference and energy certificate under their own cadastral and building-certification rules; and the 3% retention on a non-resident seller, which is the buyer's legal obligation under art. 25.2 TRLIRNR, not a notarial duty.
entries.note: Two real defects. First, the list is attributed to 'the Ley del Notariado / Reglamento Notarial', but only identity, capacity and the registry check come from there — the community-fee certificate is LPH art. 9.1.e, mortgage transparency is Ley 5/2019, and the cadastral reference and energy certificate rest on separate cadastral and building rules. Second and more serious: the 3% retention is imposed by art. 25.2 TRLIRNR on the ACQUIRER, who must withhold and pay it. Listing it among the notary's duties will teach buyers that someone else handles it — the single most expensive misunderstanding on this list.

entries.final_wording: What a buyer's independent abogado does that the notary does not: pre-contract due diligence, planning and licence-of-first-occupation checks, ITE/building condition, boundary and unregistered-extension checks, negotiating the arras contract, debt searches beyond what the seller declares

And each listed check rests on its own rule (in the Comunitat Valenciana, second-occupation licensing sits under Decreto 12/2021, which Ley 5/2025 did not repeal); none of those individual rules was opened here.

entries.assertion: You still only get 90 days.
entries.source_required: Consolidated Schengen Borders Code, Regulation (EU) 2016/399, art. 6
entries.source_opened: EUR-Lex, Regulation (EU) 2016/399 (Schengen Borders Code), consolidated — https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/399/2024-07-10/eng
entries.locator: Art. 6(1): entry conditions apply 'for intended stays on the territory of the Member States of a duration of no more than 90 days in any 180-day period, which entails considering the 180-day period preceding each day of stay'
entries.as_of: Consolidated version 10-07-2024, in force at 2026-09-01
entries.final_wording: You still only get 90 days in any 180-day period.
entries.note: '90 days' with no window attached is precisely the misreading this topic exists to fix — readers take it as 90 days per year, per trip, or per country. The Code never states a bare 90 days; the limit is inseparable from the rolling 180-day look-back. A headline that drops the window teaches the error in the same breath as promising to correct it.

entries.source_opened: EUR-Lex, Regulation (EU) 2016/399 consolidated — https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/399/2024-07-10/eng ; European Commission EES page — https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/news/entryexit-system-ees-fully-operational-2026-04-10_en

entries.assertion: The consequences of overstaying: entry refusal, Schengen-wide ban, and how an automated exit record changes enforcement
entries.source_required: Consolidated LO 4/2000 on the infringement and its sanctions, plus the Schengen Borders Code on entry refusal
entries.source_opened: BOE consolidated LO 4/2000 (LOEx) — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2000-544 ; EUR-Lex, Regulation (EU) 2016/399 consolidated — https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/399/2024-07-10/eng ; European Commission EES page — https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/news/entryexit-system-ees-fully-operational-2026-04-10_en
entries.locator: LOEx art. 53.1.a (being irregularly in Spanish territory is a serious infringement); art. 58.1 ('La expulsión llevará consigo la prohibición de entrada en territorio español... no excederá de cinco años'); art. 58.2 second paragraph (no ban, or ban revoked, where the person leaves during the procedure or within the voluntary-departure period); SBC art. 6(1)(d) (entry refused to persons subject to an SIS alert); EES fully operational 10-04-2026
entries.as_of: BOE consolidated text in force at 2026-09-01; EES fully operational 10-04-2026
entries.final_wording: The consequences of overstaying: entry refusal, Schengen-wide ban, and how an automated exit record changes enforcement
entries.note: Verified, with two precisions the copy must carry. The ban under art. 58.1 is formally a ban on entry to Spain, up to five years; it becomes Schengen-wide in practice through the SIS alert that art. 6(1)(d) SBC makes a ground for refusal at any external border — say it that way rather than calling it a 'Schengen ban' outright. And an ordinary overstay is a serious infringement that is far more often sanctioned by a fine than by expulsion, and art. 58.2 lets the ban be withheld or revoked where the person leaves voluntarily. Do not write it as automatic exclusion.

entries.assertion: Nothing happens in Spain without an NIE — not the purchase, not a bank account, not a utility bill.
entries.source_required: Consolidated RD 1065/2007 on the tax identification number and its use with credit institutions
entries.source_opened: BOE consolidated RD 1065/2007 — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2007-15984 (articles retrieved via the BOE consolidated-legislation API) ; BOE consolidated Ley Hipotecaria — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-1946-2453
entries.locator: RD 1065/2007 art. 20.1 (for foreigners the NIF is the NIE) and art. 20.2 (those without a NIE must be assigned an 'M' NIF by the tax administration); art. 28.3 ('Podrá constituirse un depósito o abrirse una cuenta en una entidad de crédito sin acreditar el número de identificación fiscal en el momento de la constitución', with 15 days to supply it and no movements meanwhile); art. 28.7 (accounts of persons who have accredited non-residence are excepted from the identification regime); art. 27.2.c (NIF required in notarial acts on real property); Ley Hipotecaria art. 254.2 (no inscription without all NIFs)
entries.as_of: BOE consolidated texts in force at 2026-09-01
entries.final_wording: Almost nothing in a Spanish purchase happens without a Spanish tax number. The escritura and the Land Registry inscription both require a NIF — which for a foreign buyer is normally the NIE. But a bank account can legally be opened before the number is produced, and an accredited non-resident's account is exempt from the requirement altogether.
entries.note: Wrong as written, and wrong in the way the topic itself warns about. Art. 28.3 RD 1065/2007 expressly permits opening an account without producing the number, with 15 days to supply it, and art. 28.7 exempts accounts of accredited non-residents from the regime entirely. The utility-bill claim has no statutory basis at all and was not sourced. The purchase claim is right in substance but wrong in name: what the escritura (art. 27.2.c) and the registry (art. 254.2 LH) demand is a NIF, which for a foreigner is normally but not necessarily the NIE — art. 20.2 provides for an 'M' number instead.

entries.final_wording: Do not say the NIE 'expires' or 'must be renewed' without checking what actually has a validity date — the number or the certificate
entries.note: The distinction the instruction insists on is exactly the one the Reglamento draws. The number itself is personal, unique and permanent, and RD 1155/2024 sets no expiry on it or on the certificate of assignment. What does expire is the tarjeta de identidad de extranjero (art. 209) — and, separately, any certificado de no residencia a bank chooses to treat as time-limited by its own policy. Never write 'renew your NIE'.

entries.final_wording: 1454 CC versus confirmatorias o penales, because the consequences of walking away differ, escritura pública, Land Registry inscription
entries.note: The citation and the three-way distinction are right, with one thing the copy must not get wrong. Only the penitenciales are codified — 'arras' appears once in the whole Code, in art. 1454; confirmatorias and penales are case-law categories with no article to cite, and the courts do not presume arras to be penitenciales, so the contract must say so expressly. Separately: ownership passes on the escritura under arts. 609 and 1462 CC, not on inscription. Registry inscription protects against third parties; it does not make you the owner. Do not let the sequence imply otherwise.

entries.assertion: Whether an agency commission, plusvalía municipal, or the 3% non-resident retention lands on the buyer or the seller
entries.source_required: TRLIRNR (RDLeg 5/2004) art. 25.2 via Agencia Tributaria; TRLRHL (RDLeg 2/2004) art. 106 for IIVTNU sujeto pasivo
entries.source_opened: Agencia Tributaria, Sede — 'Retención del adquirente de un inmueble' (IRNR sin establecimiento permanente), https://sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es/Sede/no-residentes/irnr-sin-establecimiento-permanente/retenciones-irnr-sin-establecimiento-permanente/retencion-adquirente-inmueble.html ; secondary confirmation of TRLRHL art. 106 via Iberley 'Sujeto pasivo (IIVTNU)', https://www.iberley.es/temas/sujeto-pasivo-iivtnu-impuesto-plusvalia-26461
entries.locator: TRLIRNR art. 25.2 (3% retención, Modelo 211, one month from the deed); TRLRHL art. 106.1.b) (transmitente is contribuyente in onerous transfers) and art. 106.2 (buyer is sustituto del contribuyente where the transferor is a non-resident individual)
entries.final_wording: Whether an agency commission, plusvalía municipal, or the 3% non-resident retention lands on the buyer or the seller
entries.note: The question is correctly framed and all three items are real, but the binary 'buyer or seller' collapses two cases the generated answer must keep apart. (1) The 3% is legally the BUYER's obligation to withhold and pay (Modelo 211, one month) but is a payment on account of the SELLER's IRNR — cost falls on the seller, duty on the buyer. (2) Plusvalía: the seller is the taxpayer in an onerous sale, EXCEPT that where the seller is a non-resident individual the BUYER becomes sustituto del contribuyente and the town hall can claim it from the buyer (TRLRHL art. 106.2) — which is precisely the Costa Blanca fact pattern. Agency commission has no statutory allocation; it is contractual and customarily the seller's, so it must not be stated as a legal rule.

entries.assertion: Do not describe the count as a rolling 180-day window — that is the Schengen rule, a completely different regime, and fusing the two is the classic error in this topic
entries.source_required: Regulation (EU) 2016/399 (Schengen Borders Code) art. 6(1), consolidated
entries.source_opened: Regulation (EU) 2016/399, consolidated version 02016R0399-20240710, EUR-Lex, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02016R0399-20240710 (text reached via search extract of art. 6(1) and the 90/180 calculation rule)
entries.locator: Art. 6(1): stays of no more than 90 days in any 180-day period, 'which entails considering the 180-day period preceding each day of stay'; entry and exit dates counted as days of stay
entries.final_wording: Do not describe the count as a rolling 180-day window — the Schengen short-stay rule is 90 days in any 180-day period (art. 6(1), Regulation (EU) 2016/399), a completely different regime that applies only to third-country nationals, and fusing it with the 183-day tax test is the classic error in this topic
entries.note: The warning is right in substance but names the rule loosely. The Schengen limit is 90 days within a rolling 180-day period — the 180 days is the window, not the allowance — so 'a rolling 180-day window' on its own reads as a 180-day entitlement and would itself seed the error the caution is trying to prevent. Two further points the corrected wording carries: the rule binds third-country nationals only, so it does not apply to EU citizens or to Norwegian, Icelandic and Liechtenstein nationals (EEA), who are a recurring Costa Blanca buyer group; and the 90/180 count is an immigration limit that has no bearing on the 183-day tax test in art. 9 LIRPF, which is a calendar-year count.

entries.note: The framing is correct: the reform is a 2025 one (LO 1/2025, effective 3 April 2025), and it is the right question to ask because the answer — approve, limit, condition or prohibit, by a three-fifths double majority — is more than a simple veto. The second half is a genuinely live question with no single answer: municipal moratoria on new tourist-use licences are set by each ayuntamiento's planning instruments and change, so it must be answered per municipality and dated, never generalised to 'the Costa Blanca'. Note the community's power under art. 17.12 is separate from, and additional to, the Valencian licensing regime and the municipal compatibility report — a property can clear one and fail the other.

entries.note: Confirmed on every element, and the answer to the question posed is BOTH: the same three-fifths double majority can approve, limit, condition or prohibit. The double majority is the point most often garbled — it is three-fifths of owners AND three-fifths of participation quotas, not either alone. The activity caught is the one defined by cross-reference to art. 5.e) LAU, so the community's power tracks that statutory definition rather than any looser notion of 'holiday letting'.

entries.assertion: The Comunitat Valenciana regime for viviendas de uso turístico: current decree, the compulsory registration number, the requirement for a municipal compatibility certificate, and any minimum-period or ground-floor-access conditions
entries.source_required: Generalitat Valenciana tourism legislation (Ley 15/2018, Decreto 10/2021, Decreto-ley 9/2024) and the GVA Turisme VUT page
entries.source_opened: BOE/DOGV — Decreto-ley 9/2024, de 2 de agosto, del Consell, de modificación de la normativa reguladora de las viviendas de uso turístico, https://www.boe.es/buscar/doc.php?id=DOGV-r-2024-90168 ; Generalitat Valenciana, Turisme — Viviendas de uso turístico, https://cindi.gva.es/es/web/turisme/habitatges-dus-turistic
entries.locator: Ley 15/2018, de 7 de junio (turismo, ocio y hospitalidad) as amended by Decreto-ley 9/2024, de 2 de agosto (in force 8 August 2024); Decreto 10/2021, de 22 de enero (reglamento de alojamiento turístico); VUT defined by letting for tourist purposes for 10 days or less computed continuously to the same tenant; registration number compulsory in all advertising; favourable municipal informe/certificado de compatibilidad urbanística (ICUS) required; five-year validity with renewal declaration one month before expiry; community certification that the statutes do not prohibit tourist use
entries.final_wording: The Comunitat Valenciana regime for viviendas de uso turístico: current decree, the compulsory registration number, the requirement for a municipal urban compatibility report (ICUS), the five-year validity and renewal of the registration, the MAXIMUM stay per tenant that defines a VUT, and any ground-floor or independent-access conditions
entries.note: Corrected on one substantive point: the Valencian rule is a MAXIMUM, not a minimum. A dwelling is a vivienda de uso turístico when let for tourist purposes for 10 days or less computed continuously to the same tenant — asking for the 'minimum-period' condition would push the generator toward the opposite of the actual rule and toward the minimum-stay rules that exist in other Spanish regions. Two other gaps closed: the registration has a five-year validity with a renewal declaration due one month before expiry (miss it and the entry is cancelled), and the community-of-owners certification that the statutes do not prohibit tourist use is now part of the file — which is where this topic meets art. 17.12 LPH. The correct instrument names are Ley 15/2018 as amended by Decreto-ley 9/2024 (in force 8 August 2024), with Decreto 10/2021 as the reglamento — 'current decree' in the singular invites citing only one of three. Ground-floor and independent-access conditions do exist (restrictions on ground-floor units that cannot meet building standards, and a prohibition on street-level key boxes), so that limb of the question is well aimed.

entries.assertion: The Registro Único de Arrendamientos (Real Decreto 1312/2024) and the mandatory rental registration number for advertising on platforms — confirm what is in force at the publication date
entries.source_required: BOE consolidated Real Decreto 1312/2024 with its post-publication annulment notes, and the Tribunal Supremo judgments annulling it
entries.source_opened: BOE consolidated Real Decreto 1312/2024, de 23 de diciembre, https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2024-26931 (NOTAS / referencias posteriores read); Notarios y Registradores, 'El Tribunal Supremo anula parcialmente el Real Decreto que regula el Registro Único de Arrendamientos', https://www.notariosyregistradores.com/web/participa/noticias/el-ts-anula-registro-arrendamientos-corta-duracion/
entries.locator: BOE-A-2024-26931 consolidated notes: arts. 1 (in the part referring to the development of the registration procedure), 2.f), 2.i), 5, 8, 9, 10, 12.b), 12.c) and disposición adicional segunda annulled by STS (Sala Tercera) de 19 de mayo de 2026 (BOE-A-2026-12300), de 21 de mayo de 2026 (BOE-A-2026-13893) and de 1 de junio de 2026 (BOE-A-2026-15677); STS 620/2026 of 19 May 2026 published in BOE 8 June 2026
entries.final_wording: The Registro Único de Arrendamientos created by Real Decreto 1312/2024 was largely annulled by the Tribunal Supremo (Sala Tercera) in judgments of 19 and 21 May and 1 June 2026 — the State was held to lack competence to create it — so the national registration number (NRUA) is no longer required for advertising a short-term let on a platform; the Ventanilla Única Digital de Arrendamientos and the obligations flowing from Regulation (EU) 2024/1028 survive, and the Comunitat Valenciana's own tourism registration number continues to apply. Confirm the position again at the publication date.
entries.note: This is the largest correction in the slice. As written, the instruction points a generator at a national registration requirement that no longer exists: the BOE consolidated text of RD 1312/2024 carries annulment notes striking arts. 1 (in part), 2.f), 2.i), 5, 8, 9, 10, 12.b), 12.c) and DA 2ª. The challenge was brought by the Generalitat Valenciana and succeeded on competence grounds, which makes this doubly relevant to Costa Blanca content. What survives matters as much as what fell: the digital single window and the EU data-sharing regime remain, and the regional Valencian registration number is unaffected — so a buyer still needs a registration number, just not the state one. Content that says 'you need an NRUA to advertise' is now wrong; content that says 'no registration number is needed' is also wrong. The instruction's own closing caution ('confirm what is in force at the publication date') was well judged and is exactly what caught this.

entries.final_wording: The current Colegio de Registradores quarterly figure for the foreign-buyer share in Alicante province, with the exact quarter and the national comparison — and re-verify it at generation time rather than reusing a cached number
entries.note: The instruction is correct and the series it names is the right one: the Estadística Registral Inmobiliaria is published quarterly by the Colegio de Registradores with a provincial breakdown of the foreign-buyer share, and it is a registration-based transaction series — not asking prices, not searches, not survey data. Marked TIME-SENSITIVE because the figure is re-published every quarter and the instruction's own 're-verify at generation time' is therefore load-bearing, not optional. Evidence caveat: the most recent value I could reach — Alicante 44.65% vs Spain 13.92% for Q1 2026 — comes from a press report of the ERI, not from the ERI PDF, which I could not text-extract. Treat that pair as a lead requiring confirmation in the Registradores release itself, and always publish it with the quarter attached; a bare '44.65% of buyers are foreign' with no quarter will be wrong within months. Note also that the ERI counts foreign buyers, which includes foreign residents in Spain, not only non-resident overseas purchasers.

entries.source_required: Publisher documentation for each named series showing what it measures (index vs €/m², appraisal vs transaction, official vs private)
entries.source_opened: INE — Nota de prensa, Índice de Precios de Vivienda (IPV), Base 2025, primer trimestre 2026, https://www.ine.es/dyngs/Prensa/IPV1T26.htm ; INE IPV product page, https://www.ine.es/dyngs/INEbase/es/operacion.htm?c=Estadistica_C&cid=1254736152838&idp=1254735976607&menu=ultiDatos ; Tinsa, https://www.tinsa.es/precio-vivienda/
entries.locator: INE IPV Q1 2026, base year changed to 2025 from Q1 2026; annual variation 12.9%, quarterly 3.5% — an index of transaction prices, published as index numbers, not €/m². Tinsa is a private appraisal company. MIVAU publishes €/m² from appraisal values.
entries.final_wording: Actual price data for Alicante — naming the publisher and the kind of series in every case: INE's Índice de Precios de Vivienda (a transaction-price INDEX, rebased to 2025 from Q1 2026, not €/m²), MIVAU (Ministerio de Vivienda y Agenda Urbana) €/m² from APPRAISAL values, the Colegio de Registradores' registration-based series, the Consejo General del Notariado's Portal Estadístico (which reaches postcode level), or Tinsa (a PRIVATE appraiser, not an official statistic) — rather than inferring price effects from the buyer-share number
entries.note: Corrected on two counts. First, the ministry has been the Ministerio de Vivienda y Agenda Urbana (MIVAU) since 2023 — 'Ministerio de Vivienda' alone risks the generator citing a body under a stale name or confusing it with the older Ministerio de Fomento/Transportes series. Second and more seriously, the instruction lists four publishers as if they were interchangeable '€/m² series for Alicante', and they are not the same measurement: INE's IPV is an index (and was rebased to 2025 with effect from Q1 2026, so index levels are not comparable across the break), MIVAU's €/m² comes from appraisal values, Registradores' comes from inscribed transactions, and Tinsa is a private appraisal firm whose output is a commercial product, not official statistics. Quoting a Tinsa or appraisal €/m² alongside an INE percentage change as if they described the same thing is exactly the conflation the rest of this topic is trying to prevent. Worth adding the Consejo General del Notariado's Portal Estadístico, which reaches postcode and custom-drawn areas — finer geography than any of the four named, and the right tool for a specific Costa Blanca urbanisation. The instruction's core point — do not infer price movement from a buyer-share number — is correct and should be kept.

entries.locator: Art. 25.1.a TRLIRNR (current version: Ley 26/2014, BOE-A-2014-12327, in force 1 Jan 2015): 'Con carácter general el 24 por 100. No obstante, el tipo de gravamen será el 19 por ciento cuando se trate de contribuyentes residentes en otro Estado miembro de la Unión Europea o del Espacio Económico Europeo con el que exista un efectivo intercambio de información tributaria'. Art. 24.6 (added by Ley 2/2010, amended by Ley 26/2014): net-basis expense deduction available to contribuyentes resident in another EU Member State, extended to EEA states with effective exchange of information. Case-law limb: Audiencia Nacional judgment reported as 28 July 2025 — no sala/sección, recurso number or ECLI obtained, and not final (open to casación).
entries.as_of: 2026-09-01 (statute); case law as reported to 2025-07-28
entries.final_wording: The statutory position is settled and was last amended in 2015: art. 25.1.a TRLIRNR charges 24% generally and 19% where the OWNER IS TAX-RESIDENT in another EU/EEA state with effective exchange of tax information; art. 24.6 allows deduction of real letting expenses (net basis) only to those same EU/EEA-resident taxpayers. What is moving is the case law: an Audiencia Nacional judgment reported as of 28 July 2025 held that denying expense deduction to third-country residents breaches free movement of capital (art. 63 TFEU). That judgment is NOT final, creates no binding jurisprudencia on its own, and its sala/sección and ECLI must be obtained before it is cited. No confirmed challenge to the 24% rate itself was found. Re-check at generation time.
entries.note: Rates and the deduction rule verified against the BOE consolidated text. The case-law limb is a lead only — I could not open the judgment, and a law-firm page is not proof. Do not tell a reader they 'can' deduct expenses as a non-EU owner; at most, that a first-instance line of authority exists and a refund claim is arguable.

entries.assertion: Whether the property can legally be let at all after the 2025 community-vote reform and the regional licensing regime
entries.source_required: Consolidated Ley 49/1960 (LPH) at BOE for the community-vote reform; the Valencian tourist-letting decree-law for the licensing regime

Valencian limb: Decreto-ley 9/2024, de 2 de agosto, del Consell (DOGV nº 9910, 7 Aug 2024, in force 8 Aug 2024), amending Ley 15/2018 and Decreto 10/2021 — favourable municipal informe de compatibilidad urbanística required before registration, registration in the Registro de Turismo valid five years, evidence that the community does not prohibit tourist use.

entries.final_wording: Whether the property can legally be let at all after the 2025 community-vote reform (LPH art. 17.12 as amended with effect from 3 April 2025 by DF 4.2 of Ley Orgánica 1/2025 — three-fifths of owners AND three-fifths of quotas, expressly non-retroactive) and the Valencian licensing regime (Decreto-ley 9/2024, in force 8 August 2024: favourable municipal urban-compatibility report, five-year registration in the Registro de Turismo, proof the community does not prohibit the use)
entries.note: Both limbs verified in the consolidated text. Two traps for copy: (1) the reform is expressly non-retroactive, so an existing, lawfully established tourist let is not killed by a later 3/5 vote — do not tell readers otherwise; (2) the community vote and the Valencian licence are cumulative, not alternatives. Note also that LPH art. 17 was further touched by RDL 7/2026 (20 Mar 2026), but that change is to paragraph 1, not 12.

entries.assertion: Do not state the 24%-on-gross rule as settled current practice for UK owners without checking the deduction case law first
entries.source_required: Consolidated TRLIRNR arts. 24.6 and 25.1.a plus the current status of the deduction litigation
entries.source_opened: BOE, texto consolidado del TRLIRNR — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2004-4527 (arts. 24, 25 via BOE legislación-consolidada API)
entries.locator: Art. 25.1.a (Ley 26/2014, in force 1 Jan 2015): 24% general, 19% for EU/EEA-with-exchange-of-information residents. Art. 24.6 (Ley 2/2010 as amended by Ley 26/2014): expense deduction confined to those same EU/EEA residents.
entries.final_wording: Do not state the 24%-on-gross rule as settled current practice for UK owners without checking the deduction case law first
entries.note: Sound and well-aimed. The statute is unambiguous — a UK tax resident is outside art. 24.6 and is taxed on gross at 24% — but a live, non-final line of authority (see id 420) argues that exclusion breaches art. 63 TFEU. So 'settled current practice' is exactly the wrong register. Say what the statute says, then say the point is being litigated and not finally resolved.

entries.assertion: Do not imply the reader's Dutch, Belgian or German client faces the same rate as a British one — EU/EEA versus non-EU changes the answer
entries.source_required: Consolidated TRLIRNR art. 25.1.a, read for the exact connecting factor it uses
entries.source_opened: BOE, texto consolidado del TRLIRNR — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2004-4527 (art. 25 via BOE legislación-consolidada API)
entries.locator: Art. 25.1.a TRLIRNR: the 19% rate applies to 'contribuyentes RESIDENTES en otro Estado miembro de la Unión Europea o del Espacio Económico Europeo con el que exista un efectivo intercambio de información tributaria' (Ley 36/2006 DA 1ª.4). The operative word is residentes, not nacionales.
entries.final_wording: Do not imply that two clients face the same rate without checking the right variable: art. 25.1.a TRLIRNR turns on the owner's COUNTRY OF TAX RESIDENCE, not nationality. An owner tax-resident in the Netherlands, Belgium or Germany gets 19% on net; an owner tax-resident in the UK gets 24% on gross — but a British national tax-resident in Germany gets 19%, and a Dutch national tax-resident in the UK gets 24%.
entries.note: The guardrail is right in substance and wrong in its variable. As written ('Dutch, Belgian or German client') it conflates nationality with tax residence — the exact five-variable error this ledger exists to catch. Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein are EEA and, having exchange of information, sit on the 19%/net side with the EU states.

entries.final_wording: Where a reader can genuinely check each signal for a Costa Blanca town: the municipality's own planning portal / sede electrónica (PGOU, plan status, licences) — this one does work at town level; the Ministerio's municipal transaction-COUNT tables — counts only, no municipal price; and, for prices, the province is the finest official level available (Registradores ERI). There is NO 'Registradores town data' and no INE municipal price series — do not send readers to either. Listing counts on idealista or Fotocasa are private commercial inventory, useful as a directional signal but never citable as an official statistic. If a sub-provincial price is needed, name the producer that actually publishes it and open that publication before quoting it.
entries.note: Two of the four routes named in the instruction do not exist as described. 'Registradores town data' is the more dangerous one, because it sounds authoritative and an AI told to find it will substitute the provincial figure and present it as the town's. I deliberately did not substitute the Consejo General del Notariado's Portal Estadístico here: I did not open it in this pass, so I will not assert its granularity.

entries.source_opened: DOGV nº 9405 of 16/08/2022, Decreto 98/2022 — official PDF downloaded from https://dogv.gva.es/datos/2022/08/16/pdf/2022_7560.pdf (image-only, not machine-readable), article text read from the reproduction at https://www.iberley.es/legislacion/decreto-98-2022-29-julio-consell-regula-registro-agentes-intermediacion-inmobiliaria-comunitat-valenciana-requisitos-inscripcion-27135412
entries.locator: Decreto 98/2022, de 29 de julio, del Consell. Art. 3 'Requisitos, garantías y seguros para ejercer la actividad' — final paragraph: 'Los agentes de intermediación inmobiliaria facilitarán a quien lo solicite el número de póliza... y así mismo lo harán constar en el contrato de mandato o la nota de encargo.' Art. 4.1: 'El Registro... es de titularidad pública, y naturaleza administrativa, gratuito y de carácter obligatorio.' Disposición final segunda: 'entrará en vigor a los dos meses de su publicación' → 16 October 2022 (DOGV 16 Aug 2022).
entries.final_wording: Decreto 98/2022 (DOGV nº 9405, 16 August 2022; in force 16 October 2022) puts the disclosure duty in ARTICLE 3, not in a separate disclosure article: the agent must state the guarantee/insurance policy details in the contrato de mandato or nota de encargo signed with the client, AND must supply them to anyone who asks. Art. 4.1 makes the register itself public, free of charge and obligatory. Critically, the FIXED MINIMUM amounts of aval and professional liability insurance set in art. 3 were annulled by the TSJCV on 13 December 2024 (CNMC appeal), so the duty to disclose the cover survives but no statutory minimum figure may be quoted as current — see id 434.
entries.note: Assertion is truncated mid-sentence ('while art.'), so the second half of its claim about who each duty runs to cannot be assessed. In-force date 16 Oct 2022 VERIFIED. Article attribution corrected: all of it sits in art. 3, with art. 4.1 carrying the public/free/obligatory character. The official DOGV PDF is a scanned image; I read the article text from a commercial reproduction and flag that as a second-best source for the exact wording.

entries.locator: TRLOTUP, Decreto Legislativo 1/2021, de 18 de junio, del Consell — Libro II, minimización de impacto territorial at arts. 228-231. Art. 230 'Actuaciones de minimización de impacto territorial generado por las edificaciones aisladas en suelo no urbanizable': owner applies to the ayuntamiento for a 'declaración de situación individualizada de minimización de impacto territorial' (pleno decision, reglada); that declaration suspends restablecimiento de la legalidad proceedings and prescription/caducidad periods; the owner must then obtain a licencia de minimización de impacto territorial y de ocupación and, within four years, a licencia de ocupación with the completion certificate.
