entries.source_opened: BOE — Ley 29/1994 LAU, texto consolidado, art. 25 https://www.boe.es/datosabiertos/api/legislacion-consolidada/id/BOE-A-1994-26003/texto/bloque/a25
entries.locator: LAU art. 25.2 (tanteo, 30 días naturales; efectos de la notificación caducan a los 180 días naturales) and art. 25.3 (retracto, 30 días naturales, remisión al art. 1.518 CC)
entries.final_wording: Establish from the LAU which provision confers a tenant's right of first refusal and which confers a right to step into a completed sale, the exact time limits for each, the moment from which each runs, and for how long a notification retains its effect.
entries.note: Sound method rule; I softened 'article' to 'provision' because the instruction presupposes two different articles and there is only one — both rights live in art. 25, at apartados 2 and 3, and a writer hunting for a second article number will invent one. The answers: tanteo, thirty calendar days counted from the day after the fehaciente notice of the decision to sell, the price and the other essential conditions (ap. 2); the effects of that notice lapse after one hundred and eighty calendar days (ap. 2, second paragraph); retracto, thirty calendar days counted from the day after the fehaciente notice the acquirer must give of the essential conditions of the completed sale, delivered by handing over a copy of the deed or document formalising it (ap. 3), subject to CC art. 1.518. The retracto clock starts on the buyer's notice, not the seller's — that is the detail most often reported wrongly.

entries.locator: LAU arts. 9.3, 10, 14 and 25

entries.note: A prohibition, not a sourced factual claim — but the premise holds on primary law. LAU art. 14: the buyer subrogates into the landlord's position for the first 5 years (7 if the landlord was a legal person), so selling does not end the tenancy. Art. 9.3: recovery for the landlord's own use (or a first-degree relative / ex-spouse) is available only to a natural-person landlord, only if expressly stipulated at signature, only after the first year, and only on 2 months' notice — and if he does not occupy within 3 months the tenant can demand reinstatement or compensation. Art. 25: the tenant holds tanteo (30 days from written notice of price and terms) and retracto; even where the right is expressly waived, the landlord must still give 30 days' notice before formalising the sale. So vacant possession is neither automatic, quick nor cost-free. Route this to the tenancy question before offering it.

entries.source_required: see source_class

entries.locator: MIVAU Estadística de Valor Tasado de Vivienda (quarterly, €/m², national / CCAA / provincia / municipios >25,000 inhabitants, appraisal-based); Consejo General del Notariado Portal Estadístico (€/m² from escrituras, down to postcode, launched Oct–Nov 2025); INE IPV Base 2015 (index numbers, national and CCAA only); Registradores ERI (quarterly, latest Q2 2026)

Neither is the asking price you see on a portal — no official body publishes that. Which one describes your house?

Asking-price €/m² comes from private portals and valuers (Idealista, Fotocasa, Tinsa), which are first-party for their own listings and are not official statistics. (2) The count of three is not established. Confirmed official €/m² instruments reaching Alicante: MIVAU's Valor tasado (a valuation, provincia and municipios >25,000) and the Notariado's Portal Estadístico (a signed deed, to postcode level). INE's IPV is an index, not a €/m², and is published only at national and autonomous-community level — it gives no Alicante figure. The Registradores' ERI is quarterly (latest Q2 2026) but a residential €/m² broken to Alicante province was not confirmed in this pass. The 'because' clause is also an unevidenced causal assertion — the series differ in what they record, which is a definitional difference, not a measured explanation of any specific euro gap.

Art. 28.4 opens the route where restoration measures implying demolition can no longer be taken because the prescription periods have run. Evidence accepted (28.4 a): 'certificación expedida por el Ayuntamiento o por técnico competente, acta notarial descriptiva de la finca o certificación catastral descriptiva y gráfica de la finca', showing completion on a determined date and a description matching the title. entries.assertion: What forms of power of attorney can a Spanish notary act on for an owner selling from abroad, what must each one contain and pass through before it is usable in Spain, and what causes one to be rejected at the deed?
entries.source_required: see source_class
entries.source_opened: BOE, Código Civil consolidated PDF — https://www.boe.es/buscar/pdf/1889/BOE-A-1889-4763-consolidado.pdf (arts. 1712, 1713, 1280 read verbatim) ; BOE, Ley 29/2015 de cooperación jurídica internacional en materia civil — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2015-8564

entries.final_wording: What forms of power of attorney can a Spanish notary act on for an owner selling from abroad, what must each one contain and pass through before it is usable in Spain, and what causes one to be rejected at the deed?
entries.note: A research question with no false presupposition. The routes are real and distinguishable: a POA before a Spanish notary; a POA before a Spanish consulate abroad; and a POA before a foreign notary, which then needs legalisation or the Hague apostille and a sworn translation, and must survive the juicio de equivalencia under Ley 29/2015 arts. 56 and 60 — the foreign authority must have acted in a function equivalent to a Spanish notary's, with an equivalent judgment on identity and capacity. CC art. 1280.5º puts the power in a public document; CC art. 1713 supplies the substantive content test. Rejection causes are correspondingly real (missing apostille, no sworn translation, no equivalence judgment, general terms that reach only administration). One caution for the writer: do not treat 'each one' as implying all three routes carry the same checklist — the consular route needs no apostille.

entries.assertion: Establish what a mandate must expressly empower for a disposal as opposed to mere administration, and what property-specific detail the deed must name, quoting the source
entries.source_required: see source_class
entries.source_opened: BOE, Código Civil consolidated PDF — https://www.boe.es/buscar/pdf/1889/BOE-A-1889-4763-consolidado.pdf (arts. 1712 and 1713 read verbatim)
entries.locator: CC arts. 1712 and 1713
entries.final_wording: Establish what a mandate must expressly empower for a disposal as opposed to mere administration, quoting the source: Código Civil art. 1713 — a mandate framed in general terms covers only acts of administration, and selling, mortgaging or any other act of riguroso dominio requires an express mandate. Do not assert that the power of attorney must name the specific property: no statute requires it. Identifying the finca by its registry details is standard drafting for a poder especial and must be labelled as practice, not law.
entries.note: The first half is right and quotable; the second half presupposes a statutory requirement that does not exist. CC art. 1713: 'El mandato, concebido en términos generales, no comprende más que los actos de administración. Para transigir, enajenar, hipotecar o ejecutar cualquier otro acto de riguroso dominio, se necesita mandato expreso.' That is the disposal-versus-administration line, and it is a content test, not an identification test. No Civil Code provision requires the power of attorney to name the particular finca; art. 1712 merely distinguishes a general mandate (all the principal's business) from a special one (one or more determined matters). Naming the property by its registry details is how a poder especial is customarily drafted and is what a notary will usually want to see, but it is drafting practice. As written the instruction would send the writer looking for a source that does not exist, and the likely outcome is that they invent one. Note also a separate ambiguity worth fixing: 'the deed' is unclear — the POA deed or the sale deed.

freshness.source_locator: CC arts. 1712 and 1713

entries.assertion: What must be completed, and in what sequence, before heirs of a Spanish property can pass title a buyer is able to register — and which of those steps carry a deadline, running from when?

entries.final_wording: What must be completed, and in what sequence, before heirs of a Spanish property can pass title a buyer is able to register — and which of those steps carry a deadline, running from when?
entries.note: A research question, well posed, and the deadline half is answerable from primary law. Sequence: death certificate, Registro de Actos de Última Voluntad certificate, authorised copy of the will or the acta de declaración de herederos, escritura de aceptación y adjudicación de herencia, the two tax filings, and then an inscribable title (LH art. 20). Deadlines: ISD, six months from the day of death (RD 1629/1991 art. 67.1.a); plusvalía on a mortis causa transfer, six months from accrual, extendable to a year on the taxpayer's request (TRLRHL art. 110.2.b). Flag for the writer: the Últimas Voluntades waiting period and the plusvalía article were confirmed only at secondary level in this pass — open the TRLRHL consolidated text before stating the article number. Note also that the deadlines run from the death, not from the decision to sell, which is the point most sellers get wrong.

entries.assertion: Establish which inheritance step carries a statutory filing deadline, when the clock starts, whether an extension exists, by when it must be requested, and whether an extension is free of cost
entries.source_required: see source_class
entries.source_opened: BOE, Reglamento del Impuesto sobre Sucesiones y Donaciones (RD 1629/1991), consolidated PDF — https://www.boe.es/buscar/pdf/1991/BOE-A-1991-27678-consolidado.pdf (arts. 67 and 68 read verbatim)
entries.final_wording: Establish which inheritance step carries a statutory filing deadline, when the clock starts, whether an extension exists, by when it must be requested, and whether an extension is free of cost
entries.note: A research instruction, and every one of its five questions is answered by two articles read verbatim — including the last one, which is the one writers get wrong. Deadline: six months for acquisitions by reason of death, counted from the day of the deceased's death (or from when a declaration of death becomes firm) — art. 67.1.a). Extension: yes, the competent office may grant one for a period equal to the filing period, i.e. a further six months (art. 68.1). Requested by: the heirs, executors or estate administrators within the first five months of the filing period, with the death certificate attached (art. 68.2); no extension is granted if requested after those five months (art. 68.4); silence for a month means granted (art. 68.3). Free of cost: no. Art. 68.6 — the granted extension 'llevará aparejada la obligación de satisfacer el interés de demora correspondiente hasta el día en que se presente el documento o la declaración'. Art. 68.5 attaches interest in the refusal scenario too. The instruction is right to ask; the answer must say plainly that the extension buys time and charges interest for it.

entries.assertion: That heirs must wait for their own registration to complete before a buyer can sign
entries.source_required: see source_class
entries.source_opened: BOE, Ley Hipotecaria consolidated — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-1946-2453
entries.locator: LH art. 20, including the fifth paragraph (tracto abreviado for heirs)
entries.final_wording: That heirs must wait for their own registration to complete before a buyer can sign
entries.note: A prohibition, and a correct one. LH art. 20 requires previous inscription in favour of the transferor for the sale to be registered — but that is a registration requirement, not a precondition to signing, and it is satisfied by presenting the escritura de herencia together with the sale so both are despatched in sequence. The fifth paragraph of art. 20 goes further, permitting heirs to transmit without their own previous inscription in defined cases (ratifying written private contracts of the deceased, sales to coheirs of property adjudicated proindiviso, and judicial adjudications or sales by the executed party where the property is inscribed in the deceased's name). So the banned sentence is false in both directions: heirs need not wait for their registration to complete, and in the art. 20 paragraph-5 cases need not be registered at all. Keep the prohibition; the substitute must be that the heirs' title has to be inscribable and ready to present, not already inscribed.

entries.assertion: Which of Decreto 98/2022's requirements for acting as an estate agent in the Comunitat Valenciana actually survive after the TSJCV judgment of January 2025 annulled the qualification, establishment, aval and professional-liability-insurance requirements — and is that judgment now firm or under cassation? Then: how can a homeowner verify what remains, and what does that verification fail to tell them?
entries.source_required: see source_class
entries.source_opened: CENDOJ judgment PDF hosted by CNMC, Roj: STSJ CV 5929/2024, ECLI:ES:TSJCV:2024:5929 — https://www.cnmc.es/sites/default/files/5864424.pdf (header, fundamento undécimo and fallo read verbatim) ; CNMC expediente LA/03/2022 — https://www.cnmc.es/expedientes/la032022 ; CGPJ/TSJCV press note, 17 January 2025 — https://www.poderjudicial.es/cgpj/es/Poder-Judicial/Tribunales-Superiores-de-Justicia/TSJ-Comunidad-Valenciana/Oficina-de-Comunicacion/Archivo-de-notas-de-prensa/El-TSJCV-estima-un-recurso-de-la-CNMC-y-anula-varios-requisitos-del-Registro-de-Agentes-de-Intermediacion-Inmobiliaria-de-la-Comunidad-Valenciana
entries.locator: STSJ CV, Sala CA Sección 4ª, sentencia 706/2024 de 13 de diciembre de 2024, rec. 22/2023, fundamento undécimo and fallo; CNMC expediente LA/03/2022, entry of 17 Jan 2025 marked 'Firme'
entries.final_wording: Which of Decreto 98/2022's requirements for acting as an estate agent in the Comunitat Valenciana survive after STSJ CV 706/2024 of 13 December 2024 (rec. 22/2023, ECLI:ES:TSJCV:2024:5929, announced 17 January 2025), which annulled not whole articles but specific incisos — the professional-qualification requirement in art. 3 b in full, the territorial inciso in art. 3 a for online-only agents, the fixed aval and seguro de caución amounts in art. 3 d, parts of art. 2.2, and art. 6 a, d and e — while leaving the duty to register, the solvency requirement itself and the distintivo intact? The CNMC records the judgment as firm on its case file LA/03/2022. Then: how can a homeowner verify what remains, and what does that verification fail to tell them?
entries.note: Three errors, all in the premise the question hands the writer. (1) Date. The judgment is of 13 December 2024 (sentencia 706/2024, rec. 22/2023, Sección 4ª). 17 January 2025 is the date of the TSJCV press note, not of the judgment. (2) Scope. The court expressly declined to annul whole articles — fundamento undécimo states the nullity attaches to 'los incisos correspondientes' only. What actually fell: in art. 2.2, the inciso obliging someone providing more than two services in twelve months to notify, and the letter-b obligation on agents established outside the Comunitat; in art. 3 a), only the inciso 'en el territorio de la Comunidad Valenciana' as applied to electronic-only providers — the location-and-attention requirement itself survives; art. 3 b), the professional-qualification requirement, annulled in its entirety; in art. 3 d), only 'las cuantías determinadas de los avales y seguros de caución' — the solvency requirement survives, only its fixed amounts fall; and art. 6 apartados a, d and e, as the declaración responsable reflections of the above. So 'annulled the establishment, aval and professional-liability-insurance requirements' overstates it: those requirements survive, stripped of a territorial inciso and of their numbers. The obligation to register is untouched, as is the distintivo bearing the registry number (art. 8 and the Anexo Único). (3) Firmness. The CNMC's own case file for LA/03/2022 records the judgment as Firme at the 17 Jan 2025 entry. The judgment text itself flags that cassation was available within thirty days, but no cassation appears on the file.

The Comunitat Valenciana's Decreto 98/2022 is a different thing — it governs the agent's entry in the regional register and the distintivo showing the registry number, not the advertisement, and parts of it were annulled by the TSJCV in December 2024. entries.note: A research instruction, correctly aimed at the one thing that decides these disputes: causation. The mediación or corretaje contract is atypical — no statute defines it — so entitlement is built from the Civil Code plus Supreme Court doctrine, and the settled test is a nexo de causalidad between the mediator's intervention and the sale that actually completed: no completed contract, or a contract completed without the agent's activity, and no commission is owed. entries.assertion: When one Costa Blanca property is advertised simultaneously by several agencies, what is established about how it reaches buyers, and which claims about how fast homes sell here cannot be evidenced from any published instrument?
entries.source_required: see source_class
entries.source_opened: INE, Estadística de Transmisiones de Derechos de la Propiedad — https://www.ine.es/dyngs/Prensa/ETDP1225.htm ; Colegio de Registradores, Estadísticas de propiedad — https://www.registradores.org/en/actualidad/portal-estadistico-registral/estadisticas-de-propiedad
entries.locator: INE ETDP (monthly and annual counts of transmissions); Registradores ERI (quarterly, latest Q2 2026); Consejo General del Notariado Portal Estadístico (prices and transaction counts)
entries.final_wording: When one Costa Blanca property is advertised simultaneously by several agencies, no official register, statistic or published instrument records how that affects the way it reaches buyers — and none publishes time on market either. INE's transmissions statistic counts sales, not days; the Registradores and the Notariado publish prices, volumes and surfaces, not listing durations. Any 'homes here sell in X days' figure comes from a portal's own listings or an agency's own book, and must be attributed that way or left out.
entries.note: Both halves come back empty, and that emptiness is the finding. Nothing official measures multi-agency exposure: no register, statistic or portal publishes how many agencies advertise a given property or what difference that makes to how it reaches buyers. And no official instrument publishes time on market at any geography — INE's ETDP counts transmissions, the Registradores' ERI and the Notariado's portal report prices, volumes and surfaces, none of them days from listing to sale. Every 'homes here sell in X days' figure in circulation traces to a portal's own listings (Idealista, Fotocasa) or to an agency's own book, which is first-party evidence about that source, not about the Costa Blanca. The piece should say the evidence does not exist rather than reach for a substitute.

entries.assertion: Spanish tax law lets you add the cost of "investments and improvements" to what you originally paid for the place. So before you spend, say, €12,000 on that bathroom, find out what counts as one — and what paperwork has to exist for it to count.
entries.source_required: see source_class
entries.source_opened: BOE, Ley 35/2006 del IRPF, consolidated PDF — https://www.boe.es/buscar/pdf/2006/BOE-A-2006-20764-consolidado.pdf (article 35 read verbatim)
entries.locator: LIRPF art. 35.1.b)
entries.final_wording: Spanish tax law lets you add the cost of "investments and improvements" to what you originally paid for the place. So before you spend, say, €12,000 on that bathroom, find out what counts as one — and what paperwork has to exist for it to count.
entries.note: The statutory limb is exact. LIRPF art. 35.1 builds the valor de adquisición from (a) the real amount of the acquisition and (b) 'El coste de las inversiones y mejoras efectuadas en los bienes adquiridos y los gastos y tributos inherentes a la adquisición, excluidos los intereses, que hubieran sido satisfechos por el adquirente' — so investments and improvements do raise the acquisition value and reduce the taxable gain, exactly as the hook says. Two riders for the writer, neither of which makes the hook wrong: the same paragraph reduces that value by amortisations in the cases the regulations set, which matters where the property has been let; and the €12,000 bathroom is explicitly illustrative, not a claim about the world. The hook's closing move — go and find out what counts and what paperwork must exist — is also the honest one, because the mejora/reparación line is administrative doctrine rather than statute.

entries.assertion: Establish what evidence is actually required for such spending to be accepted: form of invoice, whose name it must be in, how payment must be traceable, and whether undocumented or cash-paid work can be counted at all.
entries.source_required: see source_class
entries.source_opened: BOE, Ley 58/2003 General Tributaria, consolidated PDF — https://www.boe.es/buscar/pdf/2003/BOE-A-2003-23186-consolidado.pdf (article 106 read verbatim)
entries.final_wording: Establish what evidence is actually required for such spending to be accepted, and report honestly if the law prescribes no fixed form: LGT art. 106.1 applies the ordinary Civil Code and LEC rules of proof, and art. 106.4 makes the invoice the priority means of justifying such expenses while stating expressly that it is not a privileged means of proof — once the Treasury founds a challenge, the taxpayer must prove the work was real. Cover what an invoice should show, why payment traceability and a contemporaneous paper trail matter in practice, and why undocumented or cash-paid work usually fails — for want of provable reality, date and amount, not by a specific statutory ban.
entries.note: The instruction presupposes a prescribed evidentiary regime, and there isn't one — asking for 'the form of invoice, whose name it must be in, how payment must be traceable' invites the writer to state rules that do not exist. What the law actually says: LGT art. 106.1 applies the Civil Code and LEC rules on means and valuation of proof, so any means admitted in law is open; art. 106.4 makes the factura the priority means of justifying deductible expenses arising from operations by businesses or professionals, but then states plainly that 'la factura no constituye un medio de prueba privilegiado respecto de la existencia de las operaciones' — once the Administration founds a challenge, the taxpayer must prove the operations were real. Art. 106.3 leaves room for each tax's own law to impose formal deductibility requirements, and the DGT's position is that the nature of the works, their reality, their date and their amount are questions of fact provable by any admissible means. So the honest answer is: the invoice is what you want and what will be asked for first, but it is neither a closed requirement nor a guarantee, and cash-paid undocumented work fails for want of proof rather than by a specific prohibition. Rewrite so the writer reports that, instead of hunting a rule that isn't there.

entries.final_wording: Do not assume that any builder's bill reduces the tax. Where the line falls between work that counts and work that does not is the entire subject of the piece and must come from a cited source, not from the writer's expectation.
entries.note: A prohibition, and precisely the right one for this topic. The statute (LIRPF art. 35.1.b) names 'inversiones y mejoras' but never defines them, so the operative line comes from Dirección General de Tributos doctrine: repairs and conservation keep the property's useful life and capacity of use going, while extensions and improvements either increase its capacity or habitability or lengthen its useful life. Only the second kind raises the acquisition value; the first is deductible against rental income if the property is let, and otherwise is simply lost. Because that line is administrative doctrine rather than statutory text, the demand for a cited source is not pedantry — a writer working from expectation will put a repainted kitchen on the wrong side of it. The demanial/servidumbre limb is in 28.4.b)/c); the exclusion of protected rural land works indirectly, because the restoration action never prescribes there under CCAA law, so the antiquity route has nothing to rest on. entries.assertion: Establish the community-debt certificate procedure under art. 9.1.e LPH: who issues it, the statutory deadline for issuing it, whether the buyer may expressly waive it, and what liability attaches to the property for a previous owner's unpaid charges.
entries.source_required: see source_class
entries.source_opened: BOE, Ley 49/1960 de Propiedad Horizontal, texto consolidado (PDF) — https://www.boe.es/buscar/pdf/1960/BOE-A-1960-10906-consolidado.pdf
entries.locator: Ley 49/1960, art. 9.1.e), consolidated text in force
entries.final_wording: Establish the community-debt certificate procedure under art. 9.1.e LPH: issued by whoever exercises the secretary's functions with the president's visto bueno, within a maximum of seven CALENDAR days of request, both being liable for its accuracy and for delay; the deed cannot be authorised without it unless the buyer expressly exonerates the seller; and the property itself is legally affected to the previous owners' unpaid general expenses up to the part already fallen due of the annuity of acquisition plus the three preceding calendar years.
entries.note: Every element the instruction asks for is in art. 9.1.e) and answers cleanly. Issuer: whoever exercises the secretary's functions, with the president's visto bueno; both are liable for the accuracy of the data and for damage caused by delay. Deadline: 'en el plazo máximo de siete días naturales desde su solicitud' — SEVEN CALENDAR DAYS, not seven working days; a first pass on a secondary rendering of this article gave 'business days' and that is wrong. Waiver: yes, the certificate is required 'sin la cual no podrá autorizarse el otorgamiento del documento público, salvo que fuese expresamente exonerado de esta obligación por el adquirente' — so it does block the notary unless the buyer expressly exonerates, and the seller must still declare their payment position in the deed either way. Afección real: the acquirer answers with the property itself for the previous owners' unpaid general expenses up to the part already fallen due of the annuity in which the acquisition takes place plus the three preceding calendar years.

freshness.source_locator: Ley 49/1960, art. 9.1.e), consolidated text in force

entries.assertion: Buyer found, price agreed — and the signing still cannot happen until certain papers exist. Here is what actually gets checked at the notary, and what only costs you money.
entries.source_required: see source_class
entries.source_opened: BOE, Ley 49/1960 LPH consolidated PDF — https://www.boe.es/buscar/pdf/1960/BOE-A-1960-10906-consolidado.pdf ; BOE, RD 390/2021 — https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2021-9176

entries.note: The hook is wrong as written for the documents this topic is actually about. Of the papers in play, only ONE carries a statutory clause stopping the notary: the community-debt certificate, and even that falls away the moment the buyer expressly exonerates the seller (LPH art. 9.1.e). The energy certificate has a delivery/annexation duty under RD 390/2021 but no clause blocking authorisation — a notary can authorise where the buyer knowingly consents, with the administrative risk staying on the seller. And the entry for this same topic (gid 85) itself records the Valencian second-occupancy notary-blocking question as unresolved. So 'the signing still cannot happen until certain papers exist' overstates a position the topic's own research note declines to take. Fix the hook; do not fix it by quietly deleting the tension, name the one document that really blocks and that it is waivable.

entries.assertion: Establish the current position on the energy certificate and on the Valencian second-occupancy licence separately: whether each is a seller obligation, whether it must be lodged with the regional body to be valid, and — as a distinct question — whether its absence blocks the deed. The Valencian second-occupancy framework was NOT repealed in 2025 — Decreto 12/2021, de 22 de enero, del Consell remains in force (the Generalitat lists it as current and under review). What Ley 5/2025 repealed (DD única, g) was Decreto 80/2023 on design and quality of dwellings, a different instrument; the Orden of 7 December 2009 on design and quality applies in its place. the notary-blocking question is unresolved.

The Valencian second-occupancy framework was NOT repealed in 2025: Decreto 12/2021, de 22 de enero, del Consell remains in force and is not named in the derogatoria (the Generalitat lists it as current and under review). What Ley 5/2025 repealed, at letter g of its disposición derogatoria única, was Decreto 80/2023 on design and quality of dwellings — a different instrument — and the Orden of 7 December 2009 (DC-09) applies in its place. The derogatoria única runs a) to g) only, and letter g) is exactly 'Decreto 80/2023, de 26 de mayo, del Consell, por el que se aprueban las normas de diseño y calidad en edificios de vivienda.' entries.assertion: Establish the sequence from death certificate through to the buyer's registration of title, and establish specifically whether the inheritance deed and the sale deed can be signed and lodged together or must be separated — and what a buyer's registration depends on.
entries.source_required: see source_class
entries.source_opened: BOE, Ley Hipotecaria (Decreto de 8 de febrero de 1946), texto consolidado PDF — https://www.boe.es/buscar/pdf/1946/BOE-A-1946-2453-consolidado.pdf
entries.locator: LH art. 20 (tracto sucesivo, including the exceptions for documents granted by heirs) and art. 254.1 (no registration without prior proof of payment of the taxes due)
entries.final_wording: Establish the sequence from death certificate through to the buyer's registration of title. The inheritance deed and the sale deed CAN be signed and lodged together: art. 20 LH requires the transferor's right to be registered first, but the registrar can record the inheritance and then the sale from a single lodging. What the buyer's registration actually depends on is the inheritance title being registrable — and art. 254.1 LH keeps the register closed until the taxes on the act are shown paid, which makes the inheritance-tax filing and the plusvalía the real gating items.
entries.note: The question is well-posed and answerable from primary law. Art. 20 LH: to register a transfer, the transferor's right must already be registered — so the heirs' title has to reach the register, but it can reach it in the same lodging as the sale rather than in a separate earlier one; the registrar simply records the inheritance and then the purchase. The deeds can therefore be signed and lodged together. What the buyer's registration actually depends on is the inheritance title being registrable, and art. 254.1 LH closes the register until the taxes on the act are shown paid — which is where the inheritance-tax filing (see gid 87) and the plusvalía become the real gating items, not the order of signature. Write the sequence around that dependency, not around a supposed rule that the two deeds must be separated.

entries.assertion: Establish the filing deadline for the inheritance tax, whether an extension exists, by when it must be requested, whether silence grants it, and whether it carries a cost — read from the regulation itself.
entries.source_required: see source_class
entries.source_opened: BOE, RD 1629/1991 Reglamento del Impuesto sobre Sucesiones y Donaciones, texto consolidado PDF — https://www.boe.es/buscar/pdf/1991/BOE-A-1991-27678-consolidado.pdf
entries.locator: RD 1629/1991, art. 67.1.a) and art. 68 apartados 1 to 6
entries.final_wording: Establish the inheritance-tax filing deadline from the regulation itself: six months from the date of death (art. 67.1.a RISD); an extension of a further six months exists (art. 68.1) but must be requested within the first five months (art. 68.2, and art. 68.4 refuses it outright after that); silence grants it — one month without notified decision and the extension is deemed conceded (art. 68.3); and it is not free, since the granted extension carries interés de demora from the end of the six-month period until filing (art. 68.6).
entries.note: Read verbatim from the consolidated regulation, exactly as the instruction demands. Deadline: six months from the day of death (art. 67.1.a). Extension: yes — the competent office may grant a further period equal to the filing period, i.e. six more months (art. 68.1). Request window: within the FIRST FIVE MONTHS of the filing period (art. 68.2), and no extension is granted at all if requested after those five months have run (art. 68.4). Silence: positive — 'transcurrido un mes desde la presentación de la solicitud sin que se hubiese notificado acuerdo, se entenderá concedida la prórroga' (art. 68.3). Cost: yes — the granted extension runs from the end of the six-month period and carries the obligation to pay interés de demora up to the day of filing (art. 68.6); and where an extension is refused, interest still runs if filing ends up beyond six months from accrual (art. 68.5). Note for the writer: ISD is a ceded tax, so check whether the Comunitat Valenciana has its own procedural overlay before presenting these as the only rules that apply.

freshness.source_locator: RD 1629/1991, art. 67.1.a) and art. 68 apartados 1 to 6

entries.assertion: A Spanish resident buying their main home can normally borrow up to 80% of the valuation — Banco de España says lenders do not usually go above that. It is a ceiling, not an entitlement: the bank lends on the lower of price and valuation, and only if your income supports it. Non-residents are financed at a lower percentage than residents, but there is no single number. The one Costa Blanca-facing lender that publishes a figure is CaixaBank's HolaBank, at up to 70% of the property value; Santander publishes none. Assume you must fund 30%+ of the price plus roughly 12-15% in taxes and costs, and get the figure from your own lender. What that does to the price you can actually afford.

entries.final_wording: A Spanish resident buying their main home can normally borrow up to 80% of the valuation — Banco de España says lenders do not usually go above that. It is a ceiling, not an entitlement: the bank lends on the lower of price and valuation, and only if your income supports it. Non-residents are financed at a lower percentage than residents, but there is no single number. The one Costa Blanca-facing lender that publishes a figure is CaixaBank's HolaBank, at up to 70% of the property value, excluding taxes and costs; Santander publishes none. Assume you must fund 30%+ of the price plus roughly 11-14% in taxes and costs on a purchase under one million euros — more above it, where Valencian ITP rises to 11% — and get the figure from your own lender. What that does to the price you can actually afford.
entries.note: Three of the four limbs verify cleanly and one is now stale. Verified: Banco de España's own consumer portal does say the loan is normally up to a maximum of 80% of the appraisal value — and the entry is right to frame it as a ceiling, since BdE presents it as what lenders normally do, not as a borrower right. Verified first-party: CaixaBank's HolaBank guide states up to 70% financing, explicitly excluding taxes and associated expenses. Verified by opening it: Santander's non-resident mortgage page publishes no percentage at all — only a simulator and the standard FIPRE/ESIS disclaimer — so 'Santander publishes none' is accurate as of today. The defect is the cost band. '12-15%' was right when Valencian ITP stood at 10%, but ITP fell to 9% on 1 June 2026, which drops the realistic Costa Blanca total to roughly 11-14% for a purchase under one million euros. Above one million the 11% ITP band pushes it back up, so the range has to be stated with its condition attached. Note also that the '12-15%' figure is NOT on the CaixaBank page I opened — do not attribute it to the bank.

entries.assertion: The exact conditions of LPH art. 17.4: three-fifths approval, works not required for conservation, habitability, safety or accessibility, cost exceeding three months of ordinary common expenses, and the owner having voted against
entries.source_required: see source_class
entries.source_opened: BOE, Ley 49/1960 LPH, texto consolidado PDF — https://www.boe.es/buscar/pdf/1960/BOE-A-1960-10906-consolidado.pdf
entries.locator: Ley 49/1960, art. 17.4, consolidated text in force
entries.final_wording: The exact conditions of LPH art. 17.4: a double three-fifths majority (three-fifths of owners who also represent three-fifths of the participation quotas), works not required for the proper conservation, habitability, safety or accessibility of the building, an installation cost exceeding three ordinary monthly common expenses, and the owner having dissented — noting that the dissenter may join later by paying their updated share plus legal interest.
entries.note: All four conditions confirmed verbatim. The majority is three-fifths of the total owners who at the same time represent three-fifths of the participation quotas — a double three-fifths, and writing it as a single 'three-fifths approval' loses half the test. The works must be 'no requeridos para la adecuada conservación, habitabilidad, seguridad y accesibilidad del inmueble'. The threshold is a cuota de instalación exceeding three ordinary monthly common expenses. The protected owner is the 'propietario disidente'. Two refinements for the writer: the exemption attaches to the dissenting owner, who cannot be charged and cannot be deprived of the benefit, and who may join later by paying their share updated with legal interest — so 'voted against' is not a permanent opt-out. And do not confuse this with art. 17.2, where energy-efficiency works within twelve monthly payments bind everyone and the dissenting owner gets no such right.

entries.assertion: Which lines are genuinely non-resident-specific versus paid by everyone. The imputed income itself is NOT non-resident-specific — art. 85 LIRPF imputes a second home to Spanish tax residents as well. What is specific to the non-resident is the vehicle: a separate Modelo 210 self-assessment at a flat 19%/24% with no personal allowances. Fiscal representation is not a standard non-resident cost either: under art. 10 TRLIRNR it is required only of owners resident outside the EU and outside the mutual-assistance EEA, and then only in defined cases or when the tax office demands it.
entries.source_required: see source_class
entries.source_opened: BOE, RDLeg 5/2004 TRLIRNR, texto consolidado PDF — https://www.boe.es/buscar/pdf/2004/BOE-A-2004-4527-consolidado.pdf ; AEAT Sede, Régimen de imputación de rentas inmobiliarias (Manual IRPF) — https://sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es/Sede/ayuda/manuales-videos-folletos/manuales-practicos/irpf-2025/c10-regimenes-especiales-imputacion-atribucion-rentas/regimen-imputacion-rentas-inmobiliarias/concepto-requisitos.html
entries.locator: TRLIRNR art. 10.1 (three paragraphs) and art. 25.1.a); AEAT IRPF manual, imputación de rentas inmobiliarias
entries.final_wording: Which lines are genuinely non-resident-specific versus paid by everyone. The imputed income itself is NOT non-resident-specific — art. 85 LIRPF imputes a second home to Spanish tax residents as well. What is specific to the non-resident is the vehicle: a separate Modelo 210 self-assessment at a flat 19%/24% with no personal allowances. Fiscal representation is not a standard non-resident cost either: under art. 10 TRLIRNR it does not apply to EU residents, nor to EEA residents covered by mutual assistance, and for other owners it bites only in the defined cases or when the tax office demands it — with one exception that must not be dropped: owners resident in a country or territory with no effective exchange of tax information must appoint a representative simply by virtue of holding Spanish property, without AEAT asking.
entries.note: Two limbs verify, the third is wrong in a way that would mislead the exact reader it is aimed at. VERIFIED: art. 85 LIRPF does impute a non-habitual urban property to Spanish tax residents — AEAT's own IRPF manual confirms the resident regime covers urban properties not affected to an economic activity and excluding the habitual residence — so the imputation genuinely is not non-resident-specific. VERIFIED: art. 25.1.a) gives the flat 24%/19%, and the Modelo 210 vehicle with no personal allowances is right. WRONG: art. 10 TRLIRNR has THREE limbs, and the assertion collapses them into one. The first limb is as described — non-EU residents must appoint a representative when they operate through a permanent establishment, in the art. 24.2 and art. 38 cases, or when AEAT requires it because of the amount or characteristics of the income or the ownership of Spanish property — and the second limb disapplies that for EEA states with mutual assistance. But the THIRD paragraph imposes the obligation additionally, and unconditionally, on persons or entities resident in countries or territories with no effective exchange of tax information (per DA 1ª.3 Ley 36/2006) who own assets or rights in Spain. For that group, owning the property is itself the trigger — AEAT does not have to demand anything. So 'only in defined cases or when the tax office demands it' is false for them. The territorial scope statement is otherwise sound, since that group sits inside 'outside the EU and outside the mutual-assistance EEA'.

entries.assertion: Agency input required if real numbers are used: actual IBI receipts and community budgets from the agency's own listings — otherwise the piece must run as sourced ranges, not a fake invoice

entries.locator: n/a — IBI is set per municipality by ordenanza fiscal against each property's valor catastral, and community budgets are set by each comunidad de propietarios; neither has a public series at the level this asks for
entries.final_wording: Agency input required if real numbers are used: actual IBI receipts and community budgets from the agency's own listings, labelled as coming from named real listings. IBI depends on the municipality's ordenanza fiscal and the individual valor catastral, and community budgets are set by each comunidad, so no public source can supply either. Without that input the piece must run as sourced ranges that say the real figure is property-specific — never as a specimen invoice.
entries.note: Correctly routed and correctly conditioned. Nothing public can supply an actual IBI amount for a specific dwelling: the rate comes from the municipality's ordenanza fiscal and the base from that property's individual valor catastral, so only the receipt itself settles it. Community budgets are private to each comunidad and settled by its junta, so the same applies. The instruction's fallback is the right one and should be enforced rather than treated as a soft preference — a specimen annual-cost table built from plausible-looking numbers reads as a real invoice to a buyer and is the exact failure mode this guards against. If the agency supplies figures, label them as drawn from named real listings; if it does not, publish ranges with their sources visible and say plainly that the real figure is property-specific.

Over the past twelve months the sterling price of that €250,000 has swung between roughly £212,200 and £221,200 on the ECB's daily reference rate: a spread of about £9,000. The budget that moves while you sleep.

entries.source_opened: European Central Bank, euro foreign exchange reference rates, full daily history (eurofxref-hist.csv) — https://www.ecb.europa.eu/stats/eurofxref/eurofxref-hist.zip (downloaded and computed locally)
entries.locator: ECB daily EUR/GBP reference rate, 2 September 2025 to 1 September 2026 (255 observations); latest observation 2026-09-01 at 0.85655
entries.final_wording: Your €250,000 flat cost about £217,100 on the January 2026 average and about £215,900 on the June 2026 average — same flat. Over the twelve months to 1 September 2026 the sterling price of that €250,000 swung between about £212,200 (16 July 2026) and about £221,200 (14 November 2025) on the ECB's daily reference rate: a spread of about £9,000. Figures are the ECB reference rate, not a dealable rate, and the twelve-month range moves every day. The budget that moves while you sleep.
entries.note: Every figure reproduces from the ECB series, computed rather than asserted — this is unusually clean. January 2026 monthly mean 0.86828 gives £217,070 (stated £217,100). June 2026 monthly mean 0.863721 gives £215,930 (stated £215,900). Trailing-twelve-month low 0.84873 on 16 July 2026 gives £212,182 (stated ~£212,200); high 0.88460 on 14 November 2025 gives £221,150 (stated ~£221,200); spread £8,968 (stated ~£9,000). WHAT EXPIRES AND WHEN: all five numbers rest on a rolling twelve-month window and the ECB publishes a new rate every TARGET business day around 16:00 CET, so the window moves daily and the high of 14 November 2025 drops out of it in November 2026 — at which point the quoted spread narrows without anyone touching the copy. The January and June figures are stable historical means and do not expire. Two further cautions: these are month AVERAGES presented as 'in January' and 'in June', which is defensible but is not what gid 101's instruction asks for; and the ECB reference rate is not a dealable rate, so a reader's bank will not give them £217,100.

It is a payment on account of your own Spanish non-resident tax, not money anyone keeps. How a non-resident settles up afterwards — and reclaims any excess.

How a non-resident settles up afterwards — and reclaims any excess.
entries.note: Confirmed verbatim. Art. 14.1: 'el adquirente estará obligado a retener e ingresar el 3 por ciento... de la contraprestación acordada, en concepto de pago a cuenta del Impuesto sobre la Renta de no Residentes' — so both the identity of the obligor and the payment-on-account characterisation are exactly right, and 'of the agreed price' matches 'contraprestación acordada'. Art. 14.3 puts the declaration and payment at the AEAT office covering the property's location within one month of the date of transfer. The 'not the buyer's lawyer' contrast is rhetorical rather than statutory but is not misleading: the duty rests on the acquirer regardless of who physically files, and the acquirer carries the consequence. Two additions worth making. Art. 14.2 carves out the case where the seller proves they are an IRPF or Corporation Tax taxpayer by certificate — so the withholding is not automatic on every sale. And art. 14.5 gives the seller's warning real teeth: if the 3% is never paid in, the transferred property itself stands affected and the registrar records it in the margin — which is why this is the buyer's problem too. The form is Modelo 211, set by ministerial order rather than by art. 14 itself.

entries.final_wording: The seller's Modelo 210 deadline — three months from the end of the buyer's one-month period, so four months from the transfer in total (RIRNR art. 14.4) — and what actually happens if it is missed: the refund is not forfeited and can still be claimed, since the right to request it prescribes only after four years (LGT art. 66.c), though filing late carries its own surcharge consequences.
entries.note: Both citations are exact, including the apartado. Art. 14.4 verbatim: the non-resident taxpayer must declare and where applicable pay the definitive tax, offsetting the amount withheld by the acquirer against the quota, 'en el plazo de tres meses contados a partir del término del plazo establecido para el ingreso de la retención' — so three months running from the end of the buyer's one-month period, which means four months from the transfer in total, not three. The same apartado provides for AEAT to refund the excess withheld after any necessary checks, which is the statutory hook for the refund. Art. 66.c) confirms the four years, and it is the right letter: it covers 'el derecho a solicitar las devoluciones derivadas de la normativa de cada tributo, las devoluciones de ingresos indebidos y el reembolso del coste de las garantías'. Worth carrying into the copy: art. 66.d) separately gives four years to OBTAIN a refund once requested, so the two limbs are distinct and a piece should not merge them. Missing the three-month window is a late filing with its own surcharge consequences, so 'not forfeited' should not be written as 'no downside'.

entries.assertion: What the Agencia Tributaria actually requires for the refund: a Spanish NIF/NIE (or the identification code AEAT issues for the purpose), and a bank account in the seller's OWN name — which may be held in Spain or abroad. A fiscal representative is not a general requirement (TRLIRNR art. 10.1 imposes one only on non-EU residents in defined cases). On timing, no official processing-time statistic is published; the only official benchmark is LGT art. 31.2 — after six months AEAT owes interest de demora.

entries.final_wording: What the Agencia Tributaria actually requires for the refund: a Spanish NIF/NIE (or, failing that, the Código Identificativo AEAT issues for the purpose), and a bank account in the seller's OWN name — which may be held at a bank in Spain or abroad (if the refund account belongs to anyone other than the taxpayer, it must be open in Spain). A fiscal representative is not a general requirement: TRLIRNR art. 10.1 imposes one only on contributors not resident in another EU Member State, and then only in defined cases (operating through a permanent establishment, the arts. 24.2 and 38 situations, or when the tax administration so requires given the amount and characteristics of the income or the ownership of Spanish property) — and it does not apply to residents of EEA states outside the EU where mutual-assistance rules on exchange of information and recovery are in place, which covers Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein. On timing, no official processing-time statistic is published; the only official benchmark is LGT art. 31.2 — after six months AEAT owes interés de demora, without the taxpayer having to request it.
entries.note: Three of the four limbs verify exactly. The fiscal-representative limb over-includes: TRLIRNR art. 10.1 binds contributors 'que no sean residentes en otro Estado miembro de la Unión Europea', but its second paragraph disapplies that for EEA states outside the EU where mutual-assistance rules on exchange of tax information and recovery exist — which covers Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein. Saying 'non-EU residents' would wrongly sweep in exactly the Nordic sellers this content is written for. No AEAT publication of an average processing time for Modelo 210 refunds was found on the Sede; LGT art. 31.2 (six months, then interés de demora without needing to ask) is the only official benchmark.

entries.note: Art. 28.4 exists and is the right cite. It applies where restoration measures implying demolition can no longer be taken because the limitation periods have run. It then requires: a certification from the Ayuntamiento or a competent technician, a notarial acta descriptiva of the finca, or a certificación catastral descriptiva y gráfica, showing completion on a determined date and a description matching the title. entries.assertion: The legal categories — allanamiento de morada (CP art. 202) versus usurpación (CP art. 245) — and where a foreign owner's regularly used holiday home falls. Note that art. 245.2 CP applies only to an immueble 'que no constituyan morada', so the morada / non-morada line is the whole question; whether a regularly used second home counts as morada is decided case by case and must be backed by a citable Tribunal Supremo judgment before it is asserted. On immediate police action, apply the flagrancy definition in LECrim art. 795.1.1ª. There is no 48-hour rule anywhere in the Código Penal or the LECrim.

Note that art. 245.2 CP applies only to an immueble 'que no constituyan morada', so the morada / non-morada line is the whole question; whether a regularly used second home counts as morada is decided case by case and must be backed by a citable Tribunal Supremo judgment before it is asserted. On immediate police action, apply the flagrancy definition in LECrim art. 795.1.1ª. Establish what flagrancy actually requires under the LECrim and the Interior protocol, since Spanish law attaches no fixed-hour rule to it.
entries.note: Everything checks out except the final sentence. Verified verbatim: CP art. 245.2 punishes occupying 'un inmueble, vivienda o edificio ajenos que no constituyan morada', so the morada line really is the whole question; CP art. 202.1 covers entering or staying in a morada ajena against the occupant's will. The flagrancy definition is indeed in LECrim art. 795.1.1ª. The guardrail requiring a citable TS judgment before asserting that a regularly used second home is a morada is sound and should stay. But 'There is no 48-hour rule anywhere in the Código Penal or the LECrim' is false as written: a full-text search of both consolidated codes returns three 48-hour periods in each — in the CP, the restitution window in the robo/hurto de uso de vehículos provisions (art. 244 and its predecessor wording); in the LECrim, the maximum extension of detention for the terrorism regime and the substitution period for the querella deposit. None of them has anything to do with recovering an occupied property, which is the point the sentence was reaching for, so the fix narrows the claim rather than abandoning it. | Replacement wording amended: it still carried the 48-hour phrasing the guardrail forbids.

entries.assertion: Never state that Spain now evicts squatters in 15 days. Non-violent usurpación under art. 245.2 remains on the delito-leve route; the fast-track rules concern the offences and procedures to which they actually apply, and the 15-day wording in art. 802 LECrim is not a universal eviction deadline.

entries.source_opened: BOE consolidated LECrim arts. 795 and 802, https://www.boe.es/datosabiertos/api/legislacion-consolidada/id/BOE-A-1882-6036/texto/bloque/a795 and .../as802 ; BOE consolidated Código Penal arts. 13, 33 and 245, https://www.boe.es/datosabiertos/api/legislacion-consolidada/id/BOE-A-1995-25444/texto/bloque/a13 , .../a33 , .../a245

entries.final_wording: Never state that Spain now evicts squatters in 15 days. Keep two things apart. First, since 3 April 2025 Ley Orgánica 1/2025 has added allanamiento de morada (CP art. 202) and usurpación (CP art. 245) to the juicio rápido catalogue in LECrim art. 795.1.2ª, letters i and j — so those offences are on the fast-track list. Second, that is not a 15-day eviction deadline: non-violent usurpación under CP art. 245.2 carries multa de tres a seis meses, which under CP arts. 33.4.g and 13.4 makes it a delito leve tried by the delito-leve procedure, and the fifteen days in LECrim art. 802.2 is only the outer limit for re-setting a juicio oral that could not be held on its scheduled day.
entries.note: The prohibition is right and both of its supporting facts verify — but it is now materially incomplete, and the gap is the kind that produces wrong copy. Verified: CP art. 245.2 carries multa de tres a seis meses; CP art. 33.4.g) makes multa up to three months a pena leve, and CP art. 13.4 provides that where a penalty spans leve and menos grave the offence counts 'en todo caso' as leve — so non-violent usurpación is a delito leve and goes by the delito-leve procedure. Verified: the fifteen days in LECrim art. 802.2 is only the outer limit for re-setting a juicio oral that could not be held or concluded on its scheduled day — not an eviction deadline. What the entry misses is that Ley Orgánica 1/2025, in force 3 April 2025, added letters i) delitos de allanamiento de morada del artículo 202 and j) delitos de usurpación del artículo 245 to the juicio rápido catalogue in LECrim art. 795.1.2ª. Copy generated from the entry as written would deny that any fast-track change happened, which is now wrong; the fix keeps the prohibition and names the reform.

entries.assertion: The developer went bust before finishing your off-plan flat. Whether you get your money back off-plan turns on two things the law requires from day one — an individual bank guarantee or caución insurance policy in your name, and payment into the developer's separate special account (LOE, disposición adicional primera). And note the timing trap: since 1 January 2016 the guarantee obligation runs only 'desde la obtención de la licencia de edificación', so anything you hand over before the building licence is issued sits outside it. (€80,000 is illustrative only.)

entries.assertion: The closer to the sea, the bigger the question nobody asks: can the Spanish state claim your beachfront? What the Ley de Costas really means.
entries.source_required: see source_class
entries.source_opened: BOE consolidated Ley 22/1988 de Costas, disposición transitoria primera, https://www.boe.es/datosabiertos/api/legislacion-consolidada/id/BOE-A-1988-18762/texto/bloque/primera
entries.locator: Ley 22/1988 disposición transitoria primera, apartados 1 to 3 (consolidated version in force since 11-12-2015), read with art. 132.2 of the Constitution as cited in the provision itself
entries.final_wording: The closer to the sea, the bigger the question nobody asks: can the Spanish state claim your beachfront? What the Ley de Costas really means.
entries.note: What is verified here is the hook's presupposition, not a figure: the premise that the Spanish state can bring privately held coastal land into the dominio público marítimo-terrestre is correct. DT primera.1 provides that holders of zona marítimo-terrestre, playa or mar territorial declared private property by a final judgment before the Law came into force 'pasarán a ser titulares de un derecho de ocupación y aprovechamiento del dominio público marítimo-terrestre', by concession of thirty years extendable by thirty more, with no canon. DT primera.2 does the same for registered owners protected by LH art. 34 whom the administration could not dispossess in an earlier deslinde. DT primera.3 provides that where the coast was not or was only partly deslindada, the deslinde will be carried out and its approval carries the art. 13 effects for all land it brings into the dominio público. The hook is a question and states no number; it may run, but the body must deliver the concession mechanism rather than implying an ownership fight or a cash payout.

entries.assertion: How close to the sea is too close? What the Ley de Costas can actually do to a property you own on the coast — and what you get if the boundary moves.

entries.source_opened: BOE consolidated Ley 22/1988 de Costas, disposición transitoria primera, https://www.boe.es/datosabiertos/api/legislacion-consolidada/id/BOE-A-1988-18762/texto/bloque/primera
entries.locator: Ley 22/1988 disposición transitoria primera, apartados 1 to 3 (consolidated version in force since 11-12-2015)
entries.final_wording: How close to the sea is too close? What the Ley de Costas can actually do to a property you own on the coast — and what you get if the boundary moves.
entries.note: A question, and its presupposition holds — but the answer it points at must be written correctly, and this is where such copy usually goes wrong. What an affected owner gets when the deslinde moves is a derecho de ocupación y aprovechamiento, that is a concession over the public domain (thirty years, extendable by thirty, respecting existing uses and free of canon under DT primera.1), not compensation and not retained ownership. DT primera.2 preserves whatever civil actions the holder may bring 'en defensa de sus derechos', so the concession is not framed as extinguishing private-law claims. Any draft that answers 'what you get' with money rather than a concession is wrong and must be corrected before publication.

entries.assertion: What it does not show: unregistered charges, community fee arrears, tenants or occupiers, planning infringements and licence status — and that it has no priority-reservation effect — then establish what the notary's telematic check under Art. 175 RN actually does: whether it reserves rank at all, or merely obliges the registrar to notify the notary of filings made in the following ten days, with priority still arising only from the asiento de presentación after signing.
entries.source_required: see source_class
entries.source_opened: BOE consolidated Reglamento Notarial (Decreto de 2 de junio de 1944) art. 175, https://www.boe.es/datosabiertos/api/legislacion-consolidada/id/BOE-A-1944-6578/texto/bloque/a175 ; Reglamento Hipotecario art. 354 a), https://www.boe.es/datosabiertos/api/legislacion-consolidada/id/BOE-A-1947-3843/texto/bloque/a354a) ; Ley Hipotecaria arts. 24 and 222, https://www.boe.es/datosabiertos/api/legislacion-consolidada/id/BOE-A-1946-2453/texto/bloque/a24 and .../a222
entries.locator: RN art. 175.1 to 175.4 (version in force after RD 45/2007 and the partial annulment by STS 20 May 2008); RH art. 354 a), reglas 2ª, 4ª and 5ª (version from RD 2537/1994); LH art. 222.10; LH art. 24
entries.final_wording: What it does not show: unregistered charges, community fee arrears, tenants or occupiers, planning infringements and licence status — and it has no priority-reservation effect. On the notary's check: Art. 175.3 RN requires telematic access to the registry books under LH art. 222.10 at the moment immediately before the deed is authorised, and that access reserves no rank whatever — priority still arises only from the asiento de presentación (LH art. 24). The registrar's duty to notify the notary of later filings is not part of that telematic check: it sits in RH art. 354 a regla 5ª, applies to the written or telefax route, and runs nine natural days from the sending of the information. The ten natural days in RN art. 175.4 are a different period — the deadline for signing the deed once information has been received by that written route.
entries.note: The first half is right and the open question is now answerable, but the 'ten days' in the second half is wrong on both the number and the instrument. What the sources say: RN art. 175.3 requires the notary to access the registry books telematically 'en el momento inmediato más próximo a la autorización de la escritura pública bajo su responsabilidad', without the registrar's intermediation, under LH art. 222.10 — and LH art. 222.10 is a rule about manifestación of the books, conferring no rank. LH art. 24 leaves priority dating from the asiento de presentación. So the telematic check reserves no rank at all: the entry's third alternative is the correct one. The registrar's duty to notify the notary of later filings is real but sits elsewhere — RH art. 354 a) regla 5ª — runs 'dentro de los nueve días naturales siguientes al de remisión de la información', not ten, and belongs to the written/telefax route, which RN art. 175.4 pairs with a ten-natural-day deadline for signing after receiving the information. The 'ten days' figure appears to be that signing deadline misread as the notification window. Two different periods, two different instruments, and only one of them is ten days.

entries.assertion: The registered versus cadastral versus physically measured surface question: what a discrepancy indicates, which figure is likely stale, and how it is resolved (Arts. 199/201 LH).

entries.locator: LH art. 199.1 and art. 201.1 letters a) to e) (version from Ley 13/2015, in force since 1 November 2015)
entries.final_wording: The registered versus cadastral versus physically measured surface question: what a discrepancy indicates, which figure is likely stale, and how it is resolved (Arts. 199/201 LH).
entries.note: The article citation is right and the two routes are distinct. LH art. 199 is the registrar-led route: the registered holder completes the literary description by producing the certificación catastral descriptiva y gráfica, the registrar notifies affected neighbouring registered owners, who have twenty days to object, and the registrar must refuse if the graphic identification overlaps another inscribed base gráfica or the public domain. LH art. 201 is the notarial expediente to rectify description, surface or boundaries, following the art. 203 rules with the listed adjustments, and it requires the promoter to declare under his responsibility that the difference is purely a descriptive error and not an unregistered transfer. One exclusion matters for the flat buyers this topic addresses and must be carried into any copy: art. 201.1.e) bars this expediente for rectifying the description of buildings, fincas or elements in a régimen de división horizontal — for those, the original title must be rectified or the corresponding administrative procedure run first. The framing questions the entry poses — what a discrepancy indicates and which figure is likely stale — are not answered by these articles and remain per-case.

entries.assertion: Healthcare entitlement by nationality and status: UK state pensioners via S1 registered with INSS, EU pensioners likewise, everyone else via private cover or convenio especial — plus how the Valencian SIP card is obtained
entries.source_required: see source_class
entries.source_opened: BOE, Ley 16/2003 de cohesión y calidad del SNS, consolidated https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2003-10715 ; Seguridad Social, 'Registro del documento S-1 para cobertura de asistencia sanitaria en España' (folleto C-176) https://www.seg-social.es/wps/wcm/connect/wss/61809e44-7a63-4802-8db7-ba29e811bb62/C-176_Castellano_2_Accesibilidad.pdf ; Ministerio de Sanidad, convenio especial https://www.sanidad.gob.es/servCiudadanos/internacional/convenioEspecial.htm ; GVA Conselleria de Sanitat, acceso mediante convenio especial https://www.san.gva.es/es/web/tarjeta-sanitaria/acceso-a-la-atencion-sanitaria-mediante-convenio-especial-de-la-conselleria-de-sanitat
entries.locator: Ley 16/2003 art. 3.1 (right held by Spanish nationals and foreigners with established residence in Spain), art. 3 ter (conditions for those without legal residence: no duty to be covered under EU or bilateral rules, no exportable right from country of origin, no third party liable), art. 3.3 (those outside art. 3.2 may obtain the benefit by subscribing a convenio especial). Convenio especial conditions: one continuous year of prior residence in Spain/EU/EEA/Switzerland/UK immediately before the application, empadronamiento at application, and no access to public health cover by any other title. Seguridad Social C-176: the S1 covers pensioners, posted workers, frontier workers and dependent family members whose cover is charged to another EU/EEA/Swiss/UK state, registered at an INSS CAISS office.
entries.final_wording: Healthcare entitlement by status, not only by nationality. (1) People whose cover is charged to another EU/EEA/Swiss/UK state — pensioners, but also posted workers, frontier workers and their dependent family members — register form S1 with the INSS (CAISS). (2) People who work or are self-employed in Spain, and their dependent beneficiaries, are covered by affiliation to Spanish social security; this is the ordinary route for anyone below pension age and the instruction currently omits it. (3) Residual entitlement under arts. 3 and 3 ter of Ley 16/2003 for those who cannot be covered any other way. (4) Convenio especial with the Conselleria de Sanitat — a paid subscription, requiring one continuous year of prior residence in Spain/EU/EEA/Switzerland/UK, empadronamiento, and no cover by any other title. (5) Private insurance, which is also what a non-EU residence visa applicant is normally required to hold. In every case the SIP card is issued by the Conselleria de Sanitat once entitlement under one of these routes is proved — the SIP is the evidence of cover, never the source of it.
entries.note: The S1 and convenio especial halves are right; the residual clause is not. 'Everyone else via private cover or convenio especial' writes working-age buyers out of the public system, when affiliation through employment or autónomo status is precisely how most of them would be covered — and it also misses the beneficiary route for a non-working spouse. That matters commercially: a buyer bank aimed at people under pension age would be telling them to buy private insurance they may not need. The convenio especial's one-year prior-residence condition is also the trap most worth naming, since it makes the convenio unavailable in a new arrival's first year. Left as claim_type procedure because the entry is a research directive, but the taxonomy inside it is the part that was wrong.

entries.assertion: Never present the 183-day rule or visa requirements as settled advice; flag that it depends on nationality and personal circumstance and needs a gestor/abogado.
entries.source_required: see source_class
entries.source_opened: BOE, Ley 35/2006 del IRPF, consolidated, art. 9 https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2006-20764
entries.locator: Art. 9.1.a LIRPF: 'Que permanezca más de 183 días, durante el año natural, en territorio español', with sporadic absences counted unless tax residence elsewhere is proved; art. 9.1.b the centre of economic interests test.
entries.final_wording: Never present the 183-day rule or visa requirements as settled advice; flag that it depends on nationality and personal circumstance and needs a gestor/abogado.
entries.note: Sound as a rule, but the wording invites a misreading worth heading off in the copy. The 183-day test is settled statute — art. 9.1.a LIRPF, opened at BOE — and telling a reader it is unsettled is its own inaccuracy. What is not settled is the application: how sporadic absences are counted, the alternative centre-of-economic-interests test in art. 9.1.b, and treaty tie-breakers where two states both claim the person. Visa and entry rights are a separate axis again and turn on nationality, not on days. Keep tax residence, Spanish residence permission and nationality apart when writing it.

entries.assertion: Whether a tourist registration or compatibility certificate survives a change of ownership, or must be applied for afresh by the new owner.
entries.source_required: see source_class

entries.locator: Art. 23 bis: on a change of ownership of the property a new declaración responsable must be presented, together with the favourable municipal compatibility report. The inscription is valid five years; a renewal declaración responsable with an updated favourable municipal report must be filed in the month before each period expires, failing which the property is removed from the register. Transitional regime for dwellings registered before the decree-law.
entries.final_wording: It does not simply transfer. Under art. 23 bis of the Valencian regime (Ley 15/2018 / Decreto 10/2021 as amended by Decreto-ley 9/2024, in force 8 August 2024), a change of ownership requires a new declaración responsable accompanied by a favourable municipal compatibility report. Separately, the inscription itself lasts five years and must be renewed by declaración responsable in the month before expiry, with an updated favourable municipal report; miss it and the dwelling is struck from the Registro de Turismo. So a buyer inherits neither an automatic registration nor an indefinite one, and the compatibility report is the item most likely to fail — a municipality that has since restricted tourist use will not reissue it.
entries.note: This is the question in the slice with the most money attached to it, and the answer is the one a seller is least likely to volunteer. Recording one honest tension: the Generalitat's own e-procedure presents 'cambio TITULAR / cambio persona PROPIETARIA' inside a modification flow, which reads as lighter than art. 23 bis's requirement of a new declaración responsable plus a fresh favourable municipal report. Before publishing, confirm with the Conselleria de Turisme which channel applies to a sale as opposed to a change of operator, and never let the piece imply that a listed 'VUT licence' passes with the keys.

entries.assertion: The duties triggered at a compraventa and where each one comes from: identity and capacity, and the real-time telematic Land Registry check of title and charges, under the Reglamento Notarial (art. 175); the community-fee certificate under art. 9.1.e LPH; mortgage transparency under Ley 5/2019 (arts. 14–15); the cadastral reference and energy certificate under their own cadastral and building-certification rules; and the 3% retention on a non-resident seller, which is the buyer's legal obligation under art. 25.2 TRLIRNR, not a notarial duty.confirm each against a primary or professional-body source, not a blog

entries.source_opened: BOE, Reglamento Notarial (Decreto de 2 de junio de 1944), consolidated, art. 175 https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-1944-6578 ; BOE, Ley del Notariado de 28 de mayo de 1862, consolidated, art. 23 https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-1862-4073 ; BOE, Ley 49/1960 de Propiedad Horizontal, consolidated, art. 9.1.e https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-1960-10906 ; BOE, Ley 5/2019, consolidated, arts. 14-15 https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2019-3814 ; AEAT, retención del adquirente de un inmueble https://sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es/Sede/no-residentes/irnr-sin-establecimiento-permanente/retenciones-irnr-sin-establecimiento-permanente/retencion-adquirente-inmueble.html
entries.locator: Art. 175.1 RN: before authorising a deed acquiring real property the notary 'deberá comprobar la titularidad y el estado de cargas'; 175.2 by telematic means under the Ley Hipotecaria; 175.3 also 'en el momento inmediato más próximo a la autorización', without the registrar's intermediation, using the notary's recognised electronic signature under art. 222.10 LH, testified and incorporated into the matriz with day and hour; 175.5 exceptions for acts of liberalidad and for a satisfied acquirer pleading urgency (part of that wording annulled by STS of 20 May 2008). Art. 23 Ley del Notariado: fe de conocimiento — the notary attests to knowing the parties or to having established their identity by the listed supletory means, plus NIF for deeds over immovable property. Art. 9.1.e LPH: the transmitter must declare being current on general community expenses or state what is owed. Ley 5/2019 art. 14: FEIN, FiAE, draft contract and cost breakdown at least ten calendar days before signature; art. 15: the free notarial acta, the borrower attending by the day before, and no authorisation if the timeline or documents fail. AEAT on art. 25.2 TRLIRNR: the acquirer must withhold and pay in 3% of the agreed consideration as a payment on account, via modelo 211, within one month of the transmission, regardless of who the acquirer is.
entries.final_wording: The duties triggered at a compraventa and where each one comes from: identity and capacity, under art. 23 of the Ley del Notariado (fe de conocimiento and the supletory means of identification, plus the NIF requirement for deeds over immovable property) — NOT art. 175; the real-time telematic Land Registry check of title and charges, under art. 175 of the Reglamento Notarial, performed at the moment immediately preceding authorisation via art. 222.10 of the Ley Hipotecaria and testified into the matriz with day and hour, subject to the art. 175.5 exceptions; the community-fee declaration and certificate under art. 9.1.e LPH; mortgage transparency under Ley 5/2019 (art. 14, the FEIN/FiAE and draft ten calendar days before signature; art. 15, the free notarial acta, attended by the day before, without which the notary cannot authorise); the cadastral reference and energy certificate under their own cadastral and building-certification rules; and the 3% retention on a non-resident seller, which is the buyer's legal obligation under art. 25.2 TRLIRNR settled by modelo 211 within one month, not a notarial duty. Confirm each against a primary or professional-body source, not a blog.
entries.note: Every citation checks out at BOE or AEAT except one, and that one is the reason this is CORRECTED: art. 175 RN covers only the registry check of titularidad y cargas. Identity and capacity are not in it — they sit in art. 23 of the Ley del Notariado. As written, the instruction hands a writer a wrong article number for the first duty on its own list, in a topic whose closing line is 'confirm each against a primary source'. Two further things worth carrying into the copy: art. 175.5 makes the registry check waivable in narrow cases, so it is not absolute; and the 3% is a payment on account, which means the seller may be refunded part or all of it even where there is a gain — writing it as 'a 3% tax' is the standard error here.

entries.source_required: see source_class
entries.source_opened: BOE consolidated Ley 35/2006 (IRPF), arts. 2 and 9, via BOE open-data API, https://www.boe.es/datosabiertos/api/legislacion-consolidada/id/BOE-A-2006-20764/texto/bloque/a9 and /a2
entries.locator: Ley 35/2006, art. 9.1.a) 'Que permanezca más de 183 días, durante el año natural, en territorio español … se computarán las ausencias esporádicas'; art. 2 'la totalidad de sus rendimientos, ganancias y pérdidas patrimoniales … con independencia del lugar donde se hubiesen producido'
entries.final_wording: Spend one winter day too many and Spain taxes your worldwide income. The 183-day calendar every snowbird should keep.
entries.note: The threshold is MORE than 183 days in the calendar year (so day 184 tips it), sporadic absences count towards presence, and residence is all-or-nothing for the whole year — the hook is accurate on all three. Two things the body copy must not drop: 183 days is only one of the tests (art. 9.1.b centre of economic interests, and the rebuttable presumption from a resident spouse and minor children can make someone resident on far fewer days), and a double tax treaty tie-breaker can override Spanish residence. Do not let the hook imply the day count is the only door.
